description: Research in this topic addresses the structures and processes of crime and criminal justice, from crime detection to incarceration and rehabilitation. Case studies focused on methods for identifying and preventing crime, with particular emphasis on emerging online threats. They improved efficacy of crime prevention and policing, informing police ethics, job satisfaction and community collaboration. Research informed victim support, and shaped policy and reform in the judicial system to promote fairness and efficiency. Studies also addressed prison life, deepening understanding and supporting rehabilitation, guiding policies to foster reintegration and reduce reoffending.
narrative:
Achieving justice and improving support and protection for victims-survivors of gender-based violence

This research into how criminal justice practitioners and service providers in the UK can support victims-survivors of gender-based violence (GBV) leveraged over £7.2 million in funding to expand a GBV-prevention programme in the UK. This program is shown to reduce abuse by high-risk perpetrators by up to 88% and underpinned new UK family court guidance to protect children from domestic abuse. Read more...

Advances in the Neuroscience of Trauma & Crime: Transforming justice globally for vulnerable people in custody

Research uncovered that 42,000 people currently in UK prisons have some form of Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), which is associated with impulsivity and problems in social reasoning. This finding changed judicial and health policies in the UK and (those endorsed by the UN) UN to take account of TBI and Neurodisability. It also led to changes in practice across the prison system impacting 83,000 existing prisoners and 60,00 new entrants each year, including mandatory neurodisability screening and enhanced support and staff training Read more...

Advancing electronic monitoring: changing tagging laws and practices

This research into effective use of electronic monitoring (EM) underpinned the Management of Offenders (Scotland) Act 2019 resulting in the introduction of new EM technologies (e.g., GPS tags); EM added as an option in Community Payback Orders (alternative to prison); EM added as an alternative to bail (alternative to custody); and updated practice guidance. Read more...

Designing out Crime: Improving police and planning policy and practice to reduce crime and create safer communities

Crime Prevention through Environmental Design (CPTED) creates housing developments that are less vulnerable to crime, with housing built to Secured by Design (SBD) standards that experience 55% less burglary. This changed government planning guidance and building regulations in the UK and the United Arab Emirates and increased the number of secure homes (44% of new homes built between 2013 and 2017 were SBD), which reduced crime and increased feelings of safety. Read more...

Driving evidence-based change in ‘Citizens in Policing’ strategy, leadership and innovation

The largest-scale research programme undertaken in the field of citizens in policing helped develop evidence-based strategy and practice for a police volunteering programme, thereby shaping the national strategy across more than 38,000 volunteers in Special Constabularies, Police Support Volunteers, Volunteer Police Cadets and the Mini Police. Read more...

Evidence-based interventions to improve prisoner behaviour and reduce recidivism

Evidence-based interventions in the prison service have shown that behaviour monitoring can predict risk of reoffending after release and that digital technology terminals (for prisoners to request visits, access health care, order food, etc.) bring significant behavioural benefits and enhance rehabilitation within prisons. Enhanced Behaviour Monitoring was made mandatory in all pre-release prisons and funding of £7,000,000 for the introduction of digital kiosks in UK prisons was announced. Read more...

Improving Police Ethics Training and Practice: virtues and ethical risk in policing

This research on effective ethics training has influenced policies, practices, and training affecting at least 13,000 police officers and staff – and, by extension, the communities they serve. Police ethics training now incorporates the virtues of policing and the ethical risks of cognitive biases in a more central role. Read more...

Instigating the repeal of the Offensive Behaviour at Football Act

This research was instrumental in repealing the Offensive Behaviour at Football and Threatening Communications (Scotland) Act 2012, meaning that ‘at risk’ football fans, usually young men from deprived communities, will not be hampered by criminal records classifying them as sectarian offenders. This is particularly impactful for all football fans in Scotland, Irish-migrant populations, and civil liberty groups across the UK. The research also proposed non-legislative solutions, such as early years education. In 2019, the Scottish Government allocated £530,000 to anti-sectarianism education. Read more...

Investigative forensic linguistics: Equipping law enforcement to fight online sexual crime.

This training in linguistic methods and the provision of linguistic software to UK and international online undercover police and dark web investigators equipped law enforcement to fight online sexual crime. These efforts contributed to the identification and arrest of high-profile Child Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (CSEA) offenders. Read more...

Combating organised crime and its finances at a national and international level

This research into quantifying and mapping illicit markets has supported policymakers like the Ministry of Interior of Bulgaria, OECD, and European Parliament, as well as law enforcement officials like EUROPOL, to be more flexible and efficient in acting to address illicit market threats effectively. The research helped to expose the true nature of the harm of the illicit tobacco trade and address gaps in surveillance systems to develop early detection and warning systems. This research provided the first detailed account of smuggling illegal cigarettes, the drug market, and VAT fraud in Bulgaria. It directly influenced policymaking to better monitor higher-rate tax payers, create a register of bank accounts, and set up a reversed VAT charging system. Read more...

Safeguarding Vulnerable Adults from Financial Scams

The National Centre for Post-Qualifying Social Work at Bournemouth University provided key learning resources that have been distributed by national agencies, charities, local authorities, the NHS, financial institutions, and the government to raise scam awareness to protect vulnerable groups. These tools have saved consumers from £22,703,586 of scams. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic preserved, recorded/recorded, reinterpreted and promoted musical heritage across historical and global contexts, while pioneering new technologies in sound design, audio curation and immersive experiences. Research celebrates diverse musical traditions, building cross-cultural engagement and understanding. It also advances inclusive music-making, performance and listening experiences. Projects supported therapeutic uses of music, expanding access through innovative technological and curational practices, and enhanced music education, improving cultural understanding and creative participation.
narrative:
Student Pulse: taking classical music to a younger audience

Development of an app to introduce younger audiences to classical music. App is now used by 9 of the UK’s leading symphony orchestras and has resulted in 11,000 ticket sales. Read more...

Removing barriers to musical participation in schools – a social justice issue

Research contributed to the reform of music curricula in schools, including the introduction of modern genres such as grime and hip-hop. Research also influenced the government’s decision to continue funding Whole Class Ensemble Tuition (WCET). In 2018/19, government provided £75 million for Music Education Hubs that help fund music lessons for 700,000 children, many of whom would not otherwise have had access to music teaching and learning. Read more...

Museum Listening: Creating New Collection, Exhibition, and Audience Engagement Practices for Sound Technologies at the National Science and Media Museum

Research on sound history and museum listening inspired the National Science and Media Museum’s relaunch in 2017 as the first UK museum dedicated to sound technologies with a mission to explore ‘the transformative impact of image and sound technologies on our lives’. Read more...

Curating new expressions of Mali’s musical heritage: Trio De Kali and the Kronos Quartet

Research on music of West Africa led to the formation of an ensemble of Malian musicians to revive a now rarely performed, pre-colonial style. The ensemble has toured widely in the USA, Europe, Australia and New Zealand and collaborated with the Kronos Quartet, a US-based string quartet, generating 17,000 album sales, 3,000,000 streams, 25,000 views on YouTube, and reached nearly 5,000 people through concerts. Read more...

Digital Delius: enhancing musical understanding by creating new resources for performance, education, and interpretation

Researchers developed new interpretations of Frederick Delius' work, which led to a British Library digital exhibition that made these sources freely available alongside expert commentary and innovative multimedia resources. The project also led to the world premiere recordings of hitherto unknown Delius works. Read more...

Electroacoustic Music: Enhancing ‘Sonic Creativity’ in Schools and Communities Across the World Through eLearning and Specialist Software

ELearning site, EARS 2, and creative software, Compose with Sounds (CwS) are used for the adoption of sound-based music education in classrooms. Since late October 2013, over 4,000 people (teachers and students) around the world have attended hundreds of workshops, classroom sessions and other events. By late 2020, there were 20,000 monthly EARS 2 online visitors. Educational materials are now available in 10 languages, enabling government ministries, educators and cultural organisations in 5 countries to promote adoption of the new tools. Read more...

Bass Culture: Advancing understanding and recognition of Black British Music

This research was the first detailed retrospective of Black British music. State of Play: Grime Report played a significant role in the repeal of Form 696 by the London Metropolitan Police, which had been disproportionately used against Black music genres, specifically grime, rendering Form 696 an instantiation of racial discrimination. The Bass Culture 70/50 exhibition was attended by 3,400 people in four weeks and drew attention to the heritage of Black British music and the influence of other cultures it drew upon, such as Jamaica. The research collected through the Bass Culture project has filled gaps in knowledge identified in national and local archives and has impacted the curatorial strategies at the Museum of London to integrate marginalised cultural movements and communities. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic focus on waste management and recycling. Studies tend to consider the environmental and health impacts of waste through innovations in policy, materials, and industrial practice. They include advances in waste management across areas such as plastic, food waste, and electronic waste, alongside circular economy initiatives like carbon-negative building materials and sustainable cosmetics. The research has influenced legislation, developed British Standards, improved public understanding, and fostered commercial success in transforming waste into valuable resources.
narrative:
Transforming industry understanding and practice of designing out waste through the development of British Standards on material efficiency

Research at Loughborough University transformed industry understanding and practice by shifting construction waste management from reactive disposal to proactive prevention through design. The work led to the development of the BS 8895 multi-part British Standards series on designing for material efficiency, chaired and led by the researcher. These standards are now central references in major international sustainability certification schemes (e.g., BREEAM, Home Quality Mark, and New Zealand’s Homestar), directly influencing sustainable building practices. Adoption across the construction industry has enabled greater material efficiency, reduced waste, and contributed to environmental targets in the UK and internationally. Read more...

Improving environmental sustainability through the synthesis of novel biodegradable polymers

Research at the University of Wolverhampton has advanced the development and application of biodegradable polymers, delivering environmental and economic impact since 2014. By converting industrial waste into high-value, biodegradable plastics and developing innovative bioremediation techniques, the research underpinned the creation of new sustainable products. It informed UK government policy through contributions to the DEFRA report on biodegradable plastic bags, which was laid before Parliament in 2015. Industrial impact includes collaboration with Rozone Ltd to develop the ROwasher, an eco-friendly parts-cleaning system that sold 247 units and saved the company over £290,000 by reducing reliance on imported products. The research also enabled cosmetics SME Prima Makeup to launch biodegradable packaging and glitter, supporting export growth to 19 countries. Public awareness of sustainable plastic alternatives increased through widespread media engagement, with appearances on BBC, CBC, and ABC platforms and invitations to high-profile policy events at Chatham House. The research has directly shaped cleaner manufacturing, supported SME innovation, influenced national policy, and elevated public discourse around plastic sustainability. Read more...

Reducing consumer food waste, influencing business strategy, and increasing sales of sustainable products through co-produced research

University of Leeds researchers partnered with Asda to co-produce and trial behavioural interventions aimed at reducing household food waste and promoting sustainable product purchases. These efforts led to an estimated reduction of 48,276 tonnes of food waste and 183,449 tonnes of CO₂e, while simultaneously increasing Asda’s pre-tax profits by £5 million and strengthening customer brand loyalty. The research directly influenced Asda’s corporate sustainability strategy and sales practices, informed global Walmart initiatives, and shaped broader sector policy via WRAP and the British Retail Consortium. The methods were recognised as best practice and shared across retail and higher education sectors. Read more...

Reductions in microplastic pollution through changes to legislation, industrial innovation and societal awareness

Research at the University of Plymouth transformed global understanding and response to microplastic pollution. It was the first to identify and define microplastics in marine environments, demonstrate their widespread presence, trace key sources such as textiles and cosmetic microbeads, and show their ingestion by marine species. This evidence directly informed the UK’s 2017 ban on microbeads in rinse-off products and underpinned EU legislation banning intentionally added microplastics, projected to prevent 500,000 tonnes of pollution over 20 years. It influenced policy in Canada, New Zealand, Japan, and the UN, and supported the creation of international standards for flushable products. The research also drove industrial innovation, leading to new filtration technologies now adopted by manufacturers and supported by national regulations. Public awareness campaigns and NGO initiatives citing the research led to measurable consumer behaviour change and the formation of a parliamentary group on microplastics. The work has delivered lasting reductions in emissions and reshaped environmental legislation and corporate practice worldwide. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic addressed the commemoration and public understanding of military history by augmenting engagement with historic events, communities and individuals. Case studies developed archival records and increased accessibility though digitisation and public engagement and educational opportunities. Work engaged highlighted the ongoing relevance of historical events, shaping contemporary perceptions of certain events or experiences and informing reconciliation efforts. A key focus was on elevating the narratives of minority or marginalised communities and voices, and developing inclusive approaches to remembrance.
narrative:
Agincourt 600

Historian-led event to commemorate the 600th anniversary of the battle of Agincourt: 100 projects, including concerts, plays, educational resources, and exhibitions commemorating the battle and its place in British history were commissioned and attended by over 500,000 people. Read more...

Cartoons and the First World War

This case study looks at how soldiers serving in WWI used cartoons to comprehend and communicate what was happening around them and used this material to contribute to cultural activities during the Centenary of WW1. The cartoons provide a direct window into soldier attitudes and life at the fronts. Research about these amateur cartoons composed by the soldiers themselves was displayed, and interpreted at talks, roadshows and exhibitions such as ‘Comics and the World Wars' at the London Cartoon M. Impact is revealed by correspondence as testimonial to people’s unexpected reactions as they rediscovered–and appreciated–this unusual visual information. Read more...

description: Research in this topic encourages participation in the arts and heritage for wellbeing, education and community cohesion. Case studies used innovate curatorial and creative practices to bring artistic and historical culture to the public in new forms and settings, fostering inclusivity, co-creation and meaningful dialogue. Many engaged with underrepresented voices or histories to affirm identity, strengthen community ties and influence cultural policy. Many had lasting social and economic benefits for local areas, enhancing the visibility and value of arts and heritage in public life.
narrative:
Transforming the way art and heritage institutions document, preserve and exhibit audiences' engagement with their collections

Research into audience engagement influenced exhibitions at museums such as The Tate, and also led researchers to develop community initiatives. Among these initiatives is the first volunteer-run sporting heritage museum in Exeter, giving Exeter City Fans a space to commemorate their club’s history. Read more...

Negotiating conflict through socially engaged art and architecture

Dr. Hafeda’s work on social art practice has produced long-term benefits to communities in London (2014-present), Portugal (2017-present), and Lebanon (2019-present). The ‘Shop of Possibilities’ (SoP), an art- and play-space commissioned by the South London Gallery (SLG) improved the development of 484 children, provided training for education professionals, and employment opportunities. The SoP was cited as best-practice in an independent report advising the Greater London Authority, garnering an additional £873,299 investment for the project. Hafeda’s work with Roma communities in Portugal inspired new community-led mediations to improve community relations. Hafeda’s work has inspired artists and curators working with marginalised communities elsewhere. For example, social artworks commissioned in marginalised communities in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, and for refugee children in Lebanon on the Syrian border. The projects have helped develop social and creative skills among 696 children, young people, and adults, empowering them to assert their rights and opinions by contributing to permanent social infrastructures. Read more...

The identification of King Richard III: the economic and societal impact

Identification of the remains of King Richard III led to the enrichment of Leicester city's cultural life with the construction of a new Heritage Learning Centre, which received 347,155 visitors by 2020. The research also contributed to Leicester Cathedral's 2020-2023 £11.3 million National Lottery-funded restoration. Leicester City Council estimated that the upsurge in visitors following the discovery generated 1,012 new jobs and brought £79 million to the Leicestershire economy by 2015. Read more...

Alice's Adventures in 21st-Century Creative Industries: Enrichment, Extension and Diversification of a Victorian Icon

Research on Lewis Carroll and the evolution of the character of Alice was essential to a series of high-profile collaborative endeavours to celebrate the 150th anniversary of the publication of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland in 2015: an exhibition at the V&A Museum of Childhood, a concert suite for the London Symphony Orchestra, and a fabric collection for Liberty Art Fabrics. Read more...

description: Research in this topic informs the protection of cultural property and safeguarding of heritage and related community identities. Case studies influence foreign policy, reconciliation efforts and peacebuilding through the protection of cultural assets and promotion of heritage rights. Many projects used digitisation and novel archival techniques to preserve at-risk heritage and improve accessibility. Research also informed conservation in the context of areas of modernisation and regeneration, preserving cultural heritage while serving the needs of communities and infrastructure. International collaboration and innovative technologies and curatorial practices underpinned sustainable conservation. A strong emphasis is on increasing public access and engagement, enhancing the appreciation, resilience and global visibility of cultural heritage.
narrative:
Diversifying the global conversation about Modernist history and architectural heritage: using research to achieve UNESCO World Heritage Site status for Asmara, Eritrea

Researchers digitised and documented over 80,000 unique modernist architectural drawings, maps, and buildings in Asmara, the capital of Eritrea. This work resulted in a UNESCO Nomination Dossier, allowing Asmara to become inscribed on the World Heritage List. Read more...

Nimrud: documenting, contextualising and planning for an ancient Assyrian heritage site in post-ISIS Iraq

Research on Nimrud’s ancient and modern history conducted before, during, and after ISIS destruction of ancient Assyrian buildings and sculptures at the archaeological site, informed understanding of Nimrud’s importance as the world’s first imperial capital and its complex, politicised history over the last two centuries. The research contributed to protection and management plans, including UNESCO’s safeguarding activities at Nimrud, and UNESCO Iraq and the Iraqi State Board of Antiquities’ decision to enclose the site and install 24-hour guards to prevent further looting. Research led to the founding of the AHRC-GCRF-funded Nahrein Network in 2017 to support locally led interdisciplinary research in the role of history, heritage, and the humanities in the development of post-conflict Iraq and its neighbours. This has raised the international profile of Iraqi experts and contributed to the decolonisation of knowledge practices. The Nahrein Network is an example of successful collaboration between researchers and Iraqi stakeholders, and in autumn 2020 the network secured £11 million to continue its activities until 2031. Read more...

description: Research in this topic focuses on the preservation, protection and engagement with archaeology, material heritage and historic sites. Case studies inform policy and protection efforts, while new research methods and technologies expand archaeological discovery and curatorial and exhibition practices. Projects enhanced accessibility and visitor experiences through creative staging, performance and digital tools. Educational incentives deepened connections to cultural heritage and identity, fostering cross-cultural understanding and informing local and national narratives. Many projects also generated significant social and economic benefits for heritage sites and their communities.
narrative:
Revealing Hidden Cities: using augmented reality and geo-locative media to enhance heritage preservation, tourism experience, and historic site management

An award-winning app developed with UK art history scholars allows visitors to experience what the places they are visiting would have been like in Renaissance Florence as they tour the city. Read more...

Historic Landscape Research: supporting landscape planning and management, shaping policy, and creating new capacity for historic character assessment

Research on historic landscapes, particularly the use of a new context-based and non-site approach to the management of landscape heritage, influenced how a number of institutions created policy and implemented guidelines for practice around the world. This included providing an official method for the environmental assessment of all new major roads in the UK 2007-2019, and for projects like High Speed 2 (HS2) and airport expansions. Local authorities like Historic England, the Marine Management Organisation, and Natural England have used research datasets to inform planning for heritage management. Related guidelines have been developed in many other countries, including Belgium, Ireland, the Netherlands, Spain, and Turkey. This has been reinforced through tailored training for early-career landscape professionals, enabling these heritage protection practices to be implemented in Brazil, China, Italy, Spain, and Turkey. Read more...

Know Your Place: Discovering the Origins of Place-Names in Northern Ireland

The Northern Ireland Place-Name Project has created a database of over 30,000 names freely available for consultation online. It has promoted understanding of a multilingual heritage in a divided society through its database, social media, and a weekly newspaper column. Read more...

Corpses of mass violence: changing practice in forensic exhumations

The research of the Corpses of Mass Violence (CMV) project has helped shape the practice of exhumation as a key part of coming to terms with violent pasts and enabling transitional justice at a time when demand for exhumation is on the rise. It has contributed to the work of Doctors without Borders, the Red Cross, and the UN Human Rights Council to implement new guidance and standards for the treatment of the dead in humanitarian emergencies and the treatment of mass graves. It has changed the training of forensics students in France and medical and legal practitioners in Africa, and informed practitioners from countries including Mexico, Argentina, Spain, and the UK. It has informed excavation practices at Holocaust sites to be more sensitive to Jewish beliefs that are averse to exhumation. It has also been instrumental in informing the work of the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research in its work to address its own treatment of Holocaust victims. A documentary co-written by the researcher, Action T4: A Doctor Under Nazism (2014), was viewed by around 1,200,000 people, and won ‘Best Documentary’ at the 2016 Luchon Film Festival. Read more...

description: This topic addresses science outreach, communication and education. Case studies in this topic discuss how public understanding may be broadened through participation and access to exhibitions, outreach events, digital platforms, and media. It demonstrates increased engagement with science, for example in astronomy, quantum biology, particle physics, ethics, and evolution, often using creative formats such as museums, storytelling, and art–science collaborations. Studies in this topic also address improvements to education and have impacts in educational resources and curricula, enhancing schooling and improving equality in participation in STEM education and science communication.
narrative:
Greenfoot: Transforming Student Learning and Pedagogical Innovativeness in Programming Internationally

Greenfoot, developed through pedagogical and technical research at the University of Kent, has transformed how programming is taught and learned globally. Designed for students aged 13+, this software provides a user-friendly, visual environment for learning object-oriented programming. Since 2013, it has directly benefited over 3.9 million students and supported over 5,000 teachers in 49 countries. Greenfoot’s impact includes improving student motivation and creativity, enhancing teacher capacity and pedagogy, and informing national curricula—such as the WJEC GCSE in Wales. Widely used by Computing at School, Technocamps, and Oracle Academy, Greenfoot has become a global tool for inclusive, engaging computer science education. Read more...

Astrophysics outreach to widen participation for the socioeconomically disadvantaged

The University of Hull’s Milne Centre for Astrophysics has delivered extensive, research-driven outreach to widen participation in physics, particularly among socioeconomically disadvantaged and under-represented groups. Through over 500 education and public outreach (EPO) events—including talks, workshops, a mobile planetarium, teacher CPD, and international training—the centre reached nearly 3 million people, including 40,000 students. Targeted engagement in deprived areas of northern England increased local interest in STEM and contributed to a doubling of women studying physics at Hull. Their award-winning "Changing Face of Physics" and "Breaking Barriers" campaigns fostered gender, social, and cultural inclusion in science. Impact also includes improved teacher capacity, student coding skills, work experience opportunities, and strategic contributions to the UK’s Industrial Strategy through digital and STEM literacy. Read more...

Deep Impact: engaging public audiences and policymakers with the exploration and stewardship of biodiversity in the deep ocean

Research at the University of Southampton exploring deep-sea biodiversity has significantly increased public and policymaker engagement with the deep ocean. Working with documentary producers, the team’s discoveries featured in widely viewed broadcasts including Blue Planet II, reaching up to a billion viewers globally. They also created a Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) enrolling over 52,000 participants from 183 countries, developed popular science resources including a bestselling book (Ask an Ocean Explorer), and delivered over 70 in-person events to 94,000+ people. Their research informed UK parliamentary briefings and legislative recommendations on deep-sea mining, contributing to a policy recommendation for a moratorium on mining active hydrothermal vents. Collectively, these activities raised awareness of deep-sea ecosystems, the threats they face, and the importance of stewardship, providing cultural enrichment, supporting education, and influencing national and international policy. Read more...

Increasing public understanding of research in quantum technologies through showcasing at exhibitions and media reports

Research from the Lancaster Quantum Technology Centre significantly advanced public understanding of quantum technologies by engaging large audiences through prestigious exhibitions and extensive media coverage. Their interactive exhibits at the Royal Society Summer Science Exhibition (2017–2020) introduced key concepts such as quantum identification, random number generation, and noise isolation in quantum systems, reaching nearly 40,000 visitors in person and millions more online. Teachers reported increased confidence in teaching science and greater student interest in STEM subjects. The exhibits led to commercial gains for industry collaborators and inspired further installations at New Scientist Live and the Barbican Centre, reaching over 160,000 attendees. Online videos and global media coverage expanded the reach to over 120 million people. Media exposure from the team’s quantum memory research (ULTRARAM™) alone reached 78 million, drawing the interest of major technology companies and informing policy discussions on advanced memory technologies. Read more...

description: Research in this topic supports and informs business, entrepreneurialism, management and policies aimed at improving the founding and productivity of commercial enterprisees. Much research focuses on identifying and implementing effective tools for managing existing firms and means to make entrepreneurs successful. This includes both practices and training inside firms as well as the development of business or entrepreneurialism-friendly policies and funding. We also find several business spinoffs from research or adaptations of research into large companies. A large number of impact projects are concerned with helping small- and medium enterprises (SMEs) grow and with creating business environments, organisational practices, public policies and financial opportunities that help them thrive. Research on management reguarly informs ways to make firms more efficient and to train their staff. Several projects are also concerned with environmental and sustainable practices in business and entrepreneurialism for a greener economy.
narrative:
Accelerating the Multi-Unit Leader and Service Chain Growth

Research-based materials used to train over 800 multi-site managers across 22 big organisations to enhance their practice, progression and performance. 94 percent of managers agreed that the programme improved their performance. Read more...

Let’s Do Business Group (LDBG) – Local SME Financing

Connected 465 small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in deprived areas with GBP 1,500,000 in funding, advice, and training support. Read more...

Nurturing and Scaling Startup Businesses

Making startups and scale-ups grow: research on effective business models and the entrepreneurial life cycle supported programming for 253 startup companies. These startups have created hundreds of jobs and raised GBP 230,600,000 in grant and venture capital funding. On average, these enterprises achieved 28 percent sales growth the year after programming, with 89 percent implementing the growth plans developed during the programme. Read more...

description: Research in this topic enhances care for the elderly and those living with age-related conditions such as dementia, Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease. Case studies shaped healthcare policy and practice through innovations in early detection, practitioner training and assistive technologies. They addressed social care aspects, many involving families and communities to raise awareness and deliver social initiatives that support independent living, reduce loneliness and promote inclusion, with a key focus on changing perceptions of the elderly and their needs. A key focus in on shifting public understanding of ageing and encouraging lifelong habits and early intervention strategies that support healthy ageing and improved quality of life.
narrative:
Transforming the life quality of people with advanced dementia - and their carers - with a HUG™

This research project exploring the therapeutic value of playful objects led to the production of design guidelines for people with advanced dementia, with guidelines distributed by both Alzheimer’s UK and Care England. It also resulted in the HUG™, an artefact that improves the quality of life of people affected by advanced dementia. A six-month trial found it improved wellbeing for 87% of participants. As a result, HUG™ is now prescribed by the NHS. Its success has earned it significant media attention and the UK Tech4Good Winner of Winners’ award 2020. Read more...

description: This topic covers vision research and opthamology. In general studies in this topic demonstrate research into understanding, diagnosing, preventing, treating and supporting those with vision-threatening conditions. The topic features therapy and treament innovations as well as care and support initiatives for those affected. Research across this topic has enhanced visual care for patients, informed international guidelines, advanced identification and management of optical conditions and been commercialised. Across clinical, community, and global settings, the studies often reflect better service delivery, public health strategies, and increased quality of life for people with visual impairments.
narrative:
Counselling for sight loss: increasing the quality and availability of specialist counselling for people with sight loss in UK and Ireland

Research at Abertay University has significantly improved access to and the quality of counselling for people with sight loss in the UK and Ireland. A user-led model of counselling was developed through in-depth case study research, leading to the creation of a specialist training course for qualified counsellors. This course equips practitioners with the knowledge and skills to meet the specific psychological and accessibility needs of blind and partially sighted clients. Since its rollout, the number of trained counsellors has increased by 80% in the UK and 460% in Ireland, expanding local, face-to-face counselling provision. The course, accredited by Vision UK and delivered in collaboration with the RNIB, was recognised with a national commendation for excellence. The model has influenced professional standards, improved client choice and outcomes, supported emergency service expansion during the COVID-19 pandemic, and informed practice and service development internationally. Read more...

Improving Diagnosis and Patient Outcomes in Developmental Retinal Diseases (DRDs)

University of Leicester researchers at the Ulverscroft Eye Unit have transformed diagnosis and care for Developmental Retinal Diseases (DRDs) by pioneering genetic testing and high-resolution imaging, particularly using OCT. They discovered the FRMD7 gene, developed the world’s first nystagmus gene panel, and influenced national and international clinical testing strategies, resulting in over 1,400 patients being tested and enabling earlier, more accurate, and less invasive diagnoses. Their Leicester Grading System (LGS) for foveal abnormalities is now a globally used clinical tool, guiding diagnosis, prognosis, and genetic testing. These advances allow earlier access to resources, improve treatment planning, reassure families, and shape clinical guidelines in countries including the UK, USA, and South Korea. Read more...

NeuroEyeCoach™: achieving the gold standard for eyesight rehabilitation at home and in the clinic

NeuroEyeCoach™, developed by University of Aberdeen researchers, is an innovative vision rehabilitation therapy for stroke patients suffering from visual field loss. Unlike earlier approaches requiring clinic-based sessions, NeuroEyeCoach™ offers personalised, adaptive therapy accessible both at home and in clinics. Based on research demonstrating that inefficient eye movement strategies hinder visual recovery post-stroke, the therapy standardises training via algorithms that dynamically adjust difficulty to patient performance. It has regulatory approval in the EU and US and has become the gold standard for eyesight rehabilitation, improving visual search and daily functioning for over 500 patients to date. Used across rehabilitation clinics in Germany, Italy, Austria, and the US, and supported by major healthcare providers, it enhances quality of life while reducing delivery costs and barriers to access—marking a significant advancement in post-stroke visual therapy. Read more...

description: The research in this topic addresses reproductive, maternal, and neonatal health. Law, policy and guidance are informed by studies addressing clinical practice, access and equity, as well as the development of therapies are inlcluded here. Studies researching aspects of childbirth and reproductive health such as contraception and fertility, newborn outcomes, bereavement support, and advancements in pharmacological, psychological, behavioural, and assisted reproductive therapies are all encompassed by this topic.
narrative:
Influencing Abortion Law Reform in the UK and South Australia

This research has offered the leading legal analysis relied upon in making the case for the removal of specific criminal prohibitions against abortion and thereby formed the basis for the first three Bills – two in the House of Commons (HC), one in the House of Lords (HL)) – to fundamentally challenge the status quo in English law that criminalises abortion rather than seeing it as a matter of health law. Read more...

Improving care for women and families who have experienced miscarriage, stillbirth and elective abortion following a diagnosis of foetal anomaly

Each year in the UK, there are approximately 250,000 miscarriages, stillbirths, and terminations following a diagnosis of foetal anomaly. To improve on inconsistent levels of care for mothers and families, researchers helped develop a National Bereavement Care Pathway (NBCP); informed new UK healthcare guidelines; and transformed professional training standards for midwives, registrars, and funeral directors Read more...

description: This topic encompasses research relating to water, flood and coastal management. Studies cover flood risk management and resilience, as well as coastal and marine management, sustainable water systems and infrastructure, environmental water management initiatives as well as water access and equity. Research in this topic is broadly applied, but often showcases technology and methodology for monitoring and detection; modelling, simulation and prediction; treatment and processing; assessment and decision-making; and communication of data to public and professional bodies.
narrative:
Pioneering computer models have transformed global flood risk management

Researcher-led startup created the first high-resolution simulations of continental and global flood dynamics and risks. These simulations have been adopted by >1600 non-governmental organisations, multinational companies, governments, (re)insurers, specialist risk modelling firms, and non-commercial users for better global risk management. Read more...

Changing policy and practice for promoting flood resilience of homes and businesses

This research on making households adopt Property-level Flood Resilience (PFR) measures led to a scheme drawing on local knowledge that helped 60,000 property-owners improve their flood resilience. The research also helped convince a major UK insurer to fund PFR for its customers. Read more...

Improved capacities and standard operating procedures for tsunami early warning in Indian Ocean countries

Recent tsunami events highlighted the importance of communicating timely and accurate warnings to communities at risk. Research established critical areas of capacity and processes for effective tsunami early warning and identified recommendations for improvements to early warning processes. This work resulted in significant changes to: policy decisions on how tsunami preparedness is managed and assessed in 28 countries in the Indian Ocean region; greater priority for capacity building of national agencies responsible for tsunami early warning; and, improved national processes and practices for tsunami early warning in Indonesia and Sri Lanka, which are protecting coastal communities at risk. Read more...

description: This research topic showcases research across healthcare services, data and policy. It focuses on patient-centred care, digital health innovation, and community engagement for more inclusive, personalised, and effective services. It highlights advances in workforce and organisational transformation, policy influence, and behavioural science to improve both delivery and outcomes. Underpinning these developments are enhanced methods for ensuring safety and clinical quality, supported by rigorous data evaluation and measurement tools.
narrative:
Enabling self-administered healthcare technology through Multiple Perspective Problem Framing

Development of a Multiple Perspective Problem Framing approach to support those affected by blindness caused by diabetes. This approach helps deliver economically sustainable, self-administered healthcare. Industrial partner PolyPhotonix Ltd. produced the Noctura 400 sleep mask, a non-invasive, home-based treatment for diabetic retinophathy. As well as patients and clinicians, this technology has greatly benefited PolyPhotonix Ltd. Although in early stages of commercialisation at the time of authorship, Noctura 400 has been sold to 954 patients and 63 treatment centres (around 5,000 units), generating a turnover of £450,000 and attracting external funds for business development of £18,000,000. Read more...

NHS Investment in Social Prescribing: outcomes for individuals, communities, and the health and care system

Social prescribing (SP) is a community-based approach to health and care which aims to tackle health inequalities by addressing social determinants of health and broader wellbeing for marginalised, disadvantaged, or vulnerable people. The Centre for Regional Economic and Social Research (CRESR) undertook a programme of research demonstrating the effectiveness of social prescribing (SP). CRESR research findings informed healthcare commissioners to invest in local SP services, including £3,000,000 per year in Rotherham alone. NHS England used this research to invest £35,000,000 per year in SP through its Long Term Plan. 900,000 people per year will be referred to SP schemes, reducing the cost-burden of long-term health conditions on the NHS. Read more...

description: Research in this topic informs urban planning and transportation policy, advancing the design and implementation of more efficient, inclusive, and resilient mobility systems. Case studies shaped investment strategies and infrastructure priorities, with strong emphasis on accessibility for disabled people, the elderly, and children, as well as supporting active urban lifestyles. Many case studies focus on sustainability, addressing the challenges of climate change and uncertainty through innovative and ecologically responsible planning. Research also extended beyond urban environments to include broader logistical systems such as airport infrastructure, regional transit, and transport ticketing systems. Novel tools and technologies were developed to support planners and transport organisations in overcoming complex mobility and logistics challenges across diverse contexts.
narrative:
Connecting deprived regions in North West Europe through innovative tram projects

Research on the use of tramways for urban regeneration and accompanying shifts in travel behaviours underpinned EUR 22,300,000 in strategic investments in public transport across North West Europe. The popular, extended Blackpool tramway along the Fylde Coast is among the newly supported projects. Read more...

Delay Cost Management in European Aviation

Design, computation, and maintainance of the aviation industry’s standard delay cost values. These values are used across Europe to inform air travel management and optimization, business decisions, and airport planning. Read more...

Delivering Smart Ticketing in Great Britain

A commercial spin-out company from a university team implemented the rollout of contactless payment across UK bus networks. In 2020, over 100 million transactions across 27 local authorities were processed. Read more...

description: Research in this topic explores the cultural legacy, contemporary practice, and uses of performance across theatre, dance, and related art forms. Case studies span writing, acting, directing, choreography, design, and emerging stage technologies, highlighting the creative breadth of live performance. Work celebrates the rich heritage of British theatre, particularly the enduring impact of Shakespeare, while also exploring a diverse range of dance practices and non-theatrical performance traditions. Many projects promote inclusion and diversity in both production and participation, using performance as a platform for the expression of marginalised voices and cross-cultural discourse, building community relationships and mutual understanding. There is also emphasis on education, with theatre and dance used to engage youth, support performer training, and explore complex historical and social narratives.
narrative:
Innovating in the Production and Exploitation of Shakespeare Screen Adaptations with the Royal Shakespeare Company

Based on research about bringing theatre to the screen, the “Royal Shakespeare Company Live from Stratford-upon-Avon” project has broadened public access by bringing performances of the RSC to the screen, including during the pandemic. The project reached over 1 million viewers, including ~376,000 UK secondary education pupils. Read more...

Increasing knowledge and awareness of Black British theatre, film and television

Research on transnational Black British theatre increased knowledge and awareness of the historical contributions made by artists of African and Caribbean descent to British theatre, film and TV via an award-winning 10-part BBC Radio 4 documentary. Additionally, work with the National Theatre has restored and preserved the historical and contemporary work of Black playwrights and practitioners in the UK by documenting their contribution to British theatre’s historical record within the publicly accessible digital Black Plays Archive. Read more...

description: Research in this topic focuses on developing responsible information environments by tackling misinformation, enhancing media literacy, and promoting frameworks for impartiality and open communication. Case studies have informed global government, institutional, and corporate communication policies that protect democratic processes and ensure access to trusted information. Work supports educators, media professionals, organisations, and the public in navigating the digital information landscape. It strengthens connections between regulators, broadcasters, institutions, and audiences, shaping both public understanding and communication practices. Research also promoted diversity and representation across journalism, news, and wider media communications.
narrative:
Humanitarian Journalism: Improving Crisis Reporting for More Effective Humanitarian Response

The research contributed to a re-evaluation of The New Humanitarian (TNH), a key media news source for policymakers and the humanitarian aid sector. These changes led humanitarian agencies to pay attention to ‘forgotten crises’, leading to action that would otherwise not have been offered. Most notable is the TNH’s reporting on the ‘overlooked’ March 2018 Yazidi healthcare crisis in Iraq. This reporting resulted in immediate action from the UN migration agency and Doctors Without Borders, among others. By the end of 2018, the main hospital serving the Yazidi minority had been moved to a safer and better-equipped facility and acquired new ambulances. TNH doubled their citation of ‘local experts’ in coverage between 2015-2017 and increased the proportion of ‘investigative’ or ‘campaigning’ journalism in their outputs. This helped humanitarian professionals develop policies that address the most urgent challenges in remote crises. For example, a 2018 TNH investigation into alleged chronic corruption in the UN’s resettlement process in Sudan caused the UN’s refugee agency to suspend resettlement operations there subject to further review. TNH’s reformed reporting has impacted the aid sector at an institutional level. For example, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and others have used TNH as a source when lobbying the UN Human Rights Council for an inquiry into abuse against the Rohingya. Read more...

Visual Media Literacy for Combating Misinformation

The Visual Social Media Lab (VSML) carried out a number of impact activities, culminating in the ‘Questioning Images’ (QI) resource. QI has underpinned election-related media literacy campaigns in Canada and Colombia in 2019. These activities reached ~9,000 teachers and 1.2 million pupils in Canada (70% of all schools in Canada), and 199 school and 76,000 pupils in Colombia. The VSML also responded rapidly to COVID-19 misinformation, producing a teacher’s guide which trained 80 schools in Manchester, reaching 1,600 pupils. Read more...

topic_name_long: Brexit, UK & EU policies, Intl. Trade
description: Research in this topic shaped understanding and responses to Brexit, its legal implications, and the redefinition of the UK’s place in the world. Case studies informed the redrawing of UK legislation and legal frameworks, supported the protection of EU nationals’ rights, and guided the restructuring of Britain’s foreign relations. Scholars played a central role in communicating the consequences of Brexit to the public and in advising on the future of UK governance, trade policy, and regulatory structures. Research also supported British Overseas Territories and informed collaboration with Ireland on border and policy issues. Beyond Brexit, work on EU policymaking and trade institutions enhanced understanding of EU-specific rights and shaped evolving trade policy. Broader international trade research addressed global trade rules, WTO processes, and macroeconomic modelling to support more effective and equitable trade negotiations and policy development.
narrative:
Post-Brexit recognition for the British-Irish common travel area and for Irish citizens in UK immigration law

This research ensured post-Brexit legal protections for Irish citizens in the UK. It directly supported the forging of a formal agreement between the UK and Irish governments safeguarding reciprocal rights to live, work, access healthcare and education, and vote — affecting hundreds of thousands of residents and millions of cross-border travelers annually. Legal recommendations shaped Section 2 of the Immigration Act 2020, ensuring Irish citizens retained rights independent of EU law. Ryan’s evidence also secured ministerial commitments on family sponsorship and deportation protections, embedding long-term legal clarity and stability for Irish citizens in UK immigration law. Read more...

Informing, Developing, and Delivering the UK’s Trade Policy

This research shaped how the UK created and delivered trade policy after Brexit. Researchers from the University of Liverpool worked inside government to train over 600 civil servants across 32 departments, ensuring they could negotiate and implement trade deals effectively. Their expert advice directly supported the negotiation of four trade agreements worth over £2bn annually, and improved policymaking on complex issues like tariffs, climate, investment screening, and food safety. Their guidance informed weekly ministerial briefings and helped coordinate cross-government positions during high-stakes negotiations, including those affected by COVID-19 and the global trade landscape. Read more...

description: Research in this topic relates to climate change and environmental policy, and studies encompass climate science and modeling, carbon budgets and emissions targets, climate risk assessment, climate communication and public engagement, international climate diplomacy, climate justice and social vulnerability mapping, climate resilience and infrastructure. Research here tends to use modelling and visualisation tools, as well as assessment and data analysis tools to inform policy and organisational decisions.
narrative:
Redesigning global climate technology policy and funding to meet the needs of low- and middle-income countries

Research at the University of Sussex developed a new approach—Climate Relevant Innovation-system Builders (CRIBs)—to improve climate technology transfer to low- and middle-income countries by focusing on building local innovation systems and aligning technologies with local needs and political contexts. This approach has reshaped global climate policy: it informed the UNFCCC’s review of climate technology policy, was adopted by the Green Climate Fund (GCF) to guide funding strategy, and influenced the World Bank’s shift towards “market ecosystem creation” in its Climate Technology Program. Regionally, the African Union used CRIBs to train policymakers from 18 countries, contributing to the design of its Green Innovation Framework. Nationally, 16 policy organisations in nine African countries are applying CRIBs to secure GCF funding and inform climate strategies—most notably, Burundi received nearly USD10 million (leveraging over USD21 million) and Kenya has USD20 million in advanced-stage proposals—demonstrating CRIBs’ practical influence on mobilising climate finance and shaping sustainable development across the Global South. Read more...

Improving the effectiveness of visualisation and communication of climate science to a diverse worldwide audience

Psychological and cognitive science research at the University of East Anglia led to the creation of the ‘MADE’ principles—a set of guidelines to improve climate data visualisations for non-specialist audiences—which have been widely adopted by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) and other international bodies. These principles were directly applied to improve figures in major IPCC reports, including the Special Reports on Global Warming of 1.5°C and on Climate Change and Land, significantly enhancing figure comprehension among policymakers and the public. The guidelines have been disseminated globally, featured in IPCC style guides, communications handbooks, and African expert training, and informed visual communication strategies across multiple international agencies, thereby transforming how complex climate science is presented to and understood by diverse audiences worldwide. Read more...

Strengthening planning for urban climate change adaptation and resilience

Research at the University of Manchester through the RESIN project developed tools and spatial datasets to support climate adaptation planning in cities, most notably the European Climate Risk Typology, which helps policymakers visualise and compare regional climate risks. These tools informed climate strategies in Greater Manchester, directly shaping the Manchester Climate Change Framework 2020–2025 and the region’s Whole Place Implementation Plan. At the European level, the Typology supported the European Investment Bank’s climate risk modelling, enhanced the European Environment Agency’s data platforms and reporting, and was adopted by the Covenant of Mayors to guide adaptation assessments for over 10,000 local authorities. Read more...

Informing International and Organisational Policy and Decision-Making around Climate Change

This research into the effects of climate change underpinned a 2014 report for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change that was approved by over 100 national governments, including the UK, influencing their climate targets. The report was also a key scientific input into the Paris Climate Agreement that was signed in 2016 and aims to limit the rise in global average temperature to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels. Read more...

description: Research in this topic informed interactions with art, history and science through innovative exhibitions and technologies. Case studies shaped museum and institutional practices, promoting and enabling greater public engagement with both familiar subjects and underrepresented areas in art, heritage and science. Many used exhibitions as platforms for education, cross-cultural understanding and social inclusion, often generating significant social and economic benefits for host communities. Work in this topic highlights the role of cultural engagement in enhancing social and individual wellbeing and inspiring participation of new, diverse audiences.
narrative:
Digital Rome: inspiring access to Rome’s ancient architecture and history through 3D visualisations

Research led to the development of a highly successful Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) on the FutureLearn platform: Rome: A Virtual Tour of an Ancient City. The course provides five weeks of online content that combine documentary footage of Rome with digital reconstructions of ancient Rome, including interactive 3D models of buildings of particular historical and/or archaeological interest. The first run of the course showed higher uptake than the average for all MOOCs and for comparable history courses. Significantly higher proportions of learners completed over 90% of the course than on other MOOCs. During its 10 runs, the course has attracted over 59,000 learners from 190 countries across a range of ages and working backgrounds. It has generated £33,179.40 and has served as model for similar courses. It has also been incorporated into teaching practices, including being used as a digital training resource for Classics teachers by the Joint Association for Classics Teachers. Read more...

Caravaggio: generating cultural value through art historical research

The correct attribution of important, often newly discovered historical artworks by art history scholars, including paintings by Caravaggio, Da Vinci and Parmigianino, had considerable economic impact on the art market. Caravaggio’s Judith Beheading Holofernes achieved a market sale of around £100-150 million. The Parmigianino was estimated to be worth £245 million and subsequently purchased by the Getty Museum. Read more...

New ways of seeing: revealing the materiality of artistic practice in Medieval and Renaissance Europe

Researchers helped conceive and inform many important exhibits, such as the COLOUR exhibit (133,656 visitors) on medieval miniature paintings at the Fitzwilliam Museum and the Raphael exhibit (67,628 visitors) at the Ashmolean Museum. New forms of audience engagement were pioneered, with 58% of Raphael visitors drawing themselves during their visit, and 3,800 primary school pupils getting to engage with how monks used to illuminate paintings in COLOUR-inspired school drawing lessons. Read more...

Blood and Money: Contested cultural histories

Two major exhibitions hosted by the Jewish Museum in London, Blood: Unities & Dividing (2015/16) and Jews, Money, Myth (2019), influenced prominent collectors to open their collections and loan items to help change public understanding of Jewish history and cultural identity. Blood attracted over 11,000 people, sold over 600 exhibition books, and generated thousands of pounds in revenue. Its unprecedented acclaim created the demand for it to tour to the Galicia Jewish Museum, Krakow where it attracted more than 30,000 visitors, the most a tour exhibition has ever attracted to that musem. It then travelled to the POLIN Museum for History of Polish Jews, Warsaw, where it attracted 45,000, making it the most popular temporary exhibition the museum has ever hosted. It was covered in 628 media pieces, with an advertising value of around £1.1 million. Jews, Money, Myth reach 290 million people through media, and attracted 22,000 visitors. It won the Museums Association ‘Museums Change Lives’ award in 2019 for its impact on public understanding at a time of rising antisemitism. The responses to these exhibitions inspired Birkbeck University to develop a short course on identifying and tackling antisemitism, ‘Facing Antisemitism: Politics, History, Culture’, which was used by major institutions including the Labour Party. Read more...

description: This topic encompasses case studies relating to energy systems and decarbonisation. Studies address areas such as renewable energy technologies, policy development, building energy efficiency, decarbonization and net-zero transitions, smart energy systems, and socio-economic impacts of energy transitions. Research inlcudes both technical solutions (i.e. smart systems, materials for heat storage, solar photovoltaic monitoring, CO2 capture, AI-integrated systems), and policy tools (i.e. energy mapping, economic modeling, regulatory methodologies, community engagement). The work spans from addressing fuel poverty through targeted neighborhood mapping to supporting large-scale policy development for energy directives and decarbonisation strategies.
narrative:
Accelerating decarbonisation of the GB Whole Energy System through governance reform

This work produced policy reccomendations for decarbonising GB's energy system that influenced the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) to identify how current governance arrangements are damaging the energy market. It also supported the CMA, Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (BEIS) and regulator Ofgem to change the system of industry codes to increase opportunities for green energy innovators. Researchers also recommended a revised governance framework for the regulation of the GB whole energy system, prompting BEIS and the National Infrastructure Commission (NIC) to use this as a basis for evaluating future institutional change and inspired the creation of a “fourth principle” for energy policy: the agility principle, introduced by the BEIS Secretary of State in 2018. Read more...

Changing EU directives to improve the energy efficiency of non-residential buildings across Europe

Showing that new methods of continuous monitoring are more effective at improving building energy performance than physical inspections informed the 2018 revision of the EU Energy Performance of Buildings Directive, which defined legal standards across all 28 EU member states. Insights were also incorporated into the £4.4 billion building programme for new schools by the UK Department for Education. Read more...

Increasing energy efficiency in homes and reducing the domestic energy performance gap.

This research into energy efficient construction led to changes in UK Building Regulations, estimated to reduce 120,000 tonnes of CO2 emissions and save British households £66 million pounds in energy consumption due to higher energy efficiency. Read more...

description: The case studies in this topic cover themes in food and agricultural research, with a focus on systems and policy. Studies look at areas such as food security and resilience, sustainable agricultural transformation and practice, food safety and quality systems, and innovation and policy integration. The topic as a whole showcases developing new technologies, financial tools, and governance frameworks to support food and agricultural transformations at local and international levels.
narrative:
Building Resilience in Wetland Farming Communities in East and Central Africa

Insights from research on best practices for sustainable agricultural wetland use, codified as the Functional Landscape Approach (FLA), were incorporated by governments and NGOs in programmes that reached over 148,000 households, around one million people, across Ethiopia, Zambia, Malawi, Uganda, and Tanzania. Read more...

Food Heritage: Enabling collecting institutions and their communities to shape research and policy on food and food security and contributing to UN-Sustainable Development Goals

The BigPicnic project addressed food security issues in the context of botanic garden education by exploring the links between food security, plant diversity, and climate change. Hosted in 14 European and 1 Ugandan Botanic Garden in 2016-2019, it showed the role that trusted public institutions like botanic gardens can play in effecting changes to attitude, behaviour, and political response to food and food security. Between 2016-2018, the BigPicnic team have developed 15 exhibitions on food security issues and established 92 science cafés in 59 locations. It has altered the relationship of some European and Ugandan citizens to food and food choices, with 180,000 visitors to BigPicnic events and 6,982 science café users. The project has helped train botanic garden professionals to continue this work, and shaped policy debate around food security in Scotland and Canada. Read more...

Food Ladders: Increasing resilience and reducing vulnerability to food insecurity

A new food support framework, Food Ladders, has created institutional and policy change. Food Ladders has informed the UK’s planning responses and disaster mitigation approach and has underpinned long-term strategies in over 40 UK charities, including the UK’s largest surplus food redistributor, FareShare. FareShare has increased its long-term funding to £19million and expanded to work with Asda and Waitrose as well as Tesco. This work has also influenced major producers in the food sector, like GreenCore, whose Sustainability Report and Plan (2020) aims to introduce their community engagement programme, #StartsWithFood, to every site and to donate 100% of surplus to vulnerable communities by 2022. Local authorities have also partnered with the PI, e.g., £1.7million given by the National Institute for Health Research to PI to develop a fruit and vegetable voucher scheme in partnership with Doncaster Metropolitan Borough Council. Read more...

Improving the fortunes of small-scale agri-food producers and delivering consumer benefits via the development of quality food markets

This research has changed the practices of a major international grocery retailer, shaped the EU policy agenda on unfair trading practices and food quality policy, and developed alternative markets and short food supply chains. These impacts have improved economic returns to small-scale producers in Armenia, Hungary, Serbia, Croatia, and the United Kingdom, enabled consumers to benefit from better access to quality foods, and allowed over 30,000 children to receive more nutritious school meals. Read more...

topic_name_long: Pensions, Finances, Consumer Protection and Market Regulation
description: Research in this topic has shaped the regulation of financial services and various goods markets with the goal of protecting consumers and retail investors. Case studies informed policies of key regulatory bodies such as the Financial Conduct Authority and improved various regulations such as oversight of credit cards, payday lending, and complaint handling. Projects enhanced financial literacy and reduced risks linked to gambling, indebtedness, and financial vulnerability. Research drove reforms in insurance and pension practices and regulations, supporting better retirement outcomes and financial security. Contributions also improved market transparency and pricing in housing, pharmaceuticals, and tech products, guided merger and cartel policies, and influenced accounting standards and business regulation to safeguard consumer interests.
narrative:
Oxevision - Vision-based patient monitoring and management in mental health settings

Oxevision, developed from University of Oxford research and commercialised by spin-out Oxehealth, is the world’s first CE-marked, contact-free vital-sign monitoring system using video cameras and clinically validated algorithms. Installed in 1,277 patient rooms across 16 NHS Trusts and two Scandinavian sites by November 2020, it has transformed mental health care by enabling remote monitoring of heart rate, breathing, and movement. The system has significantly improved patient safety (e.g. 82% fewer harmful falls), privacy (98% fewer night-time disturbances), and clinical decision-making, while reducing emergency interventions and protecting staff during COVID-19. It generates over £2 million in annual recurring revenue and exemplifies research-driven digital health innovation. Read more...

Shaping Policy Learning on Regulatory Reforms: Co-Creating the World Bank’s Global Regulatory Impact Assessment Awards

Building capacity for better regulation is an important aspect of global development. To encourage bottom up innovation in regulationm UK researchers started the Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) Awards together with the World Bank. The RIA Awards represent an international learning platform, assisting policymakers in 45 developing and transition economies to share and diffuse models of best practice. Read more...

The development of the Life Market, a global capital market for transferring longevity risk.

The Life Market (LM) is a major new global capital market for transferring longevity risk from corporate pension schemes to reinsurers and capital-market investors. Mortality forecasting models together with longevity bonds and swaps, designed by UK researchers, have been integral to operating LM. To date, one $50M longevity bond, 61 UK longevity swaps (worth £105bn), and seven Dutch longevity swaps have been executed. This contributed to a reduction in the prices reinsurers charge clients by 1% and created industry savings of £1B. The reduction in risk benefits pension scheme members who now have greater confidence that their pensions will be paid in full. Read more...

Shaping Consumer Financial Protection Policy in the United Kingdom

Improving Consumer Financial Protection: Behavioural economics research influenced the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) design of a price cap on UK payday loans, protecting 4.3 million loan applicants. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic inform policy, legislation and protective measures for vulnerable workers and groups vulnerable to exploitation, including those affected by modern slavery, human trafficking, illegal sex work and the drug trade. ICSs raise awareness of often unheard or stigmatised experiences, amplifying the voices of marginalised communities to challenge public and institutional perceptions. Work in this topic advocates for more inclusive representation and reforms in national and international legal and policy frameworks to recognise and protect those most affected by exploitative systems.
narrative:
Student Sex Workers: Reducing Stigma and Improving Well-being

This research led to the UK’s first dedicated e-health service for student sex workers, offering peer support, confidential counselling, and safety advice. The service enhanced wellbeing and protection for hundreds of users. Collaboration with NHS Wales established the first sexual health clinic and outreach service for student sex workers. Awareness-raising at 30 Freshers’ Fairs reached 1,687 students - 86% reported greater awareness of stigma, and 90% said they would be more likely to challenge it. The work directly shaped NUS policy and university practices across the UK. The BAFTA Cymru-winning film Fog of Sex and related media reached over 18 million viewers. Co-produced online training has been adopted by 100+ professionals, improving responses across higher education, health, and policing sectors. Read more...

Using Earth Observation to tackle modern slavery

Boyd’s ‘Slavery from Space’ programme has revolutionised efforts to combat modern slavery by using Earth Observation to identify slavery-linked industries across multiple countries. This approach fills a critical global data gap and has been recognized by the UN, ILO, and awarded the 2020 GEO SDG Award. In South Asia, Boyd mapped over 47,000 brick kilns across 1.55m square km, enabling targeted raids that liberated 138 bonded labourers since 2019. Her data helped resolve wage disputes totalling around ₹12.1 million (~$160,000 USD) and improved conditions at nearly 20 kilns. Integrated into a UNDP GeoAI app, it supports inspections covering 30% of northern India’s brick kilns. In Greece, Boyd mapped 48 informal settlements housing 6,000 migrant workers, aiding NGOs and government efforts. Her work was incorporated into Greece’s National Action Plan following a European Court ruling and praised for advancing worker protection. Boyd’s research provides actionable data that enhances identification, rescue, policy, and compliance efforts toward ending modern slavery by 2030. Read more...

description: Research in this topic surrounds the development and utilisation of imaging and assessment techniques for diagnosis, prognosis and monitoring of conditions. Case studies encompass development of sensing and imaging technologies, as well as methods for analysis and use of procured data. Improving accuracy, patient experience and reducing risk are all key elements within the topic.
narrative:
Leeds Virtual Microscope: A New Tool for Pathologists Diagnosing Cancer

The Leeds Virtual Microscope (LVM), developed through research at the University of Leeds, transformed how pathologists diagnose cancer by enabling faster and more accurate analysis of biopsy slides using ultra-high-resolution digital displays. It was the first digital pathology software able to support gigapixel images on such screens, matching the diagnostic speed of traditional microscopes. Adopted by Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, the LVM underpinned its transition to fully digital pathology and influenced national guidelines. It also shaped the design of Roche’s uPath system—now licensed in over 100 locations worldwide—and guided scanner development at FFEI and display technologies at Barco. Its impact extends across the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia-Pacific, and helped secure major investments in UK pathology AI research and infrastructure. Read more...

Computational Cardiology Impacting on Medical Devices, Safer Drug Trials, Medical Training and Technical Standards

Ulster University’s research in computational cardiology has led to significant advances in medical technology, training, and regulation. A 3D ECG algorithm developed in collaboration with the FDA has been adopted by the agency to compute biomarkers predicting risk of drug-induced arrhythmias, shaping drug safety protocols. Ulster’s simulator for visualising ECG recording errors was integrated into a bestselling medical textbook and widely used for training, improving clinical education globally. Research into defibrillator usability and electrode misplacement directly informed the design and market approval of a novel AED and the validation of a new ECG patch system, both now in use in hospitals and emergency settings. Ulster’s findings on automation bias in ECG interpretation have informed international standards, including IEEE and IEC guidance, while its work on ECG data structure contributed to the development and deployment of PDF-ECG in hospital systems. These contributions have advanced medical practice, improved patient safety, and helped shape global technical standards. Read more...

Transforming the use of Arterial Spin Labelling for Clinical Practice

Arterial Spin Labelling (ASL) is a non-invasive MRI technique for measuring cerebral blood flow, an indicator of neurological diseases. ASL was previously underused due to lack of harmonisation in the MRI technology, despite being easily implemented, cheaper, and safer than existing alternatives. Research of this ICS produced harmonised guidelines on the use of ASL in clinical settings. The methodology has now been adopted by the manufacturers of >90% of the world’s MRI scanners. Sales of harmonised ASL clinical software packages have increased from $37,910,000 (2014) to $48,550,000 (2019). Read more...

topic_name_long: Robotics, Sensors, AI, Satellite & Image Data and Smart Systems
description: Research in this topic is applicable to advanced robotics, artificial intelligence, sensor and smart system technologies and image data across a breadth of sectors.
