Studies encompass autonomous systems for agriculture, manufacturing, and transportation, alongside sophisticated imaging and detection technologies for security, space applications, and industrial monitoring. Case studies demonstrate the commercialisation of AI-powered solutions including computer vision systems, natural language processing tools, and robotic platforms that enhance productivity and safety. The topic aslso includes sensor development for gas detection, structural monitoring, and environmental applications, as well as satellite-based monitoring systems for agricultural and urban planning. Additionally, research covers the integration of these technologies into smart systems that support decision-making, automate complex processes, and enable new capabilities in healthcare, forensics, and public safety applications.
narrative:
Oxbotica – Creating Universal Autonomy for Vehicles

Research from the University of Oxford’s Mobile Robotics Group (now Oxford Robotics Institute) established the foundational concept of ‘Universal Autonomy’—the ability for vehicles to navigate without reliance on GPS or external infrastructure and operate in all environments and weather conditions. This work led to the 2014 spinout of Oxbotica, which commercialised the research into software platforms used across industries including mining, logistics, and aviation. Oxbotica’s technology has shaped UK autonomous vehicle (AV) policy through its central role in national trials such as LUTZ, AUTODrive, and DRIVEN, and through contributions to the UK Government’s Code of Practice for AV testing. The company has grown to employ 170 staff across the UK and Canada, secured partnerships with major industrial players including Nissan, Caterpillar, and Addison Lee, and was showcased by the UK Government as an example of national leadership in AV development. Oxford’s research and Oxbotica’s deployment of it have been instrumental in positioning the UK as a global leader in autonomous mobility. Read more...

Development and commercialisation of robotic nanomanipulation of living cells

Collaborative research between the University of Bedfordshire and Changchun University of Science and Technology led to major advances in robotic nanomanipulation of living cells, resulting in the development of a multidimensional information nanoscopic detector. This technology, which enables in vitro cell manipulation and measurement across multiple physical dimensions, underpins the spin-out company Changli-nanobio Ltd, established in 2017. The detector has been used for applications such as DNA editing, drug evaluation, early cancer diagnosis, and food supplement development. Changli-nanobio provides services to hospitals and pharmaceutical companies, supporting clinical and product innovation, and has developed its own supplement, Shenpuyin. The company has attracted significant investment, grown to 60 employees, and now plays a key role in Jilin Province’s strategy to revitalise its economy through high-tech innovation, with backing from the local Economic-Technological Development Zone. Read more...

More efficient and sustainable agriculture through advanced techniques in machine vision and machine learning

Research at the Centre for Machine Vision (CMV) at the University of the West of England led to significant innovations in agriculture through the application of 3D imaging and deep learning. The ‘HerdVision’ system, developed in partnership with agri-tech firm Agsenze, automates dairy cow condition and lameness monitoring, improving welfare and productivity, and is deployed on 11 UK farms, including 10 in Arla’s sustainable farming programme. A second innovation, ‘HarvestEye’, enables real-time in-field data capture during potato harvesting, providing insights that improve crop marketing and agronomic planning; it has been successfully commercialised by B-Hive Innovations Ltd in partnership with GRIMME UK. CMV research also underpins ‘GrassVision’, developed with SoilEssentials Ltd, a smart-camera weed detection and precision spraying system that reduces herbicide use by 90%. These technologies have increased efficiency, reduced environmental impacts, created jobs, and upskilled partner companies in machine vision and AI, contributing to a more sustainable and profitable agricultural sector. Read more...

Spectral Edge Ltd.

Research at the University of East Anglia’s Colour & Imaging Lab led to the development of advanced image fusion algorithms that overcame longstanding problems of artefacts and hallucinated detail, enabling the fusion of multiple images into a single colour image with enhanced detail. These innovations were commercialised through the 2011 spin-out Spectral Edge Ltd., which secured over £6 million in funding and developed a suite of applications, including Eyeteq (enhancing video for colour-blind users), Nighteq, Vividteq, and real-time IR-visible image fusion for security. The company grew to 15 staff and gained licensing deals, including with NTT Data Italia, before being acquired by Apple Inc. in November 2019. Apple integrated the core technology into its product development pipeline and established a Cambridge facility around the Spectral Edge team, with the IP and algorithms continuing to influence next-generation imaging in consumer devices. The acquisition also delivered strong returns to early investors, including UEA and local seed funds. Read more...

Gas sensor technology: achieving global sales and developing innovative solutions for indoor air quality

Research at the University of Warwick, in collaboration with the University of Cambridge, led to the development of ultra-low-power CMOS-compatible gas sensors for detecting indoor air pollutants, resulting in the creation of the spin-out Cambridge CMOS Sensors (CCS) in 2008. Warwick-patented innovations enabled highly sensitive, compact, and cost-effective metal-oxide (MOX) sensors (CCS801 and CCS811), which significantly outperformed competitors in power efficiency and manufacturability. These sensors were adopted in industrial, automotive, and increasingly consumer devices, including smartwatches and smart home systems. Following GBP8 million in investment and growing global demand, CCS was acquired in 2016 by ams in a deal valued up to EUR31 million, and its technology underpinned the creation of the USD120 million ScioSense joint venture in 2019. Warwick’s foundational IP remains central to ScioSense’s global success and product strategy, with millions of units sold and future sensor generations under development. Read more...

New industrial electromagnetic sensor systems improve safety processes and optimise capabilities in the UK's energy, rail and manufacturing sectors

University of Manchester research revolutionised electromagnetic induction (EMI) sensor systems, enabling more accurate, non-destructive inspection across key UK industries. Their innovations in spectroscopy and tensor-based modelling are now used by EDF Energy to assess graphite degradation in the UK’s nuclear reactor fleet, enhancing safety and supporting reactor life extension. In steel production, Tata Steel adopted the EMspec™ system to monitor microstructural changes in over 30 million tonnes of steel, improving quality and reducing waste. The food industry benefits from improved contaminant detection through Safeline’s EMI-based metal detectors, while the rail sector uses Manchester’s methods to detect early-stage defects, strengthening infrastructure safety. These applications have delivered significant operational, safety, and environmental gains. Read more...

description: Research in this topic has shaped how cities, towns, and rural areas are planned, built, and governed to promote livability, inclusion, and sustainability. Case studies informed national housing policies, supported legislative reform on housing rights, and influenced regulations on building standards, property valuation, and taxation. Projects helped develop affordable and social housing and gave voice to tenants and community groups in shaping their environments. Providing social and legislative support as well as shelter for the homeless was another major research focus. Research enhanced urban development through virtual city models and spatial planning tools, while also supporting greener cities, accessible public spaces, and integration of diverse populations. In rural areas, research guided strategies to reinvigorate communities and improve local infrastructure and services.
narrative:
Improving housing law in Wales and England

This research provided the legal and intellectual underpinning for the regulation of nearly all rented accommodation in Wales, directly impacting the lives of approximately half a million private or social tenant households and their landlords. The research also provided an underpinning evidence base that directly influenced the successful passage of the Homes (Fitness for Human Habitation) Act 2018, which affects over 8 million private and social rented tenancies in England. Read more...

Homelessness: Shaping legislation in England and Wales, and informing international policy debates

Research on how to reduce homelessness via a focus on prevention resulted in new legislation: the Housing (Wales) Act 2014 and England’s Homelessness Reduction Act (2017). Read more...

Supporting planning and housing policy reform around the world

Supporting Housing Policy Reform Around the World: policy reforms aimed at improving land and housing market efficiency and affordability sparked debate in many countries, including the UK. Research and debate led to the Mortgage Interest Deduction in the USA (2017), the mortgage interest and capital deduction in Flanders (2015) and Brussels (2017), and the Ontario Housing Supply Action Plan (2019) affecting housing policies for 137,000,000 households. Read more...

description: Research in this topic focuses on approaches to viral disease prevention and control. Vaccine development, strategy and policy is an important component of this, at national and global level. Additionally new anti-viral treatments and diagnostics are included, alongside mathematical modeling and data analysis, epidemic response, and some virus-specific research (i.e. genomic studies). There is additionally a contingent of studies with focus on health policy, global health impact and access equity for virus control and vaccine deployment.
narrative:
Reducing infant deaths from rotavirus diarrhoea in sub-Saharan Africa

Research led by the University of Liverpool demonstrated that rotavirus vaccination is safe, cost-effective, and life-saving in low-income settings, directly influencing WHO’s global recommendation to introduce rotavirus vaccines in high-burden countries. Following a landmark trial in Malawi showing a 50% reduction in severe rotavirus diarrhoea, Liverpool researchers conducted further studies proving the vaccine’s effectiveness at scale: a 33% reduction in infant diarrhoea deaths and averted hospitalisations and disability. This evidence catalysed Malawi’s vaccine rollout and served as an exemplar across Africa. As a result, 38 African countries introduced rotavirus vaccination, preventing an estimated 169,400 deaths and over 40 million gastroenteritis cases between 2013 and 2020. The work continues to shape WHO policy and national vaccine programmes. Read more...

New generation seasonal influenza vaccines

Research from the University of Cambridge has fundamentally reshaped the global selection process for seasonal influenza vaccines, directly informing decisions that affect over 500 million annual vaccinations. By developing antigenic cartography and revealing the mechanisms behind antigenic shifts—including the pivotal “backboost” immune phenomenon—this work enabled accurate prediction of viral evolution and introduced the concept of using antigenically advanced strains to pre-empt circulating variants. Since 2004, Professor Smith has served on the WHO vaccine strain selection committee, and since 2012, his group has provided the WHO with near real-time analyses of thousands of global viral sequences, now integral to the vaccine decision-making process. These innovations have improved vaccine effectiveness and helped avoid critical mismatches, enhancing protection against influenza worldwide and informing national immunisation strategies in countries including Canada and the US. Read more...

Better protection against influenza through national childhood vaccination programmes

Reverse genetics technology developed at the University of Oxford revolutionised influenza vaccine production by enabling rapid, precise generation of vaccine strains, forming the foundation for AstraZeneca’s live attenuated intranasal vaccine, FluMist/Fluenz. This vaccine, introduced into the UK’s National Childhood Vaccination Programme in 2013 as Fluenz Tetra, has since been administered to over 20 million children aged 2–17, significantly reducing influenza-related GP consultations, hospitalisations, and respiratory mortality, while also providing indirect protection across the population. The programme’s phased rollout, informed by pilot studies, demonstrated that vaccinating school-aged children not only conferred direct benefits but also generated herd immunity, reducing flu incidence in unvaccinated age groups, including older adults. The technology underpinning FluMist/Fluenz has also supported national immunisation programmes in countries including the US, Canada, Finland, and South Korea, with up to 22 million doses manufactured annually in the UK. In addition to measurable public health benefits, the vaccine has contributed to a reduction in antibiotic prescriptions and is recognised as a cost-effective intervention that strengthens pandemic preparedness and alleviates winter pressures on health systems. Read more...

Prevention of epidemic meningitis in Africa

Pioneering research by LSHTM demonstrated that the MenAfriVac vaccine, designed to prevent group A meningococcal meningitis, not only protected vaccinated individuals but also halted epidemics by interrupting bacterial transmission through the prevention of carriage, leading to rapid herd immunity across the African meningitis belt. A pivotal study in Chad—where only part of the country was initially vaccinated—revealed a 94% reduction in meningitis incidence in vaccinated areas and showed near-elimination of group A carriage. These findings provided critical real-world evidence of the vaccine’s effectiveness, accelerating global rollout and influencing WHO recommendations for universal mass campaigns followed by routine infant immunisation. As a direct result, over 300 million people were vaccinated across 26 countries, virtually eliminating serogroup A meningitis from the region, preventing an estimated 142,000 deaths and more than a million cases. The research shaped Gavi policy and catalysed investment exceeding USD367 million, with MenAfriVac now a global case study in cost-effective, lifesaving vaccine deployment. Read more...

Discovery of a virus assembly mechanism using models of viral geometry: new opportunities for anti-viral therapy

Groundbreaking research at the University of York overturned long-held assumptions about virus assembly by showing that the process is not driven solely by electrostatics but instead relies on multiple dispersed RNA packaging signals (PSs) that guide capsid formation. Using mathematical tools such as group theory and Hamiltonian paths, the team developed a novel modelling paradigm that enabled the discovery of PSs in viruses including Hepatitis B, HIV, and coronaviruses. This insight has catalysed new avenues for antiviral drug development—adopted by the US National Cancer Institute to establish a high-throughput screening platform targeting RNA-protein interactions—and underpinned patents for engineering virus-like particles (VLPs) to improve drug delivery, vaccine stability, and gene therapy. The technology has attracted industry interest, including from GlaxoSmithKline, and addresses a critical bottleneck in therapeutic VLP manufacturing. Public engagement has also been extensive: the research inspired virtual reality installations viewed by thousands at international venues such as the Lowry Gallery and Centre Pompidou, enhancing public understanding of viruses and the role of mathematics in biomedical innovation, and supported fundraising for the MathsWorldUK mathematics education centre. Read more...

Anthropological insights improve the humanitarian response to Ebola

The public health response to the Ebola outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2016 faltered for a variety of reasons, many of which were social and cultural (e.g., mortuary and burial practices) but also political and economic (the sodalities managing burial practices in the region were also essential components of the political system). Researchers leveraged anthropological research to create the Ebola Response Anthropology Platform (ERAP) to provide social analysis to enable effective medical response and offer real-time advice during such outbreaks. ERAP authored 40 rapid response briefings, solicited by DFID, MOD, WHO, UNMEER, Christian Aid, and others, which drew 16,000 users to their website. ERAP’s insights aided such organisations and individuals in navigating social resistance to humanitarian responses by involving local communities. ERAP has now been renamed the Social Science in Humanitarian Action Platform (SSHAP), and this platform model is now informing the COVID-19 response. Read more...

description: This research topic focuses on cancer treatments, support and care for patients. Key themes included are early detection and screening innovations, precision medicine and targeted therapies and treatment technologies. There's a strong emphasis on patient-centered care that prioritises the overall experience and wellbeing of cancer patients. Elements of clinical guidance, policy and service management specific to cancer are also included.
narrative:
Lung Cancer Screening: Improving early detection of the commonest cause of cancer death through the UK Lung Cancer Screening (UKLS) trial catalysing implementation and unique risk modelling

Research at the University of Liverpool led to the development of the Liverpool Lung Project (LLP) risk model, a validated tool for identifying individuals at high risk of lung cancer, which underpinned the UK Lung Cancer Screening (UKLS) trial—the first randomised controlled trial in the UK to demonstrate that a risk-based approach to low-dose CT screening effectively detects early-stage lung cancers. This trial established the clinical efficiency and cost-effectiveness of targeted screening, significantly improving early diagnosis and enabling curative treatment, with 67% of detected cancers at stage I and 83% of patients suitable for surgery. The LLP model and UKLS findings directly influenced the launch of NHS England’s £70 million Targeted Lung Health Checks programme, projected to identify 3,400 early cancers by 2023 across 17 localities and laying the groundwork for nationwide rollout to 14 million people by 2028. The model has also shaped policy and implementation in Wales, Scotland, Europe, and China, where it is cited in national guidelines and used in screening pilots. The UKLS trial’s risk-based strategy and nodule management pathway have become international benchmarks for lung cancer screening, supported by economic modelling demonstrating a cost per QALY of £8,466, well below NICE thresholds, and leading to tangible health gains and reduced mortality in high-risk populations. Read more...

Specialist cancer services improve outcomes for Teenagers and Young Adults with cancer

Research at the University of Leeds identified that teenagers and young adults (TYA) with cancer faced poorer outcomes due to fragmented, non-specialised care and environments unsuitable for their age group. This led to the development of national NHS policy in 2005 mandating specialist TYA cancer services, with Leeds research providing the evidence base for both the guidance and its implementation. Following these changes, cancer mortality in TYA fell by 27% between 2001 and 2013, with national studies such as BRIGHTLIGHT showing that specialised care improves survival, quality of life, and access to multidisciplinary, fertility and rehabilitation services. Leeds research methods have shaped national data infrastructure and clinical metrics, and informed NHS service models that now support 1,400 TYA annually. Internationally, the Leeds-led approach to TYA specialisation has influenced cancer policy and services in the US, Germany, France, the Netherlands, and India, and has been integrated into European medical education programmes, transforming global standards of age-appropriate cancer care. Read more...

Lifestyle Changes to Improve Outcomes in People Living With and Beyond Cancer

Research at Sheffield Hallam University has transformed global cancer survivorship care by demonstrating that tailored lifestyle and exercise interventions significantly improve quality of life, reduce fatigue, enhance cardiovascular health, and alleviate psychological distress in people with cancer. These findings underpin international clinical guidelines, including those of the European Association of Urology, and have been adopted in national policies across countries such as Germany, Australia and the United States. The research has reshaped clinical practice in the UK, leading to the integration of exercise-based support into NHS cancer care pathways, the establishment of a dedicated rehabilitation service for cancer survivors, and the national training of healthcare and fitness professionals. These developments have improved care for thousands of patients worldwide, making evidence-based lifestyle interventions a recognised component of standard cancer treatment. Read more...

PARP inhibition in BRCA-mutated cancer: improved survival for ovarian, breast, pancreatic and prostate cancer patients

Researchers at The Institute of Cancer Research (ICR) pioneered a paradigm-shifting cancer therapy: the use of PARP inhibitors to selectively target cancers with deficiencies in DNA homologous recombination repair (HRR), especially those with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations. They showed that BRCA-deficient cells are hypersensitive to PARP inhibition—a concept they termed “synthetic lethality.” This led to the development and global regulatory approval of four PARP inhibitors (olaparib, niraparib, rucaparib, talazoparib) now used in ovarian, breast, pancreatic, and prostate cancers. Over 30,000 patients have been treated with olaparib alone, with approvals in over 70 countries. ICR's foundational science also drove more than USD 5 billion in sales for the pharmaceutical industry and informed ongoing efforts to target related DNA repair pathways (e.g., ATR, ATM). The impact spans clinical practice, health policy, patient survival, drug development, and biomarker-driven precision oncology. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic contain research surrounding neurological and neuropsychiatric diseases and their management. Studies include development of new treatments, treatment management, assessment, diagnosis and imaging. Furthermore, healthcare services for long-term support and rehabiliation are included, along with clinical practice guidelines and policy specific to this disease area.
narrative:
An app that is improving the quality of life of patients suffering with visual field defects after brain injury

Durham Reading and Exploration (DREX), a computerised training for the rehabilitation of brain injury related visual field defects, has been converted into an app to maximise accessibility and effectiveness. After implementing a consultation process with NHS professionals, patients and carers to address perceived barriers to use (e.g., tablets being a better technology for people with limited technical experience), the team developed a multiplatform app to improve the reach of this rehabilitation aid. At the time of ICS, the app has over 2,250 individual users, primarily in the UK but also in the USA, Malaysia and New Zealand. Interest in DREX increasing – it is now listed in the British and Irish Orthoptic Society's list of available rehabilitation options. DREX is also now being repurposed for other uses, such as clinical teaching in Malaysia. Read more...

Making music with brain signals to improve the quality of life of severely motor-impaired individuals

Brain-Computer Music Interface (BCMI) technology allows a person or group of people suffering from severe motor impairment to create and perform music together, significantly benefitting their mental health and wellbeing. Paramusical Ensemble, a documentary of the preparation and performance of ‘Activating Memory’ by the initial trial group, won Best Documentary at the BioFiction Science Art Film Festival in 2019, and was screen across the globe, with 104,000 views on Vimeo alone in December 2020. The ICS produced a film for the series ‘Defiant Pioneers’, showcasing the work of Rosemary Johnson, a former violinist of the Welsh National Orchestra, paralysed in a car accident. The documentary was aired during the advert break of the season finale of Game of Thrones, attracting 12,100,000 viewers. Johnson received an MBE for her services to music using the BCMI technology. Read more...

description: Research in this topic investigates malaria and tropical diseases, this includes understanding disease burden and achieving disease control through policy and strategy, awareness and prevention. Modelling of tropical diseases, healthcare access, economics and regulations are all encompassed, as are treatments, drug development and diagnostics. Studies into vector control for malaria and tropical diseases are also inlcuded.
narrative:
Overcoming regulatory barriers for the implementation of Gene Drive technology to control malarial mosquitos in Africa

Researchers at the University of Cambridge, as part of the Target Malaria consortium, were the first to demonstrate that gene drive technology could function in animals—paving the way for its application in malarial mosquito control. Building on this proof-of-concept in fruit flies, they supported the transfer of the technology into Anopheles mosquitoes, leading to the development of gene drives that suppress malaria vectors. Critically, their work helped overcome regulatory barriers in Africa: in 2016, Burkina Faso became the first African country to approve importation and later, in 2019, to permit the field release of genetically modified mosquitoes. This represented the first GM insect release in Africa and led to the development of national regulatory frameworks in Burkina Faso, Mali, and Uganda. The research also influenced international biosafety policy and public engagement strategies, contributing to capacity building and shaping responsible innovation pathways in global health biotechnology. Read more...

Improving Lives and Societies by the Targeted Treatment of Lymphatic Filariasis Morbidity in Africa and Asia

Researchers at Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine (LSTM) significantly improved the identification, treatment, and care of people suffering from lymphatic filariasis (LF)—a disabling mosquito-borne disease—in seven countries across Africa and Asia. Through innovations like an SMS-based mHealth tool, hotspot mapping, hospital assessments, and quality-of-life surveys, LSTM enabled more efficient patient identification, improved access to care (including over 11,000 hydrocoele surgeries), and demonstrated measurable gains in patients’ physical, social, and economic wellbeing. These tools and strategies are now used in national LF programmes and have helped countries like Malawi meet WHO elimination criteria, contributing to global LF eradication goals and the alleviation of poverty and disability for thousands. Read more...

Reducing the disease burden of tropical snakebite

Researchers at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine (LSTM) played a central role in tackling snakebite as a major neglected tropical disease. Their work defined the global burden of snakebite, linking it to rural poverty and long-term psychological harm, and influenced the World Health Organization’s designation of snakebite as a priority NTD in 2017. LSTM led the development and clinical testing of safer, more effective antivenoms in West Africa, which drastically reduced mortality and treatment costs. Their efforts also led to WHO establishing a prequalification system for antivenom quality, with LSTM-developed products among the first approved. These initiatives transformed international policy, improved patient care, and created lasting partnerships and commercial benefits for manufacturers. Read more...

description: Research in this topic has shaped migration policy, supported migrant integration, and amplified migrant and refugee voices in public life. Projects informed international, national and local policies, improved data on migration flows, and guided service provision for migrant youth and communities. Research supported NGOs, enhanced legal protections, and addressed challenges such as racism, trafficking, and smuggling networks. Following Brexit, studies helped adapt UK migration policy and underpinned public discourse with research based insights. Creative and co-curated initiatives—ranging from arts-based events to faith-led global efforts—helped struggling populations, raised awareness and shared the lived experiences of refugees,migrants and diasporas, fostering empathy, inclusion, and evidence-based engagement.
narrative:
‘Here to Stay’ - Influencing policy, improving public services for Eastern European migrant young people and informing public debate and attitudes to migration

Research has shown that young people born in Central and Eastern Europe who have settled in the UK are disadvantaged in rights and opportunities, particularly in access to education and support services. Working with over 1,500 of these young people, this research developed a programme of training, policy, and community activities. Events and training materials highlighted youths' understanding of their experiencing and barriers to participation in society, foregrounding discrimination and loss of rights after Brexit. This training has been accessed by over 5,000 individuals working in key services (education, social work, police, voluntary sector). The research informed social media campaigns, such as @MigrantYouth on Twitter (#heretostay #migrantyouth #migrantsrights), Instagram and Facebook. There has also been significant news coverage, such as the LSE Brexit Blog (overall monthly readership of 790,000) and Channel 4 News, where the story was viewed more than 50,000 times. Read more...

Countering the ‘Hostile Environment’ through Creative Practice: Making Space for the Stories of Immigration Detainees

David Herd’s Refugee Tales, a project culminating in a three-volume collection of first-hand accounts of refugee experience, has been instrumental in changing public perception of refugee experience. Refugee Tales has informed changes to local and national policies to support these vulnerable communities, and has been used as a lobbying tool to press for legal change. For example, Refugee Tales included accounts of indefinite detention that influenced the framing of new detention policy. 28for28.org, which filmed readings of the published tales released on social media across 28 days, had such reach that extracts from Refugee Tales I and II was used as evidence in the Joint Committee on Human Rights’ Report on Immigration Detention. The Refugee Tales are taught in over 50 universities across the world, including Oxford, Cambridge, Cornell, Leiden, and the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro. The Oak National Academy, which funded by the Department of Education and was the main provider of home-school education during lockdown, dedicated a series of online lessons for KS3 students to the Refugee Tales books, with a reach of 4.7 million visitors to the online site. Read more...

description: The case studies in this topic relate to research into cardiovascular health. This covers all aspects of cardiovascular health from treatments and management of conditions, to drug and device development, diagnosis, imaging and monitoring of conditions. It also inludes resarch informing clinical practice guielines, patient safety guidance, screening and prevention, and risk management strategies for patients. Finally, studies into public awareness and action for improved public health are included.
narrative:
A risk prediction model for sudden cardiac death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy patients (HCM Risk-SCD)

Researchers at University College London developed and validated the first statistically robust risk prediction model for sudden cardiac death (SCD) in patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), an inherited heart condition. Incorporated into European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines and endorsed in 57 countries, this model is now widely used by cardiologists to identify high-risk patients who may benefit from an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD), while avoiding unnecessary procedures for those at low risk. The model improves clinical decision-making, supports shared treatment planning between patients and clinicians, enhances quality of care, and has helped reduce inappropriate ICD use—resulting in significant health and economic benefits across global healthcare systems. Read more...

Exercise participation following stroke or transient ischaemic attack: Informing the implementation and delivery of the HELP Hampshire Stroke Clinic

Research from the University of Winchester has directly shaped the creation and delivery of the HELP Hampshire Stroke Clinic, a pioneering community-based programme supporting people recovering from stroke or mini-stroke. By demonstrating that early participation in structured exercise improves blood pressure, quality of life, and long-term health outcomes while reducing hospital admissions, the research prompted a major shift in local NHS referral practices. Instead of relying solely on GP referrals, stroke patients are now identified directly by hospital stroke units, significantly increasing access to rehabilitation. The programme has also catalyzed new collaborations, enhanced student training, supported the Stroke Association’s outreach efforts, and influenced national discussions on cost-effective stroke recovery models. Read more...

Minimally Invasive treatment for varicose veins in the legs gives patients a significantly improved quality of life

Research from the University of Hull has led to a global shift in how varicose veins and venous leg ulcers are treated, replacing traditional open surgery with minimally invasive techniques. These innovations have been adopted in NICE, European, and Royal Society of Medicine guidelines and implemented widely across the NHS and internationally. Patients now experience faster recovery, less pain, and significantly improved quality of life—over 80% report better outcomes. The approach also reduces long-term healthcare costs by preventing complications. The work has catalyzed a growing global market in endovenous technologies, benefiting patients and the medical technology sector alike. Read more...

Identifying cost-effective imaging strategies to diagnose acute stroke and to prevent secondary disabling stroke

Research influenced key clinical stroke guidelines to recommend immediate CT scanning after acute stroke, reducing the time between hospital admission and CT scanning. Immediate CT scanning in the UK has caused 42,000 more quality-adjusted life-years and a reduction in the cost of stroke patients for the NHS by £1-2billion over the REF2021 period. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic are underpinned by global health impacts in healthcare guidance and regulation. This includes reasearch studies into areas such as healthcare policy, access and equity, economics, strategy and resource management. There are also studies into medical developments, such as diagnostics and treaments, healthcare decision making, and clinical practice guidance with globally-reaching impact.
narrative:
Development of Cochrane reviews for summarizing evidence of the accuracy of diagnostic tests have improved patient care and outcomes

A new methodology for evaluating the accuracy of diagnostic tests, developed at the University of Birmingham, has transformed global healthcare decision-making. Adopted by health authorities worldwide, this approach underpins hundreds of clinical guidelines and the WHO’s Essential Diagnostics List. It has directly shaped updated WHO recommendations for diagnosing malaria and tuberculosis, enabling the rapid adoption of reliable rapid diagnostic tests in low-resource settings. As a result, millions more patients are now accurately diagnosed and treated earlier—reducing unnecessary deaths, improving outcomes, and enhancing equitable access to care in countries with the highest disease burdens. Read more...

Global surgical studies inform hospital care during the COVID-19 pandemic

A global surgical research initiative rapidly launched during the COVID-19 pandemic provided critical evidence that improved surgical care and saved lives worldwide. The collaborative’s studies revealed heightened risks for patients infected with the virus, leading to changes in clinical practice such as routine pre-operative testing and the creation of COVID-free surgical zones. These findings shaped World Health Organization and national guidelines, influenced surgical recovery planning in over 100 countries, and helped avoid millions of cancelled operations. The initiative also improved public understanding and patient confidence through accessible guidance, contributing to safer, more informed surgical care during a global health crisis. Read more...

Using Economics to Inform Budget Allocation in Global Health.

Research by the University of York has transformed how health budgets are allocated in low- and middle-income countries, helping governments and global organisations make better decisions with limited resources. Their work developed practical tools to evaluate which health interventions offer the most benefit for the money available—leading to smarter, more equitable health planning in countries like Malawi and across East and Southern Africa. It changed the way the World Health Organization sets value-for-money thresholds and directly shaped global HIV policy, improving care for millions by promoting cost-effective strategies like viral-load monitoring and HIV self-testing. This research has led to healthier populations and substantial cost savings by ensuring funds are focused on the most effective treatments. Read more...

description: This topic includes case studies pertaining to prostate cancers, including health policy surrounding prostate cancers, as well as treatments and therapies, clinical practise standards, and screening, imaging, diagnostics, prognoses for patients.
narrative:
Prostate Cancer Screening trial informs guidelines, reduces harms to men from overdetection and avoids unnecessary health service costs internationally

A major UK study led by the University of Bristol found that offering men a one-off blood test to screen for prostate cancer does not save lives and instead leads to the detection and treatment of many harmless cancers. This research changed national and international health guidance by showing that routine screening of men without symptoms causes unnecessary harm and cost without clear benefit. As a result, health authorities now recommend that men make individual, informed decisions about whether to have the test, rather than being routinely offered it—helping to avoid anxiety, side effects from unnecessary treatment, and saving the NHS an estimated £250 million in the first year alone. Read more...

Changing international practice for metastatic prostate cancer by improving survival and patient outcomes

Research led by UCL transformed global treatment for metastatic prostate cancer, demonstrating that adding docetaxel chemotherapy, abiraterone hormone therapy, or radiotherapy to standard hormone treatment significantly improves survival. Using the innovative STAMPEDE clinical trial design and STOPCAP meta-analysis approach, UCL researchers showed docetaxel extends survival by 15 months, abiraterone improves 3-year survival by 12%, and radiotherapy benefits men with lower disease spread. These results were rapidly adopted into UK and international clinical guidelines, influencing practice in over 20 countries. In the UK, an estimated 2,500 patients per year now benefit from docetaxel, potentially gaining 31,250 extra life-years over a decade. Read more...

topic_name_long: Macroeconomics, Monetary policy, Financial Markets & Banking
description: Research in this topic has strengthened the design, governance, and resilience of financial and monetary systems. Case studies informed central banks—including the Bank of England, ECB, US Federal Reserve, and others globally—on monetary policy and interventions, debt sustainability, bond auction designs and macroprudential policies. Work shaped the toolkit available for responses to financial crises through new bank rescue and stress testing schemes, and systemic risk mitigation strategies. Central Banks were equipped with improved research based tools influencing interest rate decisions, credit risk assessment, and financial market stability. Research also improved more general macroeconomic modelling, forecasting, and official statistics.. Projects also supported regulatory reform in banking and credit sectors. Many mathematical and computational research projects advanced asset and option pricing tools in financial markets. They also informed ESG investment strategies, digital banking innovation, and inclusive practices such as microfinance.
narrative:
Designing auctions to improve central bank operations

The Bank of England’s Indexed Long-Term Repo (ILTR) operation has become a key policy tool for the Bank of England to ensure sufficient liquidity for the financial system at times of stress. It is based on economic research on auction design and has been implemented and tested together with researchers. The design has led to practice changes in other central banks. Read more...

New approaches to forecasting financial markets

Forecasting Financial and Currency Markets: New forecasting models have changed key practices in both private and public sector decision making and have been used by Bank of England, the European Central Bank and major asset management companies Read more...

Enhancing the banknote security of five major currencies through the application of perception science in their design

Worked with the International Banknote Designers Association (representing 70 countries) to develop new professional standards for user testing, lead innovation, and commercial impact in banknote production. The research demonstrated that intaglio printing and 3D stereo visual cues are most commonly identified by consumers. Design decisions reflecting this are now made by central banks in England, Europe, Australia, Canada, and the USA. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic focus on educational and therapeutic initiatives and practical provisions that promote literacy and reading practices. Work provides innovative, research-informed approaches to reading comprehension, informing educational policies and supporting adoption of new teaching methods and tools across schools and adult learning settings. Many studies promote public engagement with reading at all stages of life, and underpinned provisions such as funding for public libraries and widening access to reading-related technologies.
narrative:
Enhancing children's reading comprehension by changing national and international policy and practice

Research that demonstrated the importance of including three discourse-level skills that support successful reading comprehension (inference and integration, knowledge and use of text structure, and comprehension monitoring) in early reading instruction has improved reading instruction for 4 million children in the UK by underpinning policy changes that require reading comprehension to be taught. Since 2014 and beyond, these policy changes have reached 6,000 school leadership teams, globally. Read more...

Developing effective Reading for Pleasure practices in primary schools

Research identified five key elements of an effective strategy for developing reading for pleasure within primary schools. This research has helped improve learning and practice in 308 primary schools, for 5,320 primary school practitioners (and their pupils), for 30 Initial Teacher Education Providers and for 3,858 student teachers. It has also helped guide public policy by influencing five national Reading for Pleasure initiatives. Read more...

description: This topic focuses on advances in medical treatments and therapies including the development, evaluation, and implementation of treatment options for patients. Studies encompass diagnostics, clinical decision-making, and management strategies that inform treatments and therapies used, as well as the research and development of new treatments. Case studies also often discuss policy and standards of care. The topic includes a broad range of disease areas and treatment types.
narrative:
Optimising outcomes for people with venous leg ulcers

Research at the University of Manchester has improved care and reduced costs for people with venous leg ulcers, a painful and recurring condition affecting thousands in the UK. Their systematic review confirmed that multi-layer compression bandages with elastic are most effective for healing, while a subsequent trial showed that 2-layer compression stockings are equally effective in suitable patients, reduce recurrence, and are more cost-effective. These findings have informed national and international clinical guidelines and driven significant changes in NHS practice. Prescribing of 2-layer stockings in England increased by 84% between 2013 and 2018, delivering an estimated annual saving of £7 million to the NHS and improving patient comfort and outcomes. Read more...

Radical advance in treating age-related macular degeneration leading to global impact in prevention of blindness

University of Bristol research demonstrated that the low-cost drug bevacizumab is as effective and safe as the licensed, expensive alternative for treating wet age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a major cause of blindness. The landmark IVAN trial, co-led in Bristol, provided definitive evidence that treating only active disease with bevacizumab maintains eye health while greatly reducing cost and treatment burden. These findings influenced UK NICE guidance and global health policy, including WHO recommendations and national protocols in countries such as India and Brazil. As a result, millions more patients worldwide now access effective sight-saving treatment, with substantial savings to public health systems. Read more...

Access to more effective therapies for Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma

University of Manchester research played a central role in advancing two life-extending therapies for Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma. The team was pivotal to the clinical development and regulatory approval of Brentuximab Vedotin for T-cell lymphomas, the first treatment to show improved survival in this aggressive cancer, and now a new global standard of care. In parallel, their foundational laboratory discoveries led to the development and adoption of Obinutuzumab for B-cell lymphomas, improving progression-free survival and replacing a decade-old standard treatment. These breakthroughs have transformed international clinical guidelines and expanded access to more effective therapies for tens of thousands of patients worldwide. Read more...

New sustainable technologies, support tools and standards have improved the lives of people with incontinence

Research at the University of Southampton has transformed care for people with incontinence by developing sustainable technologies, accessible guidance tools, and international standards that expand choice, improve safety, and reduce stigma. Their work enabled CE marking of the world’s first reusable, biodegradable catheter and an effective biocidal cleaning wipe, supporting more sustainable alternatives to single-use plastics. The Continence Product Advisor website and educational resources have empowered thousands globally—patients, carers, and clinicians—to make informed choices, while new international terminology and WHO procurement standards have improved access to safe, affordable products in low-income settings. Read more...

Transforming the diagnosis and treatment of ATTR amyloidosis: from a rare untreatable disease to a common remediable disorder

Research at UCL’s National Amyloidosis Centre has transformed the diagnosis and treatment of ATTR amyloidosis—a progressive, often fatal disease caused by abnormal protein deposits in the heart—into a model of precision medicine. Previously undetectable without invasive heart biopsies, ATTR amyloidosis can now be diagnosed safely and accurately using repurposed bone imaging, advanced cardiac MRI, and simple blood tests. These innovations, developed and validated by UCL, are now standard in UK and international clinical guidelines, enabling early diagnosis, patient access to new gene-silencing therapies, and improved outcomes for thousands worldwide. Read more...

description: Research in this topic has improved the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of infectious diseases and addressed the global challenge of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Work has shaped international guidelines on antibiotic stewardship, transformed national infection control policies, and reduced antimicrobial use in both human and veterinary medicine. Studies have accelerated drug discovery, including new antibiotic classes and antifungals, and advanced therapies for tuberculosis, Clostridioides difficile, and aspergillosis among others. Researchers have influenced WHO strategies, developed infection-resistant materials and hospital technologies, and improved novel genomic diagnostics. Communication, design, and systems-based interventions have also supported better public and clinical engagement with AMR.
narrative:
Pathogen whole-genome sequencing transforms healthcare-associated infection and outbreak management

Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) research at the University of Oxford has transformed global approaches to controlling healthcare-associated infections by enabling rapid identification of transmission sources and routes. This has led to safer clinical practices, such as removing reusable equipment to halt Candida auris outbreaks and redesigning surgical devices to eliminate Mycobacterium chimaera infections. Oxford’s findings also prompted international shifts in antibiotic stewardship, with fluoroquinolone restrictions helping reduce Clostridioides difficile infections. Their methods now underpin national surveillance systems and outbreak response strategies in the UK and abroad, directly influencing guidelines from Public Health England, the CDC, WHO, and other global health authorities. Read more...

Reducing Waterborne Superbug Dissemination Around the World

Research at Newcastle University fundamentally shifted global understanding of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) by demonstrating that environmental pollution—especially from untreated human waste—is a major driver of AMR spread in low- and middle-income countries. This evidence informed WHO guidance and three of its six recommended actions on AMR mitigation through water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH). It enabled countries to adopt low-cost, context-specific interventions, supported global investment and training in regions such as Ethiopia and Thailand, and influenced international AMR policy, public awareness, and response strategies, including during the COVID-19 pandemic. Read more...

Transforming understanding of antimicrobial resistance through communication design

‘Information Design and Architecture in Persuasive Pharmacy Space: combating AMR’ (IDAPPS): a design-led collaboration and creative approach to health communication, specifically related to Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR). IDAPPS has enabled pharmacists in the UK and Rwanda to provide clear advice and information on the dangers of AMR to member of the public. Organisations including Public Health England, the Commonwealth Pharmacy Association (CPA) and the Rwandan Community Pharmacists’ Union (RCPU) have adopted design-led approaches to enable effective and relevant public health communication. The Rwandan ‘Beat Bad Microbes’ campaign was recognised with an Antibiotic Guardian commended award in 2019. Design companies involved in this research have partnered on projects moving beyond the initial AMR projects. Design Science collaborated with bio-medical scientists on ‘Milk Guard’, a project in India to help treat and reduce AMR in cows and buffalo. Members of IDAPPS in bio-science and information design stimulated a campaign at Reading for public participation in developing the instructional components of home-testing kits for Covid-19. Read more...

A reduction in healthcare-associated infections through influencing policy and healthcare practice

Research at Glasgow Caledonian University significantly improved infection prevention in healthcare. It led to changes in Scotland’s screening policy for resistant organisms, increasing hospital compliance and reducing MRSA infections by 17.1% annually. At the European level, their validation of infection survey methods resulted in 450,000 more healthcare-associated infections being identified across 28 countries, improving investment and policy decisions. Globally, the research underpinned WHO guidance on national infection control programmes, contributing to an increase from 41% to 63% in countries implementing such programmes between 2015 and 2018. Read more...

Interactive Learning Resources and Behavioural Training to Improve Young Children’s Knowledge of Microorganisms and Handwashing Skills Globally

Interdisciplinary research for the co-creation of ‘A Germ’s Journey’, a resource-based intervention comprising books, web games, videos, and posters. These resources provide information on how germs spread and how to prevent it with handwashing, in particular. Resources have been utilised globally across Africa, Asia, and Europe, with 3,540 books donated to schools, museum exhibits, community centres, and refugee camps to reach 145,432 people so far. 3,000 books and 340 e-books have been sold, and the GJ website has been used across 117 countries. Programming has led to improvement in children’s handwashing and reduced diarrhoea and vomiting episodes. These resources have been developed to reflect WHO guidelines on handwashing in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic raise awareness of disabilities and offer technological and therapeutic innovations to support those living with disabilities across a range of settings. Work informs public education, institutional policy, and practical interventions aimed at changing attitudes and improving social participation for people with disabilities. Many focused on enhancing educational provisions and outcomes for disabled individuals. Work in arts and performance plays a key role in promoting inclusive practices and fostering meaningful connection between disabled and non-disabled communities.
narrative:
Transforming the inclusion of people with intellectual disabilities in elite sports across the world.

Research at Canterbury Christ Church University led to global changes in elite sport by enabling the re-inclusion of athletes with intellectual disabilities (ID) in the Paralympics and establishing new classification systems used by the IPC and Virtus. These systems expanded opportunities for over 1,000 ID athletes and introduced a new competition class for more severely impaired athletes, including those with Down Syndrome. The work has also improved professional training, changed public attitudes, and helped unlock international investment, strengthening inclusive sport infrastructure across over 30 countries. Read more...

The PBS Academy: improving understanding and enhancing the delivery of Positive Behavioural Support (PBS)

Research at the University of Warwick has transformed the national delivery of Positive Behavioural Support (PBS) for people with intellectual disabilities, establishing the PBS Academy and a nationally adopted competence framework. These standards have guided government policy, NHS commissioning, and third-sector training, improving support for thousands of individuals and carers. Widely used by regulators, service providers, and families, the framework has influenced care practice across the UK and beyond, leading to improved quality of life, workforce training, and regulatory change in the sector. Read more...

The RIX Wiki; Multimedia advocacy for young people with learning disabilities

Researchers pioneered multi-media advocacy via “The RIX Wiki'' software tool, which directly addresses inequalities faced by people with Learning Disabilities. This tool enabled them to communicate their views, wishes, aspirations and preferences to ensure improvements in the services they receive. Read more...

description: Research in this topic has advanced the design, control and resilience of modern electricity systems, supporting a global shift toward low-carbon and decentralised energy. Innovations have enhanced the efficiency and reliability of power transmission and distribution—particularly in integrating offshore renewables and balancing AC/DC networks. Projects informed smart grid development, demand-side flexibility, and equitable access through minigrids in remote and underserved areas. New modelling and simulation tools have shaped energy infrastructure planning, improved overvoltage protection, and underpinned the UK’s electricity capacity market. Work has also driven international renewable deployment, reduced emissions, and enabled novel technologies for microgeneration, such as microbial fuel cells for off-grid sanitation and lighting.
narrative:
Informing decisions and debate on low-carbon electricity

Imperial College’s research shaped UK and EU energy policy by providing the economic modelling that underpinned the European Commission’s approval of State Aid for Hinkley Point C—enabling the UK’s largest low-carbon energy project. Their open-access wind modelling tool, Renewables Ninja, is used by global policymakers and institutions including the International Energy Agency. Through Drax Electric Insights, their analysis also informs public and media debate on Britain’s electricity system, influencing both national policy and public understanding of low-carbon transitions. Read more...

Driving Siemens Gamesa’s offshore wind turbines

Research from the University of Sheffield into permanent magnet direct-drive generator technology has been integrated into all 1,049 Siemens Gamesa offshore wind turbines operating globally, supporting 23% of global installed offshore wind capacity and generating £3.5bn in turnover. This collaboration enabled five successive turbine generations, boosting output from 6MW to 14MW and helping reduce the levelised cost of offshore wind energy from £157 to £39 per MWh. These advances directly contributed to the world’s first zero-subsidy offshore wind farm and helped position Siemens Gamesa as a global market leader. Read more...

Electricity system reliability assessment and capacity procurement

Research from the Maxwell Institute underpinned critical reforms in how Great Britain ensures electricity system reliability, directly informing the design and operation of the national Capacity Market. Their statistical and decision-analysis methods improved how wind variability, energy storage, and extreme scenarios are factored into capacity procurement decisions—guiding billions of pounds in investments while enhancing supply security. Their work also led to revised risk metrics that more accurately value battery storage, preventing overpayment and ensuring fairness in auctions. Internationally, their contributions shaped the IEEE 859 standard, a foundational tool for outage data reporting used across North America, influencing decisions that affect grid reliability for hundreds of millions of people. Read more...

Pee Power – microbial fuel cell electricity generation for safe sanitation

Pee Power®, developed at UWE Bristol, uses microbial fuel cell technology to convert urine into electricity, improving sanitation safety in areas without power. Installed in schools in Uganda and Kenya and in a South African settlement, it has enhanced nighttime toilet access for thousands. The technology has also influenced humanitarian planning, with Oxfam identifying it as a potential game changer for refugee camps. High-profile demonstrations at Glastonbury Festival raised public awareness, highlighting Pee Power’s potential for sustainable, off-grid sanitation in both emergency and everyday contexts. Read more...

description: Research in this topic has transformed organ donation and transplant systems, advanced kidney and liver preservation technologies, and improved treatments for various organ conditions. Work has informed national organ allocation strategies and public health campaigns, with particular impact on reducing inequalities in donor registration. Innovations have enhanced viability and utilisation of donor organs and improved survival outcomes among others in dialysis and nephrotic syndrome care. Genetic insights and precision therapies have shaped guidelines and enabled earlier, more effective interventions for adults and children worldwide.
narrative:
Transforming the care of children and adults with nephrotic syndrome throughout the world

University of Bristol research transformed diagnosis and treatment of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) by identifying its molecular and genetic causes. Their development of a gene panel and national patient registry enabled precision medicine approaches, reducing harmful treatments and improving transplant outcomes. Over 1,000 UK patients have benefited from genetic testing, saving the NHS an estimated £5–10 million annually. The work underpinned global clinical guidelines, supported patient well-being, and catalysed over £50 million in industry investment, including the £45M launch of gene therapy spin-out Purespring Therapeutics. Read more...

OrganOx: Organ preservation to improve liver transplantation

Oxford researchers developed OrganOx metra, the world’s first normothermic liver perfusion device, enabling longer and more effective liver preservation before transplantation. Their work led to a 50% reduction in discarded donor livers and improved transplant outcomes, including halved graft injury and increased availability of viable organs. Endorsed by NICE in 2019, the device is now routinely used in all UK liver transplant centres and in 12 other countries, supporting over 850 transplants. The Oxford spinout OrganOx Ltd has generated £7M in sales and attracted further investment, creating high-value jobs and international recognition. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic focus on contemporary and historical feminist initiatives for women’s rights and histories. Work informed gender-sensitive reforms in government, legislation, and global politics. ICSs address the protection of women’s rights and celebration of women’s historic and contemporary contributions at local, national and international levels. Work also promotes public education and engagement, fostering deeper understanding of both past and present struggles and achievements in the pursuit of gender equality.
narrative:
Implementing Gender Sensitive Reforms in Parliaments: creating a more diverse and inclusive UK Parliament

Research led to The Good Parliament Report in 2016, following a 6-month House of Commons secondment. With its 40+ recommendations, the Report has driven extensive and unprecedented institutional change including the adoption of new gender and diversity sensitive formal parliamentary rules and practices, including a permanent change to the House of Common’s Standing Orders regarding proxy voting. Read more...

Expert Women on Air: Achieving greater gender parity among experts appearing on leading UK radio and television news programmes

Journalism research into gender representation in the six flagship UK news programmes revealed that men experts outnumbered women experts 4.4:1 in 2013. The Expert Women survey research and subsequent campaign for better representation inspired broadcaster equity schemes and changed the faces and voices of British broadcasting by the late 2010s. Compared to 2014, twice as many women interviewees now appear on radio and TV flagship news broadcasts in the UK. Read more...

Advancing Global Gender Equality through Educational Partnerships

Research providing robust data enabling the creation of more gender-equitable, safe schools, with far-reaching effects on the safety and well-being of girls and boys in eight African countries. The research has influenced the release of long term funding of £800,000,000 for implementation projects. Read more...

Empowering Women through Radio in the Sahel

Through a mixed-methods approach, this research demonstrated how radio can improve women’s rights and empowerment. Dozens of radio stations in Niger have implemented research-based changes to their policies and practices. As a result, women listeners now have access to newly created listening associations with saving clubs, resulting in financial empowerment and education opportunities for themselves and their daughters. The success of this project has led to its expansion into Mali, and the methodology has most recently been applied to tackle the spread of COVID-19 related misinformation in Burkina Faso. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic used research-informed performance, theatre, and creative arts as tools for therapeutics, health and education. This included drawing on historical and philosophical approaches to mental wellbeing, performance in hospice settings, and somatic arts to aid in patient care and communication as well as supporting practitioner resilience and wellbeing. Work also raises awareness of societal and environmental issues and empowers marginalised voices through innovate forms of expression and creative collaboration. These approaches contribute to cultural understanding and inform policy related to health, wellbeing and social care for specific groups.
narrative:
Changing film screening practice to bring about wellbeing benefits for the over 65s, including those living with dementia, and professional/training benefits for their carers and cultural activities providers in the UK and Brazil

Creation and application of a downloadable ‘Cinema, Memory and Wellbeing’ (CMW) Toolkit for carers. This toolkit enabled the use of films with nursing home residents, day care centre users, GP practice visitors, and dementia ward patients in the UK and/or Brazil. It also furthered the running of age-/dementia-friendly cinema screenings and the use of film with participants of film clubs for the socially isolated (Merseyside and Manchester). Read more...

Changing the lives of people living with dementia (PWD) and their families through music therapy research

Research showed how music helps memory, reduces agitation, improves relationships, and improves synchrony for people living with dementia (PWD), their families and caregivers. This research resulted in the inclusion of music therapy in NICE guidelines for the first time. Consultancy work in care homes enhanced care for ~20,000 PWD since 2014. Benefits of the therapy are documented in the 2019 BBC TV documentary "Our Dementia Choir". Read more...

Applied Theatre for Children in Hospital

Over 4,000 children at Birmingham Children’s Hospital and Heartlands Paediatrics NHS Trusts have been reached through 1:1 bedside performances. Read more...

description: This topic centres on research and practice related to neurodevelopmental conditions, such as autism, ADHD, and cerebral palsy. Case studies explore themes such as diagnosis, therapies, and ongoing support; equitable access to services; inclusive education and workplace integration; and policy frameworks promoting patient and carer well-being. Broader considerations include cultural awareness, professional training, and health and social care systems for support of neurodivergent individuals across the lifespan.
narrative:
A motor learning approach to speech therapy for children with cerebral palsy underpinned UK guidance and international teaching practice

This research showed that intensive speech therapy, based on motor learning theory, led to significant increases in children’s intelligibility. This research informed UK NICE guidelines and therapeutic practice. Read more...

Advancing multimodal evidence-based treatment of ADHD worldwide

The ADHD research programme at the University of Southampton has generated the most rigorous body of evidence synthesis available worldwide on the treatment of ADHD. This research has informed international clinical guidelines, including those adopted by the American Academy of Paediatrics (67,000 members), European guidance for ADHD management during the pandemic, and the World Federation of ADHD's (2,000 members) guidelines. This research has also benefited patients (e.g., from ADHD Europe, including 28 organisations from 23 countries). It informed the development of a parent training strategy, the New Forest Parenting Programme (NFPP), that has been included in guidelines and recommendations both nationally and internationally. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic focus on research and development of advanced physics and chemistry technology with a strong emphasis on real-world application. Studies are broad bringing together enabling technologies (i.e. quantum systems, photonics, semiconductors, electromagnetic, chemical technologies) with application-driven sectors (i.e. maufacturing, analytics, space, catalysis, healthcare, electronics). There’s also a clear through-line of commercial and entrepreneurial focus, connecting early-stage R&D with scalable industry solutions via start-ups, investment, and technology transfer. The breadth of themes within the topic to reflect interdisciplinary integration and real-world impact of the studies.
narrative:
Using plasma technology to extend food shelf-life and for safe, powerful decontaminatior

The University of Glasgow’s research on plasma-generated ozone led to a novel, safe method of sterilising sealed packages, spun out into the companies Anacail and Glanadair. This technology extended the shelf-life of over 1 million fruit packages by ~50% and reduced food waste by over 30%. It was also adapted for powerful, chemical-free sterilisation of medical devices and contaminated drains, outperforming standard techniques. The innovation has created high-value jobs, influenced EU policy on ozone use, and offers a sustainable, non-toxic alternative to conventional decontamination methods. Read more...

Driving the industrial biotechnology revolution: cheaper and more sustainable chemical manufacturing through enzyme discovery, engineering and scale-up

The University of Manchester’s CoEBio3 has revolutionised sustainable chemical manufacturing by developing over 1,000 engineered enzymes now widely used in pharmaceutical and agrochemical production. These biocatalysts—commercialised via Prozomix Ltd—have enabled greener, more cost-effective synthesis processes. Through training programmes and the online tool RetroBioCat, CoEBio3 has transformed industrial practice at companies like GSK, AstraZeneca, and Bayer. A Massive Open Online Course has trained over 38,000 learners globally, while multilingual outreach has inspired hundreds of schoolchildren. CoEBio3 researchers have also shaped UK government policy through contributions to the national bioeconomy strategy. Read more...

Teledyne: Manufacture and development of microwave semiconductor devices by the Teledyne Semiconductor Technology Centre, an embedded industrial facility

The University of Nottingham’s semiconductor physics research has driven commercial innovation at Teledyne UK Ltd, underpinning over £5.5M in sales of microwave oscillator and receiver components fabricated in an embedded facility on campus. The Teledyne Semiconductor Technology Centre (TSTC), co-located within the university, uses Nottingham-grown III-V semiconductor wafers and modelling expertise to manufacture world-leading high-frequency devices used in defence and security. Nottingham’s research has also shaped Teledyne’s strategic roadmap, leading to new superlattice-based THz technologies and next-generation receiver protectors, reinforcing the UK’s capabilities in advanced microwave systems. Read more...

Supporting the creation of a UK Quantum Industrial Revolution

The University of Oxford has been pivotal in launching the UK’s quantum computing industry, with breakthroughs in ion traps, superconducting circuits, photonics, and quantum algorithms. Their research catalysed over 10 commercial collaborations and led to four spin-out companies—Oxford Ionics, Oxford Quantum Circuits, ORCA Computing, and Quantum Dice—employing over 40 people by 2020. These ventures attracted significant venture capital and industrial partnerships with global firms such as IBM, BAE Systems, and M Squared Lasers. Oxford’s work laid the technological and commercial foundation for the UK’s emerging quantum industrial ecosystem. Read more...

A UK Quantum Technology Industrial Ecosystem in Quantum Sensors for Gravity and Optical Clocks

The University of Birmingham catalysed the UK’s industrial ecosystem in quantum sensors and optical clocks, enabling over £120M of collaborative R&D projects and 17 patent applications. Their breakthroughs in compact, robust quantum technology directly influenced the UK MOD’s Defence Science and Technology Laboratory to reorient its strategy and commit its largest-ever academic investment. The university’s leadership sparked £25M in industrial R&D, with over 70 companies—including major multinationals—engaged in quantum commercialisation, securing the UK’s position in next-generation sensing and timing technologies. Read more...

Increasing commercialisation and public awareness of ultralow-temperature technologies.

Lancaster University’s ultralow-temperature research has driven commercial innovation and global public engagement in quantum technology. Collaborating with Oxford Instruments NanoScience, researchers co-developed a compact, cryogen-free refrigerator for quantum sensors, generating £1.69M in sales. Their award-winning public outreach, including a viral LEGO®-based science documentary with over 275 million in media reach, significantly raised awareness of cryogenics and quantum technologies worldwide. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic focus on official histories, commemoration practices and the role of historical memory in reconciliation around the second world war. Many worked to document and preserve and the experience of a range of groups, often in collaboration with survivors, local archives, and communities. Particular attention is on contested cultural histories and ‘forgotten’ voices of vulnerable or minority communities in World War II. Emphasis is placed on education and open archives to inform public and institutional understandings, fostering constructive engagement with complex and sensitive histories. This includes German, Russian and Holocaust narratives, and their commemoration and reconciliation for community wellbeing.
narrative:
Enhancing public understanding and interpretations of collective violence and its aftermath: Nazi and communist rule in Germany

Research in this case study explores how people become involved in collective violence under dictatorial conditions and the socio-cultural aftermath of this, particularly in relation to the Holocaust and German dictatorships. This research was shared through an online exhibition accessed by viewers in 71 countries, educational workshops, and extensive media coverage to deepen understanding of involvement in collective violence. This research reached around 3 million people in 2019-20 through print media alone, and inspired further exhibitions, educational efforts, publications, podcasts and public lectures developing discourse and public understanding of collective violence and its legacies. Read more...

Secret History of War Crimes trials: Lessons for ending impunity today

Research on the 1943-1948 United Nations War Crimes Commission raised awareness and understandings of the wartime response to Nazi crimes. The findings of this research led to the archival records of the Commission being made public for the first time, and access boosted through public partnerships with education networks and museums. This work informed legal education, practice, and is now used as a resource informing approaches in the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic are concerned with all aspects of teaching and education, shaping policy and approaches to foster better experiences and outcomes for both teachers and learners. They focus on enhancing teaching and education through training educators and developing research-based pedagogical tools and approaches to improve learning outcomes across all education levels, from early years to universities, vocational training and apprenticeships. Case studies shaped curriculum reform and the modernisation of teaching methods, often through integrating technology in the classroom. Emphasis is placed on equity and inclusivity, informing policies and interventions that promote access to education for diverse learners and that support lifelong learning.
narrative:
Changing practice in the early years of primary schooling: Teaching and Learning Playfully

A 20 year research program on the synergies between teaching, learning, and playing led to educational reform for all 4-6-year-old children in Northern Ireland (NI), affecting 720,000 children since 2015. Read more...

Reforming Initial Teacher Education in Wales

Research into the effectiveness of teacher training has led to reforms in the training of Welsh teachers, including a changed accreditation procedure, a revised inspection framework, and extensive investment in educational capacity. All teacher trainees in Wales at the time, about 2,700, and their subsequent students were affected by this. Read more...

Transforming professional teacher development in India

The TESS-India (Teacher Education through School-based Support in India) project provided a sustainable and scalable approach to pre-and in-service teacher education, emphasising inclusive, participatory, child-centred pedagogy. The program was used in 7 state governments in India and informed the approaches of 6 non-governmental organisations (in India, Ghana, and Uzbekistan).
