It has impacted the understanding and learning of over one million trainee teachers, teaching, and teacher educators. Read more...

The Pupil Premium Toolkit: Evidence for Impact in Education

The Pupil Premium Toolkit is a synthesis of research from 200 systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and quantitative studies and provides a resource for schools on improving outcomes for learners, particularly those from disadvantaged backgrounds. It guides the work of the Education Endowment Foundation (EEF) and its funding strategy for the £200 million being spent over 15 years to reduce inequalities in school outcomes in England. Read more...

Ketso: improving professional practice and participation by embedding research findings into a physical toolkit

Ketso is a toolkit developed to improve stakeholder participation, particularly among vulnerable and marginalised groups, in service design and delivery, ensuring that diverse perspectives are included in the process. It is used by multiple public and third sector organisations and has been expanded beyond planning to include healthcare (33 examples), community development (26 examples), education (29 examples), and business (11 examples). Since 2013, the number of organisations using Ketso has increased to 625 in total, with 2,220 toolkits supporting 42,500 workshop participants in a total of 77 countries. Ketso has enabled organisations to procure resources more effectively. In 2017, it helped communities enter a successful bid for £3,200,000 million National Lottery Heritage Funding by the Lancashire Wildlife Trust for the Carbon Landscape Project. The project resulted in over 1,000 volunteers making ecological enhancements to 335 hectares. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic support the teaching, preservation and revitalisation of languages to reclaim and promote heritage and cultural identities, and to broaden horizons in an increasingly globalised world. Many focused on safeguarding endangered languages and improving access to linguistic resources through digitisation, community collaboration, and public outreach. Work also focused on education and pedagogical approaches to reading and language, promoting foreign language learning and supporting multilingualism. Many trialled innovative approaches, new technologies, and developments in teacher training to enrich language education for teachers, learners, and public worldwide.
narrative:
An Early Start to Foreign Language Learning and Literacy

Early foreign language (FL) learning in schools is a global education phenomenon but many countries report problems with learner progression and motivation. These problems are due in part to curricula uninformed by empirical evidence, a lack of age-appropriate resources, and a lack of teacher expertise and pedagogic confidence. FL learning research undertaken at the University of Southampton by Professor Ros Mitchell and Dr Alison Porter has: (A) Informed policy and addressed national implementation challenges. Mitchell’s research informed the rationale and attainment targets of the new FL requirement in the Primary National Curriculum in England, introduced in September 2014. Porter and Mitchell have since engaged with education stakeholders to ensure its sustainability and effective implementation. (B) Improved classroom practice and school provision: Since 2017, Porter and Mitchell have worked with teachers locally, nationally and globally, successfully encouraging research-informed primary FL pedagogy in participant schools. (C) Co-created original FL resources: The teacher-researcher partnerships have led to the co-construction of innovative FL literacy resources inspired by Porter’s research findings. Read more...

Informing and improving grammar teaching in English schools and beyond: the free web-based Englicious platform

Englicious, a free online platform containing a library of original English language teaching resources, enables primary school teachers to teach grammar to the 2014 National Curriculum for England standard. Over 10,000 teachers signed up to Englicious in January 2021 to improve individual ability to teach English grammar in the National Curriculum. Englicious has also had global impact, providing English language resources for over 14,000 users in 227 countries. Read more...

Language for Resilience: A global programme of language learning for refugees and migrants

This research has created a global programme of language learning initiatives, ‘Language for Resilience’, supported by the British Council. These initiatives have been developed with partners across the Middle East, Sub-Saharan Africa, and Latin America. The principles of this research are used to design and support language teaching programmes which employ trauma-sensitive methods of language learning to build resilience in refugee settings. This has changed how governments, major funding organisations (e.g., the British Council), and NGO’s (e.g., Mercy Corps) approach teaching practices in conflict and post-conflict settings. For example, Mercy Corps in Iraq drew on the pre-existing cultural practices of language teachers and multilingual pedagogies to delivery identity-affirming language programmes to Arabic-speaking displaced people from the south of Iraq, Kurdish-speaking refugees from Syria, and Kurdish-speaking host community students from Kurdistan. The British Council invited researchers to write a FutureLearn Massive Open Online Course: Migrants and Refugees in Education: A Toolkit for Teachers, that reached 7,411 learners in over 130 countries in its first two runs. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic support a range of initiatives and policies improving the care, wellbeing and legal rights and protection of women, children and families. ICSs span diverse settings, informing childcare services, early childhood interventions, support for children in care and those with disabilities, and strategies to reduce poverty and inequalities. There is strong emphasis on amplifying the voices of children ,young people and adolescents to guide social interventions and policy reform. It also informs education for parents and practitioners, contributing to national and international politics on family care and parental rights. Research also addresses legal and practical support for victims of domestic abuse and sexual violence, shaping public awareness, legislation and institutional responses.
narrative:
Domestic Violence Perpetrator Programmes – Broadening understandings, influencing public policies, and changing practice

This research changed how Domestic Violence Perpetrator Programmes (DVPPs) are understood, designed, and implemented across the world -- particularly in the UK, USA, and Australia. In the UK, this contributed to perpetrator sections of the UK Government's ‘Ending Violence Against Women and Girls Strategy’ and to an increased focus on perpetrators in the Domestic Abuse Bill, effecting changes to DVPP programme delivery. Read more...

Domestic Abuse, Child Arrangements and the Family Courts

This research shaped the Domestic Abuse Bill 2020, including the ban on cross-examination of victims by their abusers in family court proceedings, and underpinned the UK Government Plan to improve family court protection for childre and victims of domestic abuse. Read more...

description: Research in this topic has strengthened democratic institutions and expanded opportunities for citizen engagement. Projects shaped legislation and practice on freedom of information, lobbying transparency, and judicial independence, while seeking ways to improve parliamentary practices in the four nations of the UK, the EU and globally. Research enhanced democratic accountability by supporting electoral participation, public petitions, and citizen assemblies. Digital tools and arts-based initiatives promoted active citizenship and civic inclusion, especially among underrepresented groups. Studies empowered grassroots movements, influenced constitutional reform, and deepened public trust in political processes through more transparent, participatory decision-making.
narrative:
Forging a revised constitutional relationship between Wales and the UK state through the Wales Act 2017

This research reshaped the constitutional and financial foundations of Welsh devolution. Cardiff University’s work guided key recommendations of the Silk Commission, leading to the Wales Act 2017 and a more stable ‘reserved powers’ model for Welsh governance. Researchers influenced revisions to the draft legislation, prompting the UK Government to pause and rewrite critical sections, and removing legal barriers that threatened devolved autonomy. Their fiscal analysis underpinned a new funding agreement that secured an extra £360 million for Wales (2018–2021), ensuring a fairer, needs-based settlement and laying the groundwork for sustainable tax devolution. Read more...

Democratic Innovations: Citizens’ Assemblies

After a successful pilot project, ‘Democracy Matters’ (DM), the research team generated a broader programme of research into the uses and challenges of Citizens' Assemblies. They were involved in the development and design of the Citizens’ Assembly on Social Care (CASC), the first ever Citizens’ Assembly commissioned by the UK Government. Research on input and recruitment processes was essential to achieving a diversity of political opinion in this first Assembly, giving MPs confidence in the process. The research team also helped develop the Citizen’s Assembly on Brexit (CAB), and the PI served as an important consultant in the development of Climate Assembly UK. The 2018 Innovation in Democracy Programme launched by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport enables Local Authorities (LAs) to apply for funding to run a Citizen’s Assembly on any topic. Over 70 LAs expressed interest in this funding. The DM pilot won the UK Political Studies Association’s 2016 Democratic Innovation of the Year prize. Read more...

The Politics of Judicial Independence

This research reshaped how judicial independence is protected in the UK’s evolving constitutional landscape.The researchers' work led to improved engagement between judges and politicians, persuading the Lord Chief Justice to provide annual reports to Parliament and encouraging select committees to invite judicial input without compromising independence. It prompted governance reforms to reduce undue influence in judicial appointments and informed a new model for judicial involvement in court administration in Northern Ireland. The research fostered cross-branch dialogue at the highest levels, strengthening both transparency and the constitutional balance between the judiciary and government. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic focus on research pertaining to pain management and palliative care, for example considering improvement of policy, of public and professional education, and of service provision for patients. Pain assessment and management are included for a range of patient groups, from chronic to long-term conditions and young patients. End-of-life care and ethics and decision-making for patients is also incorporated in the topic.
narrative:
Improving Adolescent Chronic Pain Management

University of Bath research has transformed adolescent chronic pain care worldwide by shifting clinical focus to psychological and family-based mechanisms, enabling more effective diagnosis, treatment, and service delivery. Its assessment tools (BAPQ and BAP-PIQ) are now standard in the UK, USA, Australia, and New Zealand, used in clinical pathways and national audit systems. This work underpins key UK and WHO guidelines, and has led to new care models that improve children’s quality of life and reduce unnecessary opioid use. Read more...

Reducing inequalities in palliative care for people with non-malignant disease

Hull’s research has transformed global palliative care for patients with non-cancer conditions by improving management of chronic breathlessness, particularly in heart and lung disease. This work led to the first regulatory licence for morphine to treat chronic breathlessness, influenced 14 national and international clinical guidelines, and increased palliative care access in the UK and abroad. Novel assessment tools and service models developed at Hull are helping to reduce inequities, enabling better triage, care planning, and end-of-life support for millions previously underserved. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic used novel design and design approaches to improve accessibility and inclusion for diverse and often vulnerable groups, with a particular focus on disabled communities. Research emphasised user-centred design, driving innovation and improving understanding of varied needs across multiple settings, including the creative arts, healthcare and urban environments. Case studies demonstrate how inclusive design can foster greater participation, equity and empowerment through thoughtful, responsive design approaches.
narrative:
Embedding user-centred design into the development of innovative medical devices

Researchers in art and design helped a leading surgical robot company with the product design and development for a new radio-guided laparoscopic surgery device used in cancer patient’s treatment. Read more...

Design meets disability: changing the relationship between disability and design in business, culture, practice and education

Research transformed how disability is framed in design-led businesses and culture. Alleles, founded in 2013, creates fashion-forward prosthetic covers, empowering thousands of disabled users worldwide to express their identity. The Valuable 500, launched in 2019 at the World Economic Forum, influences nearly 400 global CEOs to prioritize disability inclusion at leadership levels, reshaping corporate mindsets on disability and innovation. Culturally, exhibitions like Hands of X at the Cooper Hewitt Museum and V&A Dundee engaged over 240,000 visitors, challenging stereotypes and fostering disability pride. Disabled artists involved reported profound personal and artistic growth. In practice and education, Microsoft’s Inclusive Design initiative, inspired by the research, has trained over 50,000 employees and influenced products. The Inclusive Design Toolkit and documentary have reached 70+ universities and 5,000+ companies globally. This work reframes disability as a source of innovation, emphasizing design’s role in identity, accessibility, and inclusion. Read more...

description: This topic includes case studies focussed on healthcare access and equity. Subject matter includes equity of health service provision, access to healthcare, social care and health information, and to community and social enterprises for health and well-being. Additionally, healthcare systems, policy, funding, investment and spending all feature in this topic with a focus on improving access and equity of healthcare.
narrative:
Ensuring Right to Health and HIV prevention, treatment and care in African prisons

Research led by LJMU has driven global policy change to uphold the health rights of women in African prisons—especially in preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission. The work informed UNODC/WHO guidance adopted in 10 countries and supported increased funding for menstrual health in Malawi’s prisons. It has shaped regional UN strategies, promoted gender-sensitive prison healthcare, and empowered incarcerated women via transformative theatre. Through global partnerships, the research continues to influence prison health reform across sub-Saharan Africa and the MENA region, aligning with efforts to end the AIDS epidemic. Read more...

Informing fairer, more transparent, and cost-effective social care policy

LSE research has informed national and international efforts to make social care fairer, more transparent, and financially sustainable. Evidence from the Care Policy and Evaluation Centre led directly to England’s new national eligibility threshold for social care, contributed to long-term funding reform debates, and supported government plans for unpaid carers. Their models shaped UK Government and WHO responses to COVID-19 in care homes. Regionally, their real-time data analysis helped London councils manage the pandemic’s impact on care services and allocate emergency resources effectively. Read more...

Mobilising knowledge from lived experiences to reduce social and health inequalities

Lancaster research has helped bring the voices of disadvantaged communities into decisions affecting their health and wellbeing. By evaluating large-scale community empowerment initiatives in England and working with local and international partners, the team influenced public health engagement policy in England, Wales, and Spain, contributed to WHO strategies on health equity, and supported co-produced local action on housing, employment, and social isolation. Through initiatives like The COVID-19 Other Front Line Alliance, the team also enabled marginalised voices to inform pandemic recovery policies globally. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic focus on higher education and universities, their policies, education practices, institutional culture and student experiences. They address issues such as preventing abuse and harassment both online and offline. There is a strong emphasis on inclusivity and widening access for underrepresented groups, promoting equity and improved participation and outcomes. Research also informed curriculum development and pedagogical innovation, such as cross-cultural collaboration and personalised learning support. Research informs policy and practice that enhances the global role of universities and their place in shaping narratives around social mobility, migration, and freedom of information.
narrative:
Healthy Universities: A Whole System Approach to Improving Health, Wellbeing and Sustainability in Higher Education

Using the ‘healthy settings’ approach, involving a holistic and multi-disciplinary method that integrates action across risk factors, the researchers created a Healthy Universities Model trialled by University of Central Lancaster. The healthy universities model has since been adopted by 86 UK HEIs, informed the publication of a Charter for Health Promoting Universities, and the establishment of an International Steering Group chaired by Dooris (an ICS researcher). The International Steering Group has overseen the adoption of the Healthy Universities Model by over 400 universities across 35 countries. This research has also influenced implementations of similar health support models. For example, the University of Sydney introduced Self-Review Tool that facilitated identification of priority areas for action by its 70,000 students and 7,500 staff, and the University of British Columbia pioneered Canadian Action for Healthy Universities, a model informed by this research to prioritise ‘health in all policies’. Read more...

Decolonising the University Across Disciplines

This research has significantly influenced universities in the UK and worldwide, particularly in the Arts, Humanities, and Social Sciences. At SOAS, a formal Vision for Decolonising was adopted in 2017, backed by annual funding of £50,000-60,000 and supported by senior committees. SOAS’s work shaped national higher education policy and was highlighted by government ministers. Between 2019 and 2020, workshops and talks led by Dr. Sabaratnam reached over 1,000 staff and students across major UK universities, improving understanding of inequality and transforming curricula and pedagogy. Internationally, the research influenced universities in Sweden, South Africa, Nigeria, and beyond, connecting scholars and helping develop African-focused curricula. In Norway, student activism grew following Sabaratnam’s keynote, leading to national policy adoption. The work received broad media attention in the UK, sparking public debate and political commitments to address colonial legacies. Additionally, Sabaratnam’s consultancy in museums helped present more balanced global histories. Read more...

Improving social mobility through evidence-informed practice and policy in Higher Education

The Centre for Social Mobility has shaped national policy and practice to advance social mobility through research-driven partnerships with universities, regulators, and practitioners. It co-developed evaluation guidance and a Self-Assessment Tool now adopted by the Office for Students (OfS) to improve how universities assess the impact of £800m spent annually on widening access. This guidance has become a sector standard, enabling institutions to critically evaluate outreach work and align with national expectations. The Centre’s research has directly led to changes in admissions policies and support for disadvantaged students at Exeter, Birmingham, Warwick, and QMUL, including targeted pre-entry and transition support. It has also influenced national conversations and professional development through resources, conferences, and a bespoke Outreach Evaluation Hub. Additionally, its work on contextualised admissions, in collaboration with the Fair Education Alliance, informed OfS-endorsed guidance promoting equity in admissions processes. This contribution was recognised in the national Social Mobility Awards. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic focus on provisions for sporting environments and opportunities safe from abuse or discrimination and promote the potentials for sport to support wider social and political change. Work highlighted sport’s potential to enhance health, social change, wellbeing and community cohesion at all levels of participation, from grassroots to elite performance. Research advanced coaching strategies and athlete development and achievement, as well as underpinning initiatives to improve the health and wellbeing of athletes and general public alike at all levels of recreational and professional participation. Case studies supported ethical practices in sport, including anti-doping measures and enforcing duties of care held by coaches and institutions, and opened discourse around harmful competitive cultures.
narrative:
Advancing regulatory frameworks within Para sport: Ensuring sport is practiced in a manner that respects fair play and protects the health of athletes globally.

Members of the PHC at Loughborough University engaged in strategic, high profile capacity building in parasport. This resulted in the establishment of new sports at the Paralympics and Commonwealth Games, including Paracanoe at the 2020 Tokyo Paralympics and Wheelchair Basketball at the 2022 Commonwealth Games. Their research informed the implementation of healthcare and practical advice for organisers, coaches, and athletes. For example, the International Triathlon Union changed their regulations concerning wetsuit use in 2019 to account for added strain when wearing a wetsuit in high water temperatures. Read more...

Changing masculinities and enhancing safety in sport.

Collaboration to establish LGBT+ Research in Sport Network with Sport England. Textbooks by ICS researchers have been adopted in UK universities. Oxford Brookes, Wolverhampton, Durham, and Southampton Solent now feature teaching on inclusive masculinities on sport-related and gender/sexuality-related courses. Anderson was one of the founders of the Sport Collision Injury Collective (SCIS), a multidisciplinary collective of academics highlighting injuries sustained in youth sport participation. The group published an open letter ‘Preventing injuries in children playing school rugby’ which petitioned to make contact sports non-compulsory. The SCIS website has received 900,000,000 hits, and the letter itself was printed in major print and online newspapers (e.g., The Guardian, The Telegraph, The Independent). New regulations regarding tackling in children’s rugby and banning heading in football for children under 12 have resulted. Read more...

Defining the autonomy and specificity of sport in EU law: Shaping the adoption of globally applicable football agent regulations and the EU’s approach to nationality-based eligibility rules in European sport.

Most impact resulted from informing various EU commissions on regulating sports discrimination. Parrish’s work on nationality discrimination in sport has helped alter the EU’s approach to this issue whilst setting the boundaries for sports bodies on questions of nationality-based eligibility rules. Related commissions created change of nationality-based eligibility regulations of 26 Olympic sports across all 27 Member States of the EU, identifying that the widespread sporting practice of denying access to sporting competitions on account of nationality was in conflict with EU law regarding non-discrimination of nationality in economic matters. Judgements informed by this research protect athletes from discriminatory nationality measures adopted by both states and private bodies, such as sporting entities, under EU citizenship rights regardless of the level of economic activity (e.g., if the athlete is an amateur). Research underpinned an enquiry into nationality in European team sport launched by the European Commission in 2012, which challenged the legality of UEFA’s home-grown player rule (introduced in 2006/7). This challenge argued that the rule created indirect discrimination on the grounds of nationality. Read more...

Enhancing practice and improving outcomes of career transition support services in elite sport

Introduction of mental health and practice support for professional athletes transitioning into non-sporting roles at the end of their competitive careers. This work has increased issue awareness in professional organisations and led to constructive outcomes. The England Rugby Players Association has introduced 8 development managers and 1 transition manager to support over 800 current and 400 former players across premiership clubs. These reforms became particularly significant during the Covid-19 pandemic, when team sports were heavily impacted and early career transition became necessary. This research prompted campaigns by the English Institute of Sport (#More2Me) and the International Federation of Professional Footballers Associations (FIFPro) to use the finding to encourage athletes to recognise the benefits of planning for life after sport. #More2Me was publicly backed by both the Minister for Sport and the Chair of UK Sport. Third sector organisations, such as the UK-based charity Switch the Play Foundation, have improved sport career transition outcomes based on this research. Read more...

Football4Peace (F4P): Building bridges in divided, unequal and unjust societies

University of Brighton research led to the creation of Football4Peace (F4P) which uses values-based coaching methodology and delivery to promote peace-building in divided and post-conflict societies. Early work in Northern Ireland, Israel and South Africa has been extended in The Gambia, Colombia and South Korea. Related NGOs have been formed to support and further this programme and its methodologies, including the formation of UNESCO clubs based on the Brighton F4P initiatives. The model has been applied to several other sports, and since 2014 has benefitted 532 coaches/volunteers, 4,699 young people, residents and pupils in 87 local communities in 7 major cities. F4P training in Columbia in partnership with Fundación Buen Punto enabled FBP to obtain international recognition through an award given by Peace and Sport in Rhodes, 2018. Read more...

Safeguarding Children in Sport

Informing safeguarding guidelines through identifying and disseminating good practice with 32 organisations across Africa, Asia, Europe and North and South America. Development of an evidence-based, flexible framework within the International Safeguards that allows people to tailor implementation to the specific cultural characteristics of their settings. Implementation guides have been produced for 126 organisations working directly and indirectly with children. These resources have affected work with around 10,000,000 children. The Commonwealth Advisory Body on Sport has recommended the adoption of the Safeguards to Sports Ministers of the 53 Commonwealth nations. In 2018, 125 organisations working with over 35,000,000 children worldwide had signed up to work towards the Safeguards. Read more...

topic_name_long: Children: Care, Development, Education, Rights, Health
description: Research in this topic supported national and international efforts to improve outcomes for children by informing child-focused policies, care systems and educational practices. Case studies underpinned governmental and non-governmental services and policies which address childcare provision, safety, education, wellbeing and legal rights, especially for children in care, with disabilities, or facing poverty. Many worked to centre children’s voices and agency, improving their participation in shaping services that impact their lives. Work also informed safeguarding practices, including protection from abuse and emerging online threats.
narrative:
Preventing and mitigating child poverty and inequality

This research on child poverty led to changes in legislation and local authority policies in Scotland. As a direct result, approximately 120,000 children who are living in poverty across Scotland now have access to a £100 annual school clothing grant. In several local authorities, they also have access to free meals through breakfast clubs and during school holidays. Read more...

Designing and implementing scalable early childhood development interventions for low and middle-income countries

This research on Early Childhood Development interventions in low- and middle-income countries provided a scalable programme that has been implemented by governments in Latin America (Colombia, Peru, Ecuador) and the largest education NGO in India to improve development and cognition for an estimated 100,000+ children between 2014-2021. The Inter-American Development Bank and the World Health Organisation have endorsed the model in published guidance. Read more...

Building global practitioner and organisational mental health services for traumatised children

This research supported mental health support for >44,000 children traumatised by war, displacement and abuse, globally. Researchers trained 1,200 front-line professionals in 14 countries to recognise trauma in children, implement psychosocial interventions, reduce stigma, and improve mental health and education. The research informed global policies and practices, including UNESCO trauma-reduction policies (2018, 2019) and The World Health Organization’s 2018 care guidance for one million children seeking asylum in the EU. Read more...

Preventing child abuse globally through research-driven parenting programmes

Researchers used randomized control trials in South Africa, Philippines, and Thailand to develop and test the world’s first evidence-based, non-commercialised, parenting programmes. Programs were estimated to have reduced cases of severe abuse by 81,000. The programmes are endorsed by the World Health Organisation (WHO), UNICEF, USAID, CDC, and the Global Partnership to End Violence Against Children. Over 3,000 local staff have been trained as parenting supporters, with programmes translated into 22 languages. Read more...

Transforming Early Education Policy and Practice

Two major longitudinal studies demonstrated the long-term benefits of early education and identified effective pedagogy. This underpinned UK government initiatives such as the provision of free early childhood education to millions of 2-4 year olds, encouraging and supporting home learning, and professional development interventions based on quality scales developed by the researchers. Read more...

description: The case studies in this topic focus on research around tobacco and smoking, this includes health research into smoke and second-hand smoke impacts, as well as for alternatives (i.e. e-cigarettes). Studies also cover policy and law, marketing ethics and public messaging, generally focussed on reducing usage and the impacts of smoking on public health and wellbeing.
narrative:
Introduction of Minimum Excise Tax (MET) on Tobacco

University of Bath research exposed how tobacco companies undermined tax policy by keeping cheap cigarettes affordable—targeting young and low-income smokers. This evidence led directly to the UK Government’s 2017 introduction of a Minimum Excise Tax (MET), ensuring a price floor per cigarette. MET raised the price of the cheapest products, reduced sales, and curbed smoking—especially among 18–24-year-olds. The work also helped counter tobacco industry lobbying and informed international tax policy debates, with global uptake and citations in over 20 countries. Read more...

Successful elimination of second-hand smoke in Scottish prisons through a comprehensive smoking ban

University of Glasgow research directly informed and supported the 2018 ban on smoking in all 15 Scottish prisons, protecting the health of over 12,000 staff and people in custody. Working in partnership with the Scottish Prison Service, researchers provided the largest ever dataset on second-hand smoke (SHS) in prisons, revealing exposures comparable to living with a smoker. These findings drove policy adoption and shaped implementation, with SHS levels reduced by 80% immediately and 91% within six months. The policy has been proven highly cost-effective and is now a model for international prison health reform. Read more...

description: Research in this topic has shaped the technologies, policies, and practices that safeguard digital infrastructure, protect privacy, and combat cybercrime. Projects have informed national and international cybersecurity standards, strengthened industrial and governmental incident response, and guided inclusive, human-centred approaches to digital risk. Work has enabled secure encryption, privacy-preserving computation, and AI-driven cyber threat detection across sectors—from aviation to healthcare. Researchers have improved online safety for children, influenced data protection regulation, and supported digital resilience for small businesses.
narrative:
Securing Data During Computation: Turning Theory into Practice

University of Bristol research made secure data computation practical, enabling data to be processed without revealing its contents to the parties performing the compuation. Advances in Multi-Party Computation (MPC) and Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) led to tools like the SPDZ protocol and SCALE-MAMBA software, now used in sectors from finance to cybercrime prevention. This work underpins over USD100 million in investment and the creation of companies including Unbound Tech, Duality, and Enveil. It has influenced global tech standards (e.g. NIST, Common Criteria) and shaped policy debates at the US Congress and United Nations, helping to enable secure data-sharing in sensitive domains like national statistics, defence, and disaster response. Read more...

Intercepting cyber-attacks using bespoke predictive AI for Airbus

Cardiff University’s research into artificial intelligence and cyber risk has significantly strengthened global cyber defence capabilities, notably through a strategic collaboration with Airbus. Facing increasingly sophisticated cyber threats, Airbus integrated Cardiff’s bespoke AI malware detection system into its frontline operations, protecting sensitive data and infrastructure across its 134,000-strong European workforce. Unlike conventional tools, the Cardiff system predicts and blocks threats in real time, detecting ransomware with 98% accuracy in seconds and reducing file damage by over 80%. In parallel, Cardiff developed a goal-oriented risk modelling tool that assesses cascading impacts of cyber incidents, now used by Airbus and its clients—including national infrastructure operators—to manage operational vulnerabilities. This partnership led to the creation of the Airbus Cyber Innovation Hub and an £8 million co-investment in the Cyber Lab in Wales. The Welsh Government cited this collaboration as central to its 2020 International Strategy, positioning Wales as a leader in cybersecurity innovation. Read more...

Protecting Employees, Children and Sensitive Data using Innovative Approaches to Cyber Security

Research at Edinburgh Napier University has led to major advances in cyber security and digital forensics, resulting in the creation of two successful spinout companies. One, ZoneFox, developed an AI-based insider threat detection system using an innovative "digital DNA" approach to track malicious activity on computer systems. This technology was adopted by the Scottish Government to protect 15,000 endpoints and was later acquired by global cybersecurity firm Fortinet for £28 million. The second company, Cyan Forensics, created breakthrough tools that enable law enforcement to detect illegal digital content—such as child abuse material—on devices up to 100 times faster than previous methods. Their technology is now in use across UK police forces and international agencies, supporting investigations into child protection and counter-terrorism. These innovations have significantly enhanced digital threat detection, strengthened national cyber defence capabilities, and accelerated justice in sensitive criminal cases. Read more...

Cryptographic Analysis of RC4 and Improvement of Transport Layer Security: Enhancing the Security of the Global Digital Infrastructure

Cryptographic research led by Royal Holloway revealed major vulnerabilities in the RC4 encryption algorithm used in the widely deployed Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol. At the time, RC4 secured about 50% of all TLS traffic—including sensitive data exchanged in web browsing, e-commerce, and banking. The work demonstrated that RC4 biases allowed attackers to recover plaintext from encrypted communications, prompting global action. Within three years, major browser vendors (Apple, Google, Microsoft, Mozilla) and service providers eliminated RC4 support, and usage dropped below 1% by 2018. The findings directly shaped global standards, accelerated adoption of stronger encryption (TLS 1.2 and 1.3), and improved the security of digital infrastructure worldwide—benefiting billions of users and protecting global e-commerce and communications systems from systemic cryptographic flaws. Read more...

description: This portfolio of research addresses neurodegenerative and genetic diseases, and particularly focuses on therapeutic development and clinical management. The research encompasses treatments and therapies, including drug development, diagnostic services, and improvements to care services, clinical guidelines and policies. It also considers holistic patient care, incorporating case studies on patient and family support for improved quality of life.
narrative:
Improving quality of life for patients with Parkinson’s disease

Research led by the University of Birmingham has significantly improved the treatment and quality of life for people with Parkinson’s disease (PD) by shaping national and international clinical guidelines and changing frontline care practices. Large clinical trials demonstrated that initiating treatment with levodopa, rather than more expensive alternatives, offers better long-term outcomes and fewer side effects. The findings also established the effectiveness of deep brain stimulation (DBS) in advanced PD and showed limited benefit of physiotherapy and occupational therapy in early disease. These insights directly influenced the UK’s 2017 NICE guidelines and Canada's 2019 national guidance, contributing to a marked rise in the use of levodopa and DBS and leading to substantial NHS cost savings—estimated at £1.8 million annually—while improving patient mobility, independence, and quality of life. Read more...

Transforming the landscape of drug development with life-changing RNAi-based drugs

The University of East Anglia’s foundational research on RNA interference (RNAi) has revolutionized the development of drugs targeting genetic diseases once deemed untreatable. Building on the discovery of small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), the research enabled the creation of four first-in-class RNAi-based therapeutics: ONPATTRO®, GIVLAARI®, OXLUMO™, and LEQVIO®. These drugs have provided transformative clinical benefits for over 1,300 patients with conditions such as hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis and acute hepatic porphyria. The RNAi technology, licensed to Alnylam Pharmaceuticals, generated over £10 million in royalties and underpinned a rapidly growing therapeutics market, valued at over USD 1 billion by 2018. This research not only improved health outcomes globally but also reshaped drug development by enabling precision gene silencing to treat previously intractable diseases. Read more...

Advancing treatments for lysosomal storage disorders

University of Manchester researchers led pioneering work developing treatments for lysosomal storage diseases (LSDs), rare, life-limiting childhood conditions. Their research was central to the development and licensing of two enzyme replacement therapies: Sebelipase Alfa for lysosomal acid lipase deficiency and Elosulfase Alfa for Morquio A syndrome. These therapies are now approved worldwide and have benefitted over 1,000 patients globally, including more than 90 in England. In parallel, their gene therapy research contributed to the founding of Orchard Therapeutics, a major gene therapy company that has grown from 33 to over 250 employees and secured $33 million in early-stage investment. These breakthroughs have extended and improved the lives of affected children and built commercial capacity for rare disease therapeutics. Read more...

Development and validation of the first treatments for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy and Spinal Muscular Atrophy

Research at University College London (UCL) has led to the development and validation of the first effective treatments for two devastating childhood neuromuscular disorders: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) and Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA). UCL scientists pioneered the use of antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) to restore expression of key proteins missing due to genetic mutations, directly enabling the approval of Exondys 51 and Vyondys 53 for DMD, and Spinraza for SMA. These therapies now benefit thousands of patients worldwide, significantly prolonging life and improving motor function. UCL also played a key role in securing access to Spinraza through the NHS and in training healthcare professionals to deliver it effectively. The research has generated over $5.5 billion in drug sales, reflecting substantial economic and clinical impact. Read more...

Changing mental health care to improve wellbeing in people with cystic fibrosis and their caregivers

Research on the mental health of people with cystic fibrosis and their caregivers has created new jobs and guidelines for provision of mental health care and support. This research also contributed to the founding of US and European Mental Health Working Groups and $20,000,000 committed to fund 138 mental health coordinators. New guidelines for mental health professionals by the Mental Health Advisory Committee resulted in 25,000 patients and carers entering screening programmes, 10,000 individuals bring referred for treatments, and 1,000 people being urgently referred for suicidal ideation by 2019. The PI received the Richard and Carolyn Mattingly Award for Leadership in Mental Health Care in the first year the award was open to researchers and clinicians outside the US. Read more...

description: Research in this topic has advanced the use of biometric data for security, identity verification, health, and justice. Projects enabled reliable speech and facial recognition, forensic voice and DNA analysis, and the creation of realistic synthetic speech and animation. Innovations have supported refugee identification, border control, and forensic investigations, while also transforming accessibility and communication for people with speech impairments. Work shaped public and commercial use of biometric technologies, influenced policing practice, and guided policy on ethical and algorithmic governance of biometric systems.
narrative:
Personalised speech synthesis improves quality of life, changes health legislation, and leads to new commercial products

Research in personalised speech synthesis at the University of Edinburgh has significantly enhanced the lives of individuals who have lost their voice due to conditions like motor neuron disease, enabling them to communicate using synthetic voices that retain their unique vocal identity. This work led to the creation of SpeakUnique Ltd, a spin-out company providing personalised voices globally, supported by major health charities and the NHS. It also influenced Scottish health legislation, mandating access to communication support. The research has further powered commercial innovations, supporting product development at ObEN and Papercup, which use synthetic voice technology in digital avatars, patient care, and multilingual media content. Read more...

Iris recognition technology transforms the speed and security of refugee aid distribution, and access to critical benefits and services

Iris recognition algorithms developed through research at the University of Cambridge have become the global standard for biometric identification systems, enabling rapid and highly accurate identity verification. Since 2013, over 800 million additional individuals have been enrolled using these systems, which have significantly improved the efficiency, fairness, and security of aid distribution, especially in refugee settings. In Jordan and Uganda, the technology supports World Food Programme and UNHCR operations, streamlining food assistance and reducing fraud. In India, it underpins the Aadhaar biometric ID system, facilitating access to benefits and services for over a billion people, including those previously lacking official identification. Read more...

EvoFIT Facial Composites: Helping police identify serious criminal suspects

A new system of software and procedures helps police identify suspects of serious crimes, such as rape and assault, with identification rates of around 60 to 70% compared to 5% for traditional systems. During the REF period, it has been used by 26 police forces in 11 countries for over 2,500 investigations, assisting in the identification and arrest of an estimated 1,500 serious offenders. Read more...

Developing character animation techniques to improve production practice in the animation sector and create economic impact on Humain Ltd.

Research to improve techniques for character animation for film and video games reduced the time needed to create a facial rig from several weeks to several minutes. Developed techniques were used by private sector firm humane ltd and were used to attract over 1,000,000 GBP in investment including contracts with HBO and Microsoft. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic informed public health policy, physical activity guidelines and education initiatives, supporting long-term behaviour change and improved population health. They promoted physical activity in the general population through the creation of supportive, inclusive environments and improved health education, underpinning efforts to increase participation among underrepresented groups, including women, children and disable individuals. Research also aided the integration of physical activity into healthcare strategies for treatment and prevention, including physiotherapy and post-surgical care to improve patient outcomes, and promoting regular movement to lower the risk of sedentary-lifestyle-related diseases.
narrative:
Placing Physical Activity at the Heart of the NHS: Co-locating Healthcare and Physical Activity Services within Bespoke Facilities in Economically Disadvantaged Communities

Research on physical activity led to a £10 million Department of Health and Social Care grant, supporting three NCSEM sites in Sheffield. Located in underserved areas, these centres co-locate NHS services with leisure facilities, enabling over 100,000 NHS appointments annually, including 60,000 for musculoskeletal care. The model improves access, reduces anxiety, and embeds care in supportive, activity-focused settings. Referrals now come from both secondary and community care, streamlining treatment. Over 150 NHS staff report that the environment encourages patient engagement and fosters collaboration, such as a chronic pain pathway combining physiotherapy and mental health services. Staff also benefit from better wellbeing and a stronger sense of community. The centres have seen major growth in use, boosting jobs, business, and investment in inclusive facilities. The model has shaped policy locally, nationally, and internationally. During COVID-19, the centres resumed face-to-face care early and supported national physical activity efforts, proving both resilient and sustainable. Read more...

LifeLab: increasing health literacy and inspiring positive health-related lifestyle and behaviour choices among teenagers.

LifeLab is a hospital-based education programme that has reached over 11,500 students and 340 teachers across 66 Wessex schools. Designed to improve health literacy and science engagement among teenagers, it combines classroom lessons, teacher training, and hands-on experiences in a clinical research setting. Evaluations show sustained improvements in students’ understanding of how lifestyle affects long-term health and increased motivation to adopt healthier behaviours. Students make health pledges, supported by teachers and a bespoke behaviour-change app. LifeLab has influenced career aspirations, with students reporting greater interest in health and science. It is embedded in local public health strategies, recognised by councils, endorsed by the Royal Society for Public Health, and cited in parliamentary debates. During COVID-19, the programme adapted to support national testing efforts through a DHSC-funded science-for-health-literacy curriculum. LifeLab’s model has been adopted internationally and continues to shape public health and education policy. Read more...

description: Research in this topic has shaped global efforts to prevent, resolve, and recover from violent conflict. Case studies supported peace and reconciliation efforts in regions such as Afghanistan, Syria, and Colombia, informed international diplomacy and post-conflict reconstruction, and guided UK policy towards conflict as well as UN peacekeeping strategies. Projects promoted inclusive peace processes, advancing new global norms and laws to strengthen women’s participation and civil society leadership. Research contributed to transitional justice and reconciliation efforts—from documenting genocide in Rwanda and Indonesia to shaping school curricula and community healing. Partnerships with governments, NGOs, and international agencies are a recurring aspect of research impact in this domain. Researchers also influenced terror prevention and counter-radicalization efforts in the UK. Statistical work improved conflict prediction through data science and created more solid evidence bases for the analysis of violent conflict. Work ranged from high-level political advice for peace processes to very direct practical efforts such as demining post-war landscapes.
narrative:
Case Study 1: Constitution-Making as a Tool for Ending Conflict and Supporting Peace Processes

This research mapping the connections between peace processes and constitution-making informed more effective peace processes around the world. This research supported peace processes (2013-2018) to end conflict between the Ethiopian Government and the Ogaden National Literation Front (ONLF) by supporting the ONLF to represent the international self-determination law and the Ethiopian constitution as linked rather than in opposition. The research was also used by both the Colombian Government and Revolutionary Armed Forces of Columbia (FARC) to reach a peace agreement. The research was used for sub-state constitution drafting in meetings of Ethnic Armed Organisations (EAOs) during Myanmar’s complex transition from authoritarian to democratic state. Read more...

Countdown to Annihilation: Shifting the global discourse on the genocide of the Rohingya

The International State Crime Initiative’s (ISCI) research influenced offices of the UN which had initially resisted any ‘genocide determination’ to recognise the persecution of the Rohingya as ‘genocide’. The researchers briefed and worked closely with the UN Fact Finding Missions (FFM) on Myanmar in 2018, and the ISCI report is cited in the FFM recommendation of ‘genocide’ recognition. The ISCI advised The Gambia’s legal team in The Gambia’s Genocide case against Myanmar before the International Court of Justice. NGOs, such as the Burmese Rohingya Organisation UK, have testified that the ISCI’s work in supporting the recognition of ‘genocide’ status has empowered them to speak out on behalf of the effected minority groups to raise awareness. The ICSI worked with global media to encourage the use of the terminology of ‘genocide’ in reporting on atrocities against the Rohingya. They briefed journalists and organisations, leading to widespread change to terminology by media organisations including CNN, Nikkei Asian Review, LA Times, and TIME. Sky News Television, who won a BAFTA Award for their Rohingya coverage, cited the fundamental importance of the ISCI research input. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic focus on the production, exhibition, and curation of film and television as a means of preserving heritage, shaping public understanding, and informing societal and political discourse. Case studies celebrate the history and culture of film and cinema, examining its role in commemoration, representation, and reclaiming marginalised or ‘hidden’ histories. A number of studies focus on improving access to film and television archives, enhancing curatorial practices to encourage engagement and preservation. Research also highlights the potential of film for reframing both past and future narratives, foster cross-cultural engagement and inclusive storytelling.
narrative:
Transforming the Accessibility and Discoverability of Millions of Archival Television Programmes

Much of recent historical heritage is stored in television programs. This project built databases of 2,500,000 TV content items. Almost all UK HEIs subscribe to the database, and use content from news and documentaries to sitcoms and reality shows, to enhance teaching. In total there are about 1,700,000 programme streams per year. Read more...

Beyond Fact or Fiction: enhancing documentary discussions

Collaboration between researchers and the Edinburgh International Film Festival (EIFF) enriched the cultural conversation about documentary film and media. A public discussion (a ‘DocSalon’) on the subject of documentary in the age of fake news was held at the EIFF in 2017. This allowed public exchange between the audience and documentary professionals, including festival programmers, filmmakers, and commissioning editors. The EIFF adopted the DocSalon as a permanent annual feature. It has now taken place three times as of 2020 and sold out immediately. The DocSalon has been adopted by other film festivals, such as the Documentary International Human Rights Festival (Glasgow). The research highlighting the links between artists’ film practice and documentary production has inspired the creation of documentary art installations produced in Vietnam and exhibited in Scotland, Hong Kong, Switzerland, and The Netherlands. Read more...

description: Research in this topic encompasses epidemiology and COVID-19. Case studies span epidemiology from detection, characterisation, monitoring and surveillance of disease, to modelling and public health protection strategies including policy development. Furthermore, studies into specifically COVID-19 are included in this topic, covering areas such as diagnosis, transmission, intervention and treatments, as well as risk management, response, and policy.
narrative:
Understanding disease spillover from wildlife to improve public health outcomes in a changing world

Research from UCL and the Institute of Zoology significantly advanced global understanding of the ecological and socio-economic drivers of zoonotic disease spill-over. This work shaped international research and policy priorities by identifying emerging disease hotspots and promoting the ‘One Health’ approach. It guided over $1.5 billion in USAID investments (e.g. PREDICT), influenced UK and global research agendas (e.g. DFID ZELS, IPBES, Trinity Challenge, EU PREZODE), and informed responses to Ebola and COVID-19. Findings supported the UN’s 2020 pandemic prevention efforts and contributed to UK government planning and communications. Public understanding was also enhanced through widespread media engagement and contributions to major documentaries and briefings. Read more...

Shaping national policy to reduce the rate of COVID-19 transmission in care homes

Research by UCL’s Institute of Health Informatics rapidly influenced UK national policy to reduce COVID-19 transmission in care homes. Drawing on pre-existing expertise and access to large-scale care home datasets, UCL researchers led key studies during the first wave, identifying critical factors driving infection such as low staffing ratios, use of agency staff, and lack of sick pay. Their findings informed government decisions to prioritise staff testing, limit cross-site work, and implement the £600m Infection Control Fund. The research underpinned the national weekly testing strategy for care home staff, supported real-time surveillance through an interactive dashboard used across government, and shaped national vaccination prioritisation for care home residents and staff. Read more...

Demographic and Sociological interventions during COVID-19

LCDS’s research influenced national and international policies during the COVID-19 pandemic. These findings were extensively cited as an underpinning for the decision to allow people living alone to form a ‘support bubble’ with one other household. The dissemination of this research also informed social bubble implementation around the world by organisations such as the European Centre for Disease Prevention. The initial study on the demographics of COVID-19 mortality rates in Italy, England and Wales gained attention from policy-makers and the media, shaping public understanding. Newspapers covering the research findings included The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, News18 India, II Post, The Sydney Morning Herald, National Geographic España and The Economist. It was also circulated through the Dear Pandemic initiative, with Facebook posts reaching 1,022,226 viewers from August-September 2020. Read more...

description: Research in this topic has advanced global efforts to protect biodiversity, manage ecosystems sustainably, and align conservation with social justice. Projects informed international frameworks and national policies, guiding the design of biodiversity indicators, invasive species management, and carbon offset strategies. Work amplified Indigenous knowledge, strengthened protected area governance, and developed community-based and participatory conservation models. Studies shaped responses to climate change impacts on ecosystems, enhanced restoration and land-use practices, and improved the integration of conservation with rural livelihoods, resource use, and environmental justice. Research has supported better decision-making tools, novel monitoring technologies, and sustainable practices across forests, wetlands, rangelands, and peatlands globally.
narrative:
Improving sustainable oil palm

Research at the University of York has significantly influenced sustainable oil palm policies through evidence demonstrating the ecological value of forest patches within plantations. This work informed the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil (RSPO)’s High Conservation Value (HCV) and High Carbon Stocks Approach (HCSA) standards, leading to the protection of approximately 790,000 hectares of tropical forest and avoiding around 1.4 million tonnes of CO₂ emissions annually. York’s findings on patch size, biodiversity, carbon storage, and landscape connectivity shaped RSPO’s certification requirements and smallholder guidelines, contributing to more effective deforestation-free commitments and improved habitat protection for numerous threatened species across tropical regions. Read more...

Pheromone Traps: providing new Tools across Europe for the Prevention of Spread of Pine Wood Nematode, an Invasive Disease of Pine Forests

Research at the University of Greenwich led to the development of a pheromone-based trapping system that has transformed EU policy and practice for controlling the pine wood nematode (PWN), a major invasive threat to pine forests. By identifying the pheromone compound “monochamol” used by the beetle vector Monochamus galloprovincialis, the team enabled early detection and population suppression through baited traps. These tools informed EU regulations, reducing costly clear-felling and surveillance zones while improving eradication success rates in countries like Spain and Portugal. The traps have been widely adopted across Europe and internationally, with at least seven SMEs—including Spanish company SEDQ—benefiting economically from commercialising the patented technology, generating over €1.5 million in sales and enhancing forest biosecurity across the continent. Read more...

Protecting tropical peatlands and their ecosystem services

Research at Liverpool John Moores University has significantly influenced international efforts to protect tropical peatlands—vital carbon sinks threatened by agricultural expansion. Through the TROCARI consortium, the research generated field-based data that doubled previous UN IPCC greenhouse gas emission factors for peatland conversion and fire, contributing to global emissions inventories (IPCC, NCAR, GFED). These findings informed key policy documents, including the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil (RSPO) guidelines, which now require subsidence monitoring and promote the eventual phase-out of oil palm cultivation on peat. The work directly supported the protection of over 1,000 hectares of Malaysian peat swamp forest, preserving an estimated five million tonnes of carbon, and influenced the management of an 81,000-hectare forest reserve. The research has been cited in Indonesian restoration policy and featured in UK-Southeast Asia climate diplomacy, contributing to evidence-based decision-making on land use and emissions reduction. Read more...

Biodiversity Indicators to inform international policy

Research at the Institute of Zoology and University College London led to the creation and refinement of global biodiversity indicators—specifically, the Living Planet Index, Red List Index, and Biodiversity Intactness Index—which have become cornerstone tools for tracking biodiversity change worldwide. These metrics are now embedded in international policy frameworks and are used by major organisations including the UN Convention on Biological Diversity, IPBES, and the IUCN to monitor progress toward global biodiversity targets. They have shaped global reports such as the UN’s Global Biodiversity Outlook and WWF’s Living Planet Report, informed UK and Canadian policy, and underpinned biodiversity assessments across diverse ecosystems, from the Arctic to Australia. The indicators have also driven new species-level conservation actions, helped guide climate-related extinction risk assessments, and catalysed political responses, such as UK parliamentary debates on biodiversity. This work has fundamentally changed how biodiversity is measured, reported, and acted upon at global, regional, and national levels. Read more...

Amplifying Indigenous knowledge within environmental management and governance in South America

Research at Royal Holloway has empowered Indigenous communities in South America to use participatory video as a means of documenting and sharing their environmental knowledge, strengthening their role in environmental management and governance. This work has built capacity among Indigenous groups in Guyana and Venezuela, enabling them to articulate how their knowledge systems contribute to biodiversity conservation and climate resilience. It also transformed how NGOs and government agencies engage with Indigenous communities—shifting practices towards more inclusive and respectful collaborations. At policy levels, the research helped influence new frameworks such as Guyana’s Traditional Knowledge National Action Plan and informed fire management strategies in Venezuela, where ancestral fire knowledge is now formally recognised. Through intercultural dialogue, training, and advocacy, the research has amplified Indigenous voices in environmental policy, challenged knowledge hierarchies, and supported more equitable, sustainable governance of natural resources. Read more...

description: Research in this topic has advanced the decarbonisation of transport through innovations in electric mobility, hydrogen systems, and low-emission propulsion technologies. Projects shaped the development of electric vehicles and batteries, supported the use of alternative fuels, and informed industrial design and strategy. Researchers enabled reductions in carbon and resource intensity by improving motor efficiency, fuel systems, and materials. Work also supported the rollout of hydrogen infrastructure and smart energy integration, influencing national transport and energy policy. Further contributions improved freight logistics and vehicle control systems, supporting a broader transition to sustainable and low-carbon mobility.
narrative:
National and international strategy development and implementation of hydrogen systems for low emission transport and industry

Research at the University of South Wales has played a central role in advancing hydrogen as a viable low-emission energy source for transport and industry. By pioneering cost-effective and renewable hydrogen production—particularly through PEM electrolysis—the work directly enabled commercial deployment by ITM Power and helped scale global electrolytic hydrogen production more than tenfold between 2010 and 2020. The research has shaped UK and Welsh hydrogen policy, informed national strategies via the UK Hydrogen Advisory Council, and influenced industrial decarbonisation plans through the South Wales Industrial Cluster. Internationally, it impacted Chinese energy infrastructure by integrating hydrogen into grid-balancing and transport systems. The work has also fostered wide adoption of hydrogen refuelling technologies and supported decarbonisation in hard-to-abate sectors like steelmaking, helping drive a strategic transition to a hydrogen-based low-carbon economy. Read more...

Transitioning to the 'new normal' of electric vehicles

Research at Oxford Brookes University has played a key role in accelerating the transition to electric vehicles by addressing both the technological and behavioural challenges of adoption. Through collaboration with industry, particularly BMW, and public stakeholders, the work influenced the design and development of the BMW i3 and MINI Electric, informing battery management, cabin design, charging behaviour, and consumer uptake strategies. It also shaped UK policy on electric mobility and infrastructure planning by providing critical insights into driver psychology, energy use, and life cycle emissions. This research has supported the commercial success of electric vehicles, improved public infrastructure, and contributed to policy initiatives aimed at decarbonising transport. Read more...

Reducing the requirement for rare earth metals in high performance magnets for Hybrid Cars

Research on magnetic materials has significantly advanced the sustainability and efficiency of hybrid electric vehicles by reducing reliance on scarce and environmentally damaging rare earth elements. Collaborative work with industrial partners led to the development of magnets requiring less neodymium, dysprosium, and terbium, which have since been integrated into approximately 6.5 million hybrid vehicles. This innovation has cut rare earth metal usage by an estimated 450 tonnes, reduced CO₂ emissions by 11 million tonnes globally since 2016, and contributed to $108 million in production savings. The improved materials also enhanced motor efficiency and durability, yielding benefits for manufacturers, consumers, and the environment alike. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic shaped more effective strategies for self-harm and suicide prevention through improvements in identifying and safeguarding vulnerable individuals in a range of contexts. Case studies inform targeted interventions strategies through improved understanding and regulation of social media and access to harmful substances. Work supported vulnerable individuals through direct care, clinician and community training, and policy reform across sectors including healthcare, the military and prisons. Research also played a key role in shaping public understanding and governmental and institutional practices to reduce stigma and improve mental health outcomes.
narrative:
Preventing Railway Suicide

59% of Transport for London (TfL) staff have received suicide prevention training at date of ICS authorship. Has resulted in an unprecedented drop in suicide of a third in two years (the first two-year consecutive drop for almost 20 years, despite a rise in UK suicide rate by all methods). The PI of the project received a ‘Lifesaver Award’ by TfL in 2019. A team led by the PI received recognition as a ‘Nation’s Lifesaver’ for research carried out between 2018-2020 (‘the top 100 individuals or groups based in universities across the country whose work is saving lives and making a life-changing difference to our health and wellbeing’). The award-winning Small Talk Saves Lives media campaign launched in November 2017 was developed by the Samaritans and RSSG with direct and ongoing input from the research team, based on their findings that suicidal thoughts at railways are often temporary. Extensive media coverage created 158 million opportunities for people to see or hear the campaign. This has inspired similar campaigns in the Netherlands (where railway suicides reduced by 10% in 2019), Germany, and Japan. It also inspired the Thames Water Safety Forum to create a new Drowning Prevention Strategy. Read more...

The development and evaluation of a self-help app (BlueIce) to prevent adolescent self-harm

Research at the University of Bath created the first self-harm prevention app designed for high-risk young people (ages 12-17) who self-harm. The BlueIce app is endorsed on the NHS app library and is prescribed by 18 Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services across the UK. It was used by 2,520 young people at time of ICS authorship. 73 percent of users report reduced self-harm, equivalent to a reduction of 10 episodes per user over a 12-week period. Improvements in the trial sample alone saved the NHS an estimated £69,923. National roll-out would save the NHS an estimated £1,700,00 per year. Read more...

description: The case studies in this topic encompass the optimisation of the medication lifecycle, from development of drug dosing strategies, to prescribing frameworks and policy, and provision to patients. Studies may consider ares of benefit-risk ratios, population diversity, reduction of prescribing errors, as well as access and adherence to treatments, and service provision to particular patient groups.
narrative:
Improving medicines adherence in chronic illness

The outcome of the New Medicine Service (NMS) review, led by University of Nottingham researchers, underpinned the decision by NHS England to adopt the service delivered by community pharmacists. Between September 2014 and September 2020, over 5,348,000 NMS consultations have been delivered in England to patients starting a new medicine for a chronic condition. Increased medicine adherence afforded by NMS has provided £558,000,000 long-term cost savings to the NHS and 213,952 quality adjusted life years (QALYs) gained. The study’s success and impact within England influenced equivalent services introduced internationally, therefore benefitting patients’ health in Europe and Australia. Read more...

A Single-Drop Blood Test to Identify Patient Nonadherence to Cardiovascular Medication, Change Care Delivery and Optimise Treatment Plans

De Montfort University developed a world-first single-drop blood test to objectively detect nonadherence to cardiovascular medication, transforming care for hundreds of patients in Iraq and Kenya. The test enabled personalised treatment adjustments, improved blood pressure control, reduced emergency admissions, and triggered systemic changes in clinical practice. It also exposed serious concerns about counterfeit drugs in Kenya, prompting national regulatory review—demonstrating the test’s power not only to enhance outcomes but also to safeguard medicine quality at scale. Read more...

Opioid prescribing in Scotland: stemming the epidemic

Research led by the University of Dundee defined the scale and risks of opioid prescribing for chronic pain in Scotland, directly shaping the development of SIGN 136—the world’s first comprehensive evidence-based guideline for chronic pain management. Since its 2013 publication and 2019 update, SIGN 136 has underpinned national prescribing strategies and policy, contributing to an 18.8% reduction in opioid prescribing across Scotland, with local and national adoption improving safety, reducing dependence, and reversing rising trends in opioid use. Read more...

Implementing PINCER to reduce medication errors in general practices

Researchers at the University of Nottingham developed PINCER, a pharmacist-led, IT-based intervention proven to reduce clinically significant medication errors in general practice—particularly those causing gastrointestinal bleeding. Endorsed by NICE and embedded in multiple NHS policies, PINCER has been implemented in nearly 2,700 practices, covering 40% of England’s population. With over 25 million patient records searched and more than 2,000 clinicians trained, PINCER has led to measurable reductions in hazardous prescribing and is credited with preventing hospital admissions and patient harm, transforming medication safety at national scale. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic contain research pertaining to greenhouse gas emissions, atmosphere and climate. The studies discuss climate change mitigation through improved greenhouse gas measurement, refined emissions reporting, and the development of decision support tools. They include research validating CO₂ emissions, accounting for methane and hydrocarbon impacts, and shaping global and national policies—including UK Net Zero targets, the UN Paris Agreement, and the Montreal Protocol. Advances also focus on satellite observations, carbon capture and storage (including negative emissions and cryogenic methods), emissions reduction in agriculture, shipping and aviation, and the environmental benefits of novel technologies such as aerosol valves and the CarbFix system.
narrative:
Carbon Capture and Storage including Negative Emissions to deliver UK Net Zero Emission

University of Edinburgh research on Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) and negative emissions underpinned the UK’s strategy to reach Net Zero emissions, informing the 2019 Net Zero legislation and major government investments in CCS infrastructure. This work supported the development of the Acorn CCS cluster in Scotland, guided over £15M in UK, Scottish, and EU investment, and influenced UK and EU industrial decarbonisation policy. It also contributed directly to national climate targets, including the commitment of £1B to CCS deployment and support for Direct Air Capture and negative emissions technologies. Read more...

Evidence-based international standards and regulation to mitigate the environmental effects of aviation emission

Research from Manchester Metropolitan University on the climate impacts of aviation emissions has directly shaped global standards and policy instruments to reduce CO₂ from international aviation. This work informed the EU Emissions Trading Scheme for aviation, credited with avoiding 193MtCO₂, and underpinned technical decisions adopted by ICAO, including the global CORSIA offsetting scheme, which will mitigate over 3GtCO₂ to 2035. It also drove the creation of new aircraft CO₂ and particulate emissions standards, influencing technological design and regulatory compliance in all 191 ICAO member states. Read more...

New measurements of trees and forests: improving global observations for climate and carbon studies and extending public understanding

UCL’s development of 3D terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) has revolutionised how forest carbon is measured, enabling more accurate estimates of carbon stocks and improving validation of satellite data used by NASA and the European Space Agency. This work directly informed updates to UN IPCC guidelines for national greenhouse gas reporting, supporting global climate policy under the Paris Agreement. It has also strengthened the case for preserving both tropical and urban forests, empowering environmental charities, informing urban planning, and engaging mass public audiences through exhibitions, media, and awareness campaigns. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic address respiratory health, including asthma, allergies and respiratory diseases. Research covers drug development and therapies, treatments and disease management, as well as prevention and care. Studies in this topic often discuss best clinical practice, therapy development, healthcare delivery and service provision, and healthcare policy. Studies in this topic also extend to respiratory conditions such as breathlessness and sleep apnoea.
narrative:
Improving outcomes for people experiencing seasonal respiratory allergies through refining pollen and fungal spore forecasts

Research at the University of Worcester has transformed the management of seasonal respiratory allergies by refining pollen and fungal spore forecasts used by millions across the UK and Ireland. Through advanced modelling, allergen mapping, and species-level detection, the University’s forecasts—delivered via the Met Office, Met Éireann, media, and direct online platforms—help sufferers plan activities and medication, reducing symptoms, hospitalisations, and missed workdays. Clinicians, charities, and businesses use these data to personalise treatment, raise awareness, and enhance customer services, improving health outcomes and quality of life for allergy sufferers nationwide. Read more...

Chronic cough: defining a “new” disease and producing a novel class of effective drugs

University of Hull research redefined chronic cough as a distinct disease, transforming diagnosis, treatment, and drug development globally.
