The Hull Airway Reflux Questionnaire (HARQ), now used in over 39 countries, has improved patient identification and reduced misdiagnosis. Hull’s leadership shaped the 2020 European Respiratory Society’s international guidelines and uncovered key mechanisms in cough hypersensitivity, catalysing the first effective antitussive drugs in over 40 years. This underpinned Merck’s $1.25 billion acquisition of Afferent Pharmaceuticals and led to global phase 2 and 3 trials of five novel compounds, directly benefiting millions of previously untreated patients. Read more...

description: This research addresses HIV prevention and treatment, and sexual health. Research encompasses clinical practice, public health policy, prevention, and community interventions, as well as scientific developments, diagnostic tools, and therapies to reduce HIV transmission and improve treatment outcomes. Frequent themes include healthcare access and equity, community engagement, and public health policies. Sexual health, relationships and education studies are also incorporated in this topic.
narrative:
Cash + Care: Transforming HIV outcomes for adolescents in Africa through social protection.

Research demonstrating that combinations of social welfare, cash transfers, and caregiving support led to 50-70% reductions in HIV infection risk behaviours, such as transactional sex, reduced HIV infection risks and improved health for 2,000,000 adolescents across Southern and Eastern Africa. These findings have been directly translated into policy and service delivery for adolescents by USAID's President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), UNICEF, UNAIDS, and national governments including South Africa, Kenya, Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. Read more...

HIV policy formulation and prevention: driving the decision for and implementation of publicly-funded pre-exposure prophylaxis in Scotland

Researchers contributed essential data and understanding needed by Scottish policymakers to plan and fund pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV prevention. In July 2017, Scotland became the first UK nation to fund PrEP on the NHS. In the first three years, 4,100 people received PrEP, reducing HIV incidence five-fold in men who have sex with men (MSM) with high risk behaviour. Read more...

description: Research in this topic has transformed how scientific knowledge is produced, shared, and accessed. Case studies informed national and international open access policies, strengthened GDPR-compliant data practices, and improved editorial standards and transparency across scientific publishing. Projects advanced open, scholar-led, and experimental publishing models and worked with libraries and publishers to broaden public access to research. Researchers developed influential open databases—from genetics to socio-economic data—as well as open-source tools and data ressources for digital humanities and open research software abroad many scientific fields. Citizen science initiatives empowered public participation in data collection, while efforts in knowledge organization and publishing reform shaped the future of accessible, ethical, and high-quality research dissemination.
narrative:
The Openness Agenda: Re-Shaping the Governance of Science, Digital Technologies and Research Infrastructure in Europe

This research reshaped how Open Science is governed across Europe and beyond. Work on data practices and scientific infrastructure directly influenced the European Commission’s Open Science policy, including the Plan S framework and the creation of the EU’s Open Research Platform. The research underpinned major shifts toward inclusive, sustainable, and equitable open access and open data practices. The insights were used to advise over a dozen national governments, shaped high-level EU recommendations, and contributed to UNESCO’s global Open Science guidelines. Countries reformed research incentives, evaluation, and infrastructure, enabling wide adoption of open knowledge systems. Read more...

The miRBase microRNA database – driving the development of commercial microRNA research tools, diagnostics and therapeutics

miRBase, an open access database developed at the University of Manchester, has become the global reference for microRNA gene sequences, powering research, diagnostics, and therapeutics worldwide. Used by over 20,000 monthly users—including 10% from industry—it underpins commercial products from biotech leaders, guides clinical trials of microRNA-based therapies, and shapes international genomic standards. With over 34,000 entries added, miRBase directly supports a USD160M+ market in experimental tools and has enabled breakthroughs in disease diagnostics, drug development, and genome policy globally. Read more...

Zooniverse: harnessing Citizen Science for Global Impact

Zooniverse, developed from Oxford Physics’ Galaxy Zoo project, is the world’s largest citizen science platform, engaging over 2.1 million volunteers across 248 projects spanning science, the arts, history, and medicine. Enabled by cutting-edge research in human-machine collaboration, Zooniverse has transformed research and public engagement globally. It has informed disaster relief by rapidly analysing satellite images after hurricanes, influenced environmental policy through penguin population data, inspired digital art and museum exhibits, and enhanced science learning in schools. Projects like Planet Hunters and Penguin Watch demonstrate its scientific, educational, and societal reach and impact. Read more...

topic_name_long: Public Services, Civil Service & Local Governance
description: Research in this topic has strengthened the design, delivery, and governance of public services, and local government. Projects informed evidence-based policymaking and evaluation, supported public service reform, and improved civil service workforce training, communication and strategy. Researchers developed outcome-focused models for service innovation and helped local authorities adopt peer-led improvement approaches. Case studies enhanced both local and national procurement practices, supported small business participation in local decision-making, and shaped reforms to civil service workforce planning. Work also guided local government initiatives and revenue generation, simplified public administration across sectors, and reduced corruption—promoting more transparent, accountable, and effective governance across the UK.
narrative:
Responding to a post-austerity economics by improving procurement policy and practice in Wales

University of South Wales research has transformed procurement policy and practice across the Welsh public and private sectors, significantly enhancing economic outcomes in a post-austerity context. Their work led to major reforms in Welsh Government procurement strategy, including a 100% increase in SME bids and a 400% rise in contract wins. Knowledge Transfer Partnerships with public bodies like Cardiff City Council and firms such as Airbus generated substantial savings (£40m at Cardiff; projected €35m annually at Airbus). The university’s CIPS-accredited training and national leadership in procurement education further support sustainable public service delivery and regional economic development. Read more...

Empowering Communities in Public Service Reform in Scotland

University of Edinburgh researchers helped transform public service reform in Scotland by embedding community empowerment into legislation, policy, and practice. Through sustained collaboration with government, local authorities, and civic partners, their research: (i) informed the Community Empowerment Act (2015); (ii) helped mainstream participatory budgeting, leading all councils to commit 1% of budgets to citizen-led processes; (iii) shaped NHS engagement strategies, including the creation of a Citizens’ Jury and national citizens’ panel; and (iv) drove a new governance framework based on fiscal, functional, and community empowerment, now central to Scotland’s ongoing Local Governance Review. Read more...

Improving the effectiveness of policy making through an innovative model of knowledge mobilisation in Wales

Cardiff Business School created a demand-led knowledge mobilisation model that embedded academic expertise into Welsh Government decision-making. By tailoring rapid evidence reviews to ministerial priorities through the Public Policy Institute for Wales and later the Wales Centre for Public Policy, the model improved policy outcomes in areas including childcare, youth homelessness, and COVID-19 recovery. Impacts included £80M annual savings from revised childcare policy, a £4.8M youth housing innovation fund, and stronger evidence-based strategy across Welsh Government. Cardiff’s model has influenced UK-wide practice through the What Works Network and was recognised by the OECD as exemplary. Read more...

description: This topic covers marine and aquatic research with case studies examining environmental conservation, sustainable management, and protection strategies for aquaculture, fisheries and marine environments. Studies include aspects of statistical analysis, species conservation, aquaculture development, fisheries regulation, biodiversity assessment, and marine planning approaches. Key themes are environmental protection, strengthened policy development, and improved sustainability. Some coastal management, and community engagement research is also incorporated.
narrative:
Using Lumpfish to Control Sea Lice in Salmon Farming

Research at Swansea University enabled the large-scale captive breeding and welfare optimisation of lumpfish, a natural predator of sea lice in salmon farming. This work has transformed industry practices by reducing the need for chemical treatments by up to 100% on some sites, saving millions and improving fish welfare. The team developed genetic tools to breed elite, lice-eating lumpfish, standardised operating procedures used internationally, and the first lumpfish welfare index. Their research led to over 6.5 million lumpfish deployed in the UK, created 12 new jobs in Wales, and helped regenerate the regional aquaculture economy while boosting sustainability across Europe’s £15 billion salmon industry. Read more...

The Conservation of Coral Reefs in the Face of Climate Change

Research at the University of Derby pioneered the first-ever successful laboratory-induced coral spawning and juvenile survival techniques, enabling full coral life cycles in captivity and revolutionising global reef restoration practices. These innovations have been adopted by leading institutions including the Florida Aquarium, AIMS in Australia, and aquaria across Europe and the US, enhancing large-scale coral propagation and reef recovery. The work shaped United Nations environmental policy, upskilled conservation practitioners in the Maldives and Israel, and engaged millions via museum exhibits, TV, and online platforms. Derby’s coral research now underpins a global model for reef resilience in the face of climate change. Read more...

The social, economic and environmental impacts of a Marine Protected Area (MPA): Lyme Bay

Pioneering research by the University of Plymouth led to the designation and long-term ecological and socio-economic monitoring of the Lyme Bay Marine Protected Area (MPA), transforming UK reef conservation. By evidencing the benefits of excluding bottom-towed fishing across an entire site, the research informed national fisheries policy, triggered new byelaws protecting 2,179 km² of reef, and helped shape the UK’s post-Brexit marine strategy and 25 Year Environment Plan. The work demonstrated ecological recovery, increased shellfish catch and income for local fishermen, boosted marine tourism, and fostered a model fisher-science partnership now replicated across the UK and internationally. Read more...

Adapting terrestrial property management law to protect the marine environment

This research on using terrestrial property law to better manage maritime resources influenced the UK government's post-Brexit maritime regulations, a ban on electric pulse trawling throughout Europe, and the establishment of new Marine Protected Areas around Ascension Island and in Scotland. Read more...

description: This topic focuses on telecommunications with case studies covering network technologies, wireless systems, and connectivity solutions. Research encompasses 5G development, wireless communication protocols, optical fiber technologies, internet infrastructure improvements, and 'Inernet of Things' connectivity systems. Case studies may demonstrate enhanced network performance, improved communication standards, or commercial innovations across telecommunications policy, infrastructure development, and digital service delivery.
narrative:
Millimetre wave technology enables fast, reliable WiFi on the move

University of Bristol research into millimetre wave wireless technology enabled FirstGroup’s evo-rail to deliver the world’s first gigabit-speed onboard WiFi via trackside-to-train connectivity, offering passengers throughput 100 times faster than cellular networks. This work directly influenced UK Government 5G policy on rail connectivity and catalysed commercial deployment on the Isle of Wight and the busy Basingstoke–Waterloo line. It also underpinned the growth of Blu Wireless Technology Ltd, whose products, co-developed and tested with the University, secured £12M investment and global contracts, expanding their team from 7 to over 110 and their revenue by over 200% in 12 months. Read more...

Enabling the 5G Networked Society

Research by the University of Bristol’s Smart Internet Lab has played a pivotal role in enabling 5G technology in the UK and globally. Their work shaped UK Government policy, securing £200M for 5G testbeds and influencing the UK’s telecom supply chain strategy. Technical innovations in Massive MIMO, mobile edge computing, orchestration, and quantum-secure networks were adopted by standardisation bodies (e.g. 3GPP, ETSI), telecom providers (e.g. BT), and major corporates (e.g. Samsung). Their spin-out, Zeetta Networks, commercialised 5G virtualisation software now deployed across cities and venues. Public showcases and collaborations helped raise awareness and drive early adoption across industry sector Read more...

SpaceWire and SpaceFibre

The University of Dundee’s research led to the development and standardisation of SpaceWire and its high-speed successor SpaceFibre, now core technologies in global spacecraft data systems. SpaceWire, used in over $40 billion worth of missions, enables reliable onboard data handling across telecommunications, environmental, and exploration satellites. The University’s spin-out, STAR-Dundee, has commercialised this globally. SpaceFibre, offering up to 100× faster data rates with advanced fault recovery, is being adopted by major space agencies and aerospace companies and is embedded in international standards, supporting next-generation, high-performance space missions. Read more...

Hollow Core Fibres: Delivering economic impact via the commercialisation of a disruptive optical fibre technology for next-generation communications systems.

Pioneering research at the University of Southampton’s Optoelectronics Research Centre led to the development of hollow core optical fibre (HCF) technology with world-record performance, enabling significantly faster, lower-latency data transmission. This breakthrough underpinned the creation of spin-out company Lumenisity Ltd in 2016, which has since attracted substantial investment (including foreign direct investment), generated revenues from HCF product sales, and created over 50 high-skilled UK jobs. Lumenisity’s technology is being used commercially, including by financial services firms seeking latency advantages, and has spurred trials in data centre interconnect and 5G backhaul. The success of HCFs—proven by record-setting attenuation levels and robust IP licensing—has influenced strategic investment decisions across the global telecoms industry, with expanding applications in laser delivery and gyroscopic navigation, demonstrating widespread technological and economic impact. Read more...

topic_name_long: Occupational, Transport & Fire Safety & Emergency Responses
description: This portfolio of research addresses critical challenges in occupational, transport, and fire safety, as well as emergency preparedness and response. It demonstrates how academic expertise has influenced legislation, policy, design, training, and technological innovation to protect lives, improve public safety, and enhance emergency response systems across sectors.Key impacts include: improving fire safety engineering through advanced computer modelling and smoke toxicity assessments; shaping emergency response protocols for spontaneous volunteers; informing evacuation and blast safety strategies; reducing risks in hazardous occupations through behavioural science and materials research; and enhancing road safety through innovations in driver training, vehicle technology (e.g., Intelligent Speed Assistance), and road safety improvements based on AI collision modelling. The research has also led to more targeted fire prevention through novel informatics, and improved public safety policies.Through interdisciplinary methods—spanning engineering, psychology, data science, and policy research—this work has strengthened safety and resilience frameworks and technology both in the UK and internationally.
narrative:
Improving and Protecting the UK Governments largest asset – the Strategic Road Network

Loughborough University’s research transformed the accuracy of collision data used by Highways England (HE), improving location precision from 82% to 99% through AI-based modelling. This enabled HE to implement a data-driven Safe Systems model, leading to more effective targeting of road safety interventions across the Strategic Road Network (SRN). Between 2014 and 2019, the approach supported over £17bn in safety improvements, helped reduce collisions by 20% despite rising traffic volumes, and saved over £500m by preventing road closures. Accurate modelling also enabled more nuanced responses—such as identifying suicides rather than traffic-related deaths—shaping appropriate strategies. The evidence base built through this work supported HE in meeting its government-mandated casualty reduction target and secured £27.4bn in funding for future road safety investment (2020–2025). Read more...

Newly developed mobile traffic collision reporting improves road safety data, increasing the efficiency of UK police services

This research revealed systematic cognitive bias and inefficiencies in police officers’ recording of road traffic accidents that undermines the reliability of accident statistics used to inform road safety policy. Researchers transformed the reporting of road traffic accidents via the development and evaluation of a mobile app reporting system used by police officers at the incident scene. The new reporting practices provided to police forces in November 2018, are already in use by 24 of the 45 police forces in England, Wales, and Scotland. These measures improved the reliability of collision data, and reduced police costs associated with the incident reporting and data processing that informs the Department for Transport and Transport Scotland's road safety policies. Read more...

Making Tall Buildings Safe from Fire

Research at the University of Central Lancashire played a key role in shaping UK fire safety policy following the Grenfell Tower fire. By demonstrating the flammability and toxicity of widely used façade materials—including polyethylene-cored aluminium composite panels (ACP) and combustible insulation—the team provided critical evidence that informed government decisions. Their findings directly influenced the ban on combustible cladding for high-rise residential buildings (December 2018) and supported a £3.5 billion remediation programme. Further evidence on the risks of high-pressure laminates (HPL) helped prompt an additional £1 billion commitment to remove unsafe non-ACM cladding. Their work was presented to government bodies, parliamentary groups, and the Grenfell Inquiry, contributing to major shifts in construction practice, including a market shift towards non-combustible materials like mineral wool Read more...

description: This body of research addresses poverty alleviation, social mobility, and international development, influencing how governments, NGOs, and international bodies design, implement, and evaluate policies aimed at improving the lives of marginalised populations.Internationally, the work has transformed approaches to poverty measurement and financial aid effectiveness, informed major anti-poverty initiatives—including programmes targeting the ultra-poor and international microfinance schemes—and shaped global frameworks such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. It has empowered marginalised voices in economic governance, enhanced land rights for women, and informed humanitarian responses in complex political economies such as South Sudan. Innovative interdisciplinary approaches, including evolutionary anthropology, have also advanced development policy and influenced fields from agricultural policy to reproductive health.In the UK, the research in this cluster focused on poverty, often seeking ways to reduce child povertyand ensure mobility, including direct influence on relevant legislation. Across all contexts, the work supports co-produced, equitable governance and evidence-led policy to tackle poverty and promote inclusive, sustainable development.
narrative:
Improved Effectiveness and Impact of an International Microfinance Programme

Research by the University of Portsmouth significantly improved the effectiveness of CARE International’s microfinance platform, Lendwithcare (LWC). Insights into lender behaviour informed a 2015 website redesign, helping grow the lender base from 20,794 to 66,002 and increase loan capital from £5.5M to £31.5M, enabling over 120,000 new loans to low-income entrepreneurs. Fieldwork with microfinance partners led to operational changes: Pakistan introduced new social performance tools, Zimbabwe streamlined training and oversight, and Ecuador adjusted loan targeting to reach more marginalised borrowers. CARE has since expanded its investment in impact evaluation and prioritised academic partnerships as a result. Read more...

Improving the lives of the ultra-poor

Research led by LSE and UCL demonstrated that “graduation” programmes—a form of anti-poverty intervention that provides extremely poor households with a productive asset (such as livestock), skills training, and temporary financial support—can create lasting improvements in income, savings, and wellbeing. The evaluation focused on a flagship programme in Bangladesh run by BRAC, the world’s largest non-governmental development organisation, and showed that 95% of participants maintained better living conditions years after the programme ended. These findings provided the first long-term evidence that such programmes work at scale and have since influenced global poverty policy. As a result, graduation-style programmes are now being implemented by BRAC and others in over 45 countries, supported by governments, major NGOs, and international agencies including the World Bank and UNHCR, helping millions of the world’s poorest people achieve greater stability and self-reliance. Read more...

Tackling Child Poverty Policy in Scotland

Research by Glasgow Caledonian University’s Scottish Poverty and Inequality Research Unit (SPIRU) significantly shaped Scotland’s approach to tackling child poverty. Their studies revealed major gaps in local authority responses under previous UK legislation, prompting the Scottish Government to include statutory duties in the 2017 Child Poverty (Scotland) Act. SPIRU was appointed as an official partner to support local authorities in producing annual Local Child Poverty Action Reports (LCPARs), offering expert guidance, analytical tools, and feedback frameworks. Their work improved the quality, focus, and evidence use in these reports across Scotland. SPIRU’s research also informed national strategy, including the introduction of the Scottish Child Payment, and helped foster collaboration between local government, health boards, and civil society to address the root causes of poverty. Read more...

Sowing seeds; Transforming land rights for women and other disadvantaged groups

Research on gender, human rights, and land tenure has significantly shaped global approaches to making land access more equitable for women and disadvantaged groups. This work influenced UN strategy on land governance, contributed to the creation of an international network promoting inclusive land tools, and led to the development of practical frameworks and training initiatives used in over 40 countries. These efforts directly improved land rights for more than 200,000 households, particularly through the application of gender-responsive tools and legal pluralism in land administration. The research has also informed policy reforms in regions affected by conflict and displacement, supported the integration of inclusive land governance into global development agendas, and provided training to over 2,400 professionals, embedding more equitable practices into national and international land management systems. Read more...

description: This topic focuses on pollinator with case studies researching protection strategies, policy and regulatory frameworks, and land management practices. Research encompasses pollinator protection measures, pesticide control policies, biodiversity support initiatives, and evidence-based intervention development.
narrative:
Ecological “BEEHAVE” models deliver benefits for pollinators - improving European regulation, reducing risks and informing land management

Research at the University of Exeter developed BEEHAVE and Bumble-BEEHAVE, advanced ecological models simulating honeybee and bumblebee colony dynamics, enabling long-term, landscape-scale assessment of stressors such as pesticides, disease, and habitat loss. These models have transformed EU regulatory practice, underpinning EFSA’s revision of bee protection goals and guiding new risk assessment tools for plant protection products. Major agrochemical companies including Syngenta, Bayer, and BASF now use the models to improve environmental safety and reduce pollinator harm. Locally, the models—integrated into the BEE-STEWARD software—have enabled pollinator-friendly land management across over 900km² in the UK, influencing strategies by Cornwall Council, the Duchy of Cornwall, and Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty. Widely adopted by regulators, industry, and land stewards, the models have become pivotal tools for pollinator conservation policy and practice across Europe. Read more...

Informing policy to mitigate insect pollinator decline

Research at the University of Leeds has been instrumental in shaping UK and international policies to address insect pollinator decline. By providing the first robust evidence of widespread losses in bee diversity and associated declines in pollinated plants, Leeds influenced National Pollinator Strategies in the UK and US, agri-environmental policy changes, and restrictions on harmful pesticides. Their findings have supported planting schemes across thousands of hectares, improved urban land management, and helped design national pollinator monitoring programmes, including the UK’s Pollinator Monitoring Scheme. The work also contributed to the European Red List for bees and significantly raised public awareness, helping to embed pollinator protection in environmental and conservation strategies. Read more...

description: This topic encompasses a wide range of research aimed at improving employment conditions, labour standards, and wage policy. Case studies focus on reducing wage inequality, supporting low-paid and precarious workers, and promoting inclusive labour markets, but also focus on labour market efficiency and ensuring high employment rates. Research has informed minimum wage legislation and pay-setting bodies in the UK and internationally, encouraged adoption of the Living Wage, and contributed to reforms in unemployment and employment policies. Other work has advanced understanding of occupational regulation, Universal Basic Income, and digital transformation of work. Studies have also adviced on trade unions and their role in the political economy, promoted decent work principles through international institutions, and improved employability programmes for disadvantaged groups. Workplace well-being, and the rights of ageing and migrant workers are further particular labour market aspects that the research advised on.
narrative:
Detecting and improving the recovery of unpaid wages

This research showed the scale of non-payment of wages, amounting to £3.1 billion annually. Findings led to employment rights policy through the ‘Good Work Plan’, regulating enforcement of entitlement to holiday pay, improvements to payslip entitlement, and greater efforts to pursue directors evading employment obligations. Improved enforcement directly benefited over 2 million of Britain’s lowest paid workers. Read more...

Improving our understanding of the National Minimum Wage to benefit low-paid workers in the UK and Ireland

Research exploring effects of the UK National Minimum Wage (NMW) on low-paid workers informed the Low Pay Commission’s recommendations to the UK Government to increase the NMW in 2014, 2015 and 2016, which were accepted in full. These measures raised the pay of around 1,000,000 workers by as much as GBP355 per annum. Read more...

Abolishing Employment Tribunal Fees

Economics and law research was instrumental in the UK Supreme Court's July 2017 ruling that employment tribunal fees introduced by the UK Government in 2013 were unlawful. This research provided the legal arguments underlying the court decision. Tribunal fees were abolished with immediate effect, affecting many thousands of potential claimants who had been deterred from bringing their cases before the courts. By September 2019, the Ministry of Justice had refunded more than £18,000,000 in illegally levied fees. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic cover dental and oral health, including research into product development, prevention and treatment of dental diseases, child healthcare, and service provision improvements. Common themes include improved clinical outcomes, reduced health inequalities, policy improvements and service provision improvements.
narrative:
Improved oral healthcare using biomimetic peptide technology

University of Leeds research developed a biomimetic self-assembling peptide (SAP) technology that has transformed minimally invasive dental care. The patented peptide, P11-4, enables the regeneration of enamel and periodontal tissue by mimicking natural mineralisation processes. Initially launched for treating early tooth decay ("filling without drilling"), the technology now underpins a growing portfolio of CE-marked and FDA-compliant products, including Curodont Repair, D’Senz, and Protect. These are used across Europe, the US, and Switzerland in both professional and over-the-counter formats, including high-volume toothpaste lines. The technology has proven more effective than fluoride varnish in clinical trials, offers an aerosol-free alternative to traditional fillings, and reduces treatment cost and patient anxiety. Following successful licensing and global distribution deals, including with Straumann AG, and the acquisition of its original distributor by vVardis, SAP technology is now driving commercial innovation and improving oral healthcare worldwide. Read more...

Improving the oral health of UK children in deprived communities through policy and practice change

Cardiff University’s research significantly improved oral health policy and practice for children in deprived UK communities. Their landmark randomised controlled trial demonstrated that fluoride varnish is as effective but more cost-efficient than fissure sealants, leading the Welsh Government to shift its national oral health programme, Designed to Smile (D2S), away from sealants and toward early intervention with fluoride varnish and daily brushing in children under five. Cardiff’s epidemiological studies showed a 12% drop in caries in five-year-olds over nine years, supporting continued £3M+ annual investment in D2S. Their work also shaped NICE guideline PH55 and informed Public Health England’s national oral health strategy. Read more...

topic_name_long: Gender, Race & Class Equity at Work
description: This topic brings together research focused on advancing workplace equity across dimensions of gender, race, class, sexuality, and belief. Case studies explore the drivers of the gender pay gap and support organisations in embedding change through pay analysis, positive action, and taking into account female lifecourses from childbearing to menopause. Research has influenced board-level gender diversity in UK companies, shaped women’s enterprise and entrepreneurship policy, and informed strategies for career progression among minority ethnic professionals. Work has also tackled barriers to social mobility in elite professions and the creative industries, improved workplace experiences for LGBTQ+ employees, and supported policy development to prevent discrimination based on religion or belief.
narrative:
Encouraging Women in the Scottish STEM Sector

Research on barriers that prevent women progressing in STEM education and careers recommended holistic approaches to increasing female engagement, employment, and retention that directly influenced Scottish Government policies on education and employment. This research has also informed educational establishments such as The Open University and City of Glasgow College, where the proportion of women studying engineering rose from 4% to 28%. Read more...

Diversity and Entrepreneurial Outcomes in the UK: A case study transforming policy and practice

Research into ethnic and migrant entrepreneurship in the UK led to a pioneering model of inclusive business support that directly improved the performance of around 100 previously unreached ethnic minority businesses in Birmingham. Drawing on long-term data from the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor, the project demonstrated the economic and social value of ethnic minority firms and influenced national and local support structures. It informed the development of new programmes by NatWest, Citizens UK, and other partners, helped secure £31m in new contracts for a refugee-focused housing organisation, and contributed to inclusive growth strategies across sectors. Findings also shaped national policy dialogue, with recommendations taken up by the Federation of Small Businesses and informing government and bank-led initiatives to support underrepresented entrepreneurs. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic focus on Ireland’s history, culture, and political landscape, with emphasis on reshaping entrenched socio-political narratives to drive reconciliation and foster a shared sense of history and identity. Research informs policy, education, and practical initiatives aimed at promoting collaboration, peacebuilding, political engagement, economic development, and cultural vitality within conflicted and/or marginalised communities. Many case studies use arts and history to address the complexities of Northern Ireland’s historic and contemporary sectarianism, helping to bridge community divides through commemoration, reconciliation and justice, particularly for those affected by conflict and marginalisation.
narrative:
Improving Collection and Curatorial Practices at the National Museum of Ireland and Emphasising Social Value and Creativity in Older Irish Women

Sorcha O’Brien’s research on the history of the electrification of rural Irish homes and its effects on women’s lives led to an exhibition, ‘Kitchen Power’, at the National Museum of Ireland (NMI). The exhibition prompted developments in museological practice, and a change in emphasis for NMI Country Life from folklife to social history to include the late 20th century, a gap in its coverage. This change in emphasis included the acquisition of 16 of the mass manufactured domestic appliances on display in the exhibition (out of 51 objects in the exhibition in total), adding to the 8 already in the NMI collection. It also prompted conceptual developments among the NMI curatorial staff, particularly the integration of oral histories as part of new permanent displays. The changes to curatorial and acquisition practices highlighted engrained issues of communication between departments and led to the creation of a Head of Operations position in NMI Country Life’s organisation. NMI visitor numbers increased significantly during the ‘Kitchen Power’ exhibition, rising from a previous 5-year average of 13,532 in July and 15,560 in August, to 15,060 in July and 18,002 in August. As of February 2020, 73,426 people had visited the exhibition, and 22,748 visitors attended in the break between COVID-19 restrictions from June 2020-October 2020. Read more...

The Belfast Mobility Project: Transforming everyday mobility patterns in a divided city

The Belfast Mobility Project has demonstrated how and why the everyday movements of city residents can both reproduce and reform systems of segregation within Belfast. It has been particularly impactful in informing government policy decisions by giving policymakers from various sectors (including the Northern Ireland Housing Executive, the Good Relations Unit, the Department of Justice, and the Northern Ireland Executive Office) better understandings of the psychology of sectarian divisions in the city and areas where access to public spaces and facilities remains shaped by these divisions. This work has shaped the approaches of the Neighbourhood Services and City Regeneration and Development teams of Belfast City Council. It has informed the Council’s encouragement of residents to live in the city centre, and the creation of a new campus site for Ulster University to support this. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic cover research into treatments and rehabilitation across orthopaedics, biomechanics and kinesiology practice. Studies include areas such as joint replacement procedures, trauma management, rehabilitation services, biomechanical analysis, prosthetic development. Case studies demonstrate improvements in patient outcomes, healthcare cost reduction, and clinical practice guidelines and policy.
narrative:
Orthopaedic implant analysis changed which implants were used and how they are monitored

nan Read more...

From molecule to mouse to man: transforming the clinical management of all alkaptonuria patients in the UK with molecular and whole-body level approaches

Liverpool John Moores University’s research has transformed the management of alkaptonuria (AKU), a rare and debilitating metabolic disease. Preclinical studies and international clinical trials led by LJMU contributed to the licensing of nitisinone, the first approved treatment for AKU, now available to all adult patients across Europe. Complementary gait analysis research developed innovative methods to quantify movement impairment and revealed that AKU affects patients from a younger age than previously believed. These findings directly inform the clinical management of all 72 UK AKU patients via the NHS National Alkaptonuria Centre, where LJMU's gait reports guide personalised care. The work also changed clinical teaching practices: LJMU-developed methods are now integrated into the annual ESMAC Gait Course and widely used via the ‘Moments’ app in clinics and universities. This integrated molecular-to-movement approach enhances quality of life for patients, informs earlier intervention strategies in children, and is influencing international best practice. Read more...

Advancing Regenerative Medicine: from the bench to a NICE-approved treatment for early osteoarthriti

Keele University’s research has transformed the clinical management of early knee osteoarthritis by advancing regenerative medicine from lab to patient care. Their interdisciplinary team developed and validated autologous chondrocyte implantation (ACI), a cell-based therapy that uses a patient’s cultured cartilage cells to repair joint defects. Pioneering long-term studies demonstrated ACI’s safety, efficacy, and cost-effectiveness, leading to NICE approval in 2017—the first such approval for a cell therapy in the UK. The team also developed the ORKA-1 prognostic tool and web app to personalise treatment, helping surgeons identify patients most likely to benefit. Their internationally adopted cartilage repair scoring system (ICRS II) set a clinical benchmark for evaluating outcomes. Over 500 patients have received ACI at Keele/RJAH, with significant improvements in mobility and quality of life. The research has shaped policy, NHS practice, international trials, and clinical training, establishing Keele as a leader in orthopaedic regenerative medicine. Read more...

Advanced Pre-clinical Simulation Methods Enabling the Development of Longer Lasting Total Joint Replacements

Since 2014, the University of Leeds has transformed joint replacement design and testing through advanced pre-clinical simulation methods. Working with Simulation Solutions, Leeds developed new six-axis simulators and led the creation of ISO14242-4, the first international standard to account for real-world surgical variation and edge loading. Adopted globally, these innovations have supported new hip and knee implant products from DePuy Synthes, Mathys, and Invibio. More than 300,000 joint replacements each year—over 10% of the global market—now benefit from Leeds-based simulation. DePuy doubled its ceramic head sales and launched the ATTUNE knee (used in over 950,000 patients), while Leeds’ methods also enabled Mathys’ ceramic hips and Invibio’s all-polymer knee. This work has significantly improved implant durability and patient outcomes worldwide. Read more...

description: This topic encompasses agricultural plant research across disease management strategies, crop improvement technologies, and food security solutions. Case studies cover plant disease epidemiology, crop breeding techniques, pest management approaches, genetic modifications, sustainable farming practices, environmental protection strategies, and biotechnology applications. Case studies often demonstrate policy influence, agricultural productivity enhancements, and environmentally sustainable crop protection across global food production systems.
narrative:
‘More crop per drop’: exploiting plant hormone signalling in agricultural technologies that enhance water and food security.

Lancaster’s research on plant hormone signalling transformed water use in agriculture by enabling low-cost practices and microbial products that significantly improve water use efficiency (WUE) and crop yields. By uncovering how root-to-shoot hormone signals regulate plant responses to soil drying, the team pioneered deficit irrigation techniques such as alternate furrow irrigation (AFI), now used by over 100,000 farmers across China, India, Iran, and California. These methods reduced crop water use by up to 40%, restored degraded water systems like China’s Qingtu Lake, and boosted yields by up to 30%. In China alone, adapted rice irrigation on 5.4 million hectares generated nearly GBP200 million in seasonal farmer income. Building on these insights, microbial products developed with Lancaster’s partners manipulate hormone signalling via root bacteria to sustain crop growth under water stress. Such biofertilisers, now widely adopted in Pakistan, India, and Russia, yield 10–30% increases in crops like wheat, sugarcane, and potatoes, improving farmer incomes by up to 25%. Together, these innovations have enhanced food and water security for farmers in some of the world’s most water-scarce regions. Read more...

Mitigating the devastating impact of cassava virus diseases on African smallholder farmers and the cassava value chain by transforming policy and practice

Research at the University of Greenwich has significantly mitigated the impact of two devastating cassava virus diseases—CMD and CBSD—on smallholder farmers across Sub-Saharan Africa. Through innovative diagnostic protocols and tissue culture techniques, the team cured over 2,500 cassava plants and enabled the first regional exchange of virus-free, improved varieties across five countries (Kenya, Malawi, Mozambique, Tanzania, Uganda). This intervention led to increased cassava yields, benefitting over a million Tanzanian farmers and catalysing the emergence of commercial cassava seed enterprises. The work directly informed a 2017 amendment to Tanzania’s Seed Act, institutionalising laboratory virus testing and tissue culture for seed certification. The protocols have since been adopted in Rwanda, Burundi, and Eastern DRC, shaping national policies and seed systems. These efforts underpinned a 25% rise in cassava production in Eastern Africa between 2010 and 2018, while improved varieties are now used in multiple breeding programmes continent-wide. Funded by major donors including the Gates Foundation, the research has reshaped cassava disease control, seed policy, and farmer behaviour across the region. Read more...

Protecting global food production and woodland environments: forecasting and managing plant disease through epidemiological modelling

Epidemiological models developed at the University of Cambridge have informed global strategies to manage major plant diseases, protecting crops, ecosystems, and livelihoods. In Ethiopia, an early warning system based on these models enabled up to 500,000 smallholder farmers to act against wheat rust. Across ten West and Central African countries, forecasts of cassava brown streak disease guided national surveillance and policy, safeguarding a key food source for 500 million people. In Australia, modelling averted a harmful policy change, protecting a AUD605M banana industry. In the UK, the models shaped government responses to ash dieback, larch disease, and oak processionary moth. In California, they helped authorities contain citrus greening disease, protecting a USD3.84B industry and over 21,000 jobs. These models have driven cost-effective, real-time disease control globally. Read more...

description: Research in this topic highlighted and enabled the crucial role of translation and multilingual communication in global collaboration, diplomacy and cultural exchange. Case studies supported the training, support and professionalisation of translators across diverse international contexts. Work celebrated multilingual engagement in literature and performance, using translation as a tool for preserving and sharing heritage, fostering cross-cultural understanding and promoting inclusive, multicultural interaction.
narrative:
Improving conditions for subtitlers and increasing Netflix’s subtitled content coverage

Development of the first ever online subtitling test and indexing system, Hermes. Capable of working with 33 languages, Hermes increased Netflix’s language coverage from 16 to 32 languages in a year. A novel accreditation system measuring translation performance – the ‘Hermes number’ has become the de facto standard of accreditation in the industry and led to an increase in demand for subtitles and in subtitlers’ financial remuneration. Read more...

The Translator as Creative Writer: Transforming the Training, Professional Practice, and Public Status of Literary Translator

Project aimed at transforming the role of the literary translator from that of linguistic technician to publicly recognised creative writer. This project is based on an innovative model of translator training that has achieved global reach through collaboration with international cultural organisations, training events in countries from China to Mexico, and the publicly funded European framework for literary translator training (PETRA-E). The training programmes and Emerging Translator Mentorships, delivered in partnership with the National Centre for Writing (NCW), have led directly to the publication of newly translated novels, poetry, and non-fiction by highly regarded publishers. Read more...

description: This topic focuses on geology, fossil fuels and mining research, including policy development, extraction technologies, environmental protection measures, and resource management strategies across oil, gas, and mineral industries. The research encompasses studies on hydrocarbon reservoir management, geological exploration methods, mining techniques, as well as environmental impact mitigation, decommissioning strategies, safety protocols, digital analysis tools, and mathematical modeling approaches. Case studies often consider regulatory frameworks, industrial efficiency improvements, and sustainable resource extraction practices for energy and mining operations.
narrative:
Building on the success of mercury capture to drive change in the petroleum industry

A collaboration between Queen’s University Belfast and PETRONAS led to the industrial deployment of HycaPure™, an ionic liquid-based mercury removal technology, across thirteen Malaysian gas processing plants by 2017. The system captures all forms of mercury with significantly higher capacity and longer operational life than conventional scrubbers, reducing downtime, cutting replacement costs, and enhancing worker safety. Its success enabled PETRONAS to treat over 2.5 million tonnes of gas per plant annually while removing up to 700kg of mercury per train. HycaPure™ received the 2016 IChemE Oil and Gas Award and was licensed globally by Clariant. The collaboration also shifted PETRONAS’ research strategy, catalysing a new £2.4M programme on low-carbon technologies and embedding Queen’s-led innovation into the company’s long-term transition beyond conventional oil and gas. Read more...

Geoteric - Deep Learning for Hydrocarbon Exploration

A collaboration between the University of Lincoln and UK software company Geoteric led to the development of a deep learning-based system, “AI Faults,” which transformed geological fault detection in seismic surveys used for hydrocarbon exploration. Based on Lincoln’s research in image segmentation, the system enables rapid, automated interpretation of seismic data, dramatically accelerating the fault-mapping process from months to days while increasing accuracy. Licensed in 2018, the technology helped Geoteric expand its team, launch a new software-as-a-service business model, and complete 10 commercial projects in its first year. “AI Faults” has allowed clients to reduce drilling risks and avoid costly mistakes, including identifying a missed fault that previously led to £1 million in wasted drilling. It has strengthened Geoteric’s competitive position globally and enabled oil companies to extend asset life while improving environmental and operational efficiency. Read more...

New pyrolysis techniques delivering improved fuel additives and contributing to UK energy policy development

High-pressure pyrolysis techniques developed at the University of Nottingham have delivered major commercial and policy impacts. Global chemical company Innospec used the technology to analyse diesel injector deposits, enabling the development of 10 new fuel additives and influencing the direction of its USD600 million fuel additive business. This led to over USD200 million in sales and helped protect the company’s reputation by confirming its additives were not responsible for harmful engine deposits. The same pyrolysis techniques enabled a more accurate assessment of the UK’s shale gas reserves, revealing they were significantly lower than previously estimated. This evidence was cited by the Scottish Government in its 2019 parliamentary decision to reject support for fracking, and it played a key role in shaping public debate and influencing UK energy policy. Read more...

New geological approaches drive exploration strategies and accelerate economic growth in the minerals industry

New geological modelling and mineral fingerprinting techniques developed at the University of Leicester have transformed exploration and processing strategies in the mining industry, contributing over £408 million in gross value added to companies and regional economies in the UK, Greenland, and Zambia. In Zambia, these methods enabled the reopening of the Munali Nickel Mine, which had been closed due to uneconomic operations, by improving orebody understanding and guiding mining redesign—leading to the creation of around 500 jobs and generating over £37 million annually in nickel production. In Greenland, the identification of high-potential mineralisation zones led to new investment and the acquisition of an exploration company for £1.76 million, while also significantly expanding licensed exploration areas. Additionally, the application of these techniques at the Kitumba Copper Project in Zambia helped avoid £173 million in capital expenditure by optimising processing strategies, strengthening investment potential, and accelerating project development. Read more...

topic_name_long: International Law, Human Rights, Indigenous & Environmental Justice
description: Case studies in this topic inform the protection and enforcement of human rights and international legislation across a range of global contexts, including prisons, conflict and post-conflict zones, border, and authoritarian regimes. Collaborating with NGOs, governments, policy groups, and communities, this work contributes to reforming justice systems and establishing legal presidents, making human rights more universally definable, enforceable and recognised. The research informed conflict resolution, international law, and legal accountability for human rights violations, while raising awareness of the experience of persecuted groups, victims on historical and ongoing abuses, and those working to defend human rights. There is also a key focus in advocating for indigenous rights and environmental justice, supporting self-representation, land rights, and sustainable access to resources.
narrative:
The recognition of Aboriginal land and resource-related rights and claims, primarily in the common-law jurisdictions of Australasia and North America, as matters of legal status, political and historical treatment.

This research has caused widespread change in the concept of aboriginal land/resource title and has fundamentally changed the relationship between aboriginal people and the state. It has underpinned the reversal of the conception that aboriginal territories held by the British Crown were terrae nullius (nobody’s land), rather than territories subject to the authority of indigenous polities. The impact of this work since 2013 include landmark legal decisions which resolve both contemporary and historical claims to traditional resource rights. For example, the 2014 reinterpretation of the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi in New Zealand (between the British Crown and the Māori), the 2016 recognition of Maori title over the foreshore and seabed in the Re Tipene case, and the 2018 Alderville case settlement of £640 million, benefitting 3,800 members of the seven First Nations in Canada. Read more...

Effective torture prevention? Detention safeguards and the reduction of torture

Research showing that the best protection against torture is provided by safeguards when people are first arrested improved on previous policy which focused on monitoring detention places and prosecuting torturers. This research led UN anti-torture bodies and two prominent international NGOs to changed their approach to torture prevention and shaped policy and practice in the Republic of Georgia, Uruguay, Ethiopia, and the United Kingdom, leading to greater protection for thousands of people previously at risk of torture. Read more...

description: This topic addresses nuclear science, engineering, and policy research and their translation into safety standards, regulatory frameworks, and operational improvements across the nuclear sector. The research encompasses studies on reactor safety, materials, radioactive waste management, as well as radiation protection, decommissioning strategies, risk assessment, software, and modeling tools. Some case studies also consider tools for facilitating conversation and awareness in the nuclear sector.
narrative:
Innovative technology for radioactive waste managemen

Sheffield’s research transformed radioactive waste management by developing novel vitrification and hot isostatic pressing technologies that safely immobilise intermediate-level waste (ILW), including plutonium-contaminated materials previously lacking viable disposal routes. This work directly influenced UK nuclear waste policy and investment, leading to the planned construction of a new £100M thermal treatment plant and three demonstrator projects at Sellafield. It informed strategy at the Ministry of Defence for decommissioning nuclear submarines and underpinned key decisions by Radioactive Waste Management (RWM) and the US Department of Energy, where Sheffield’s durability testing method shaped revised standards and reduced vitrification costs at Hanford, the USA’s most contaminated nuclear site. The research, led by Professor Hyatt and his team, ensured compliance, improved safety, and significantly reduced waste volumes, while extensive public engagement raised awareness about nuclear waste risks and solutions among over a million people through media coverage and outreach. Read more...

Award-winning earthquake experiments underpin GBP4bn safe life extension of the UK’s fleet of Advanced Gas-cooled Reactor nuclear power stations

Groundbreaking earthquake simulation research by the University of Bristol directly enabled the continued safe operation of the UK’s Advanced Gas-cooled Reactor (AGR) nuclear fleet, safeguarding over £4 billion in low-carbon electricity generation. By constructing and shaking a high-precision, ¼-scale model of a cracked AGR graphite core, Bristol provided the first physical validation of EDF and Atkins’ GCORE seismic safety modelling. This evidence persuaded the UK’s Office for Nuclear Regulation to approve safety cases for reactor life extensions—preventing premature closure of multiple AGR stations and ensuring 14% of the UK’s electricity supply remained online. The research also strengthened EDF’s long-term strategic planning and built modelling capability at consultancy partner Atkins, while raising public awareness through major industry awards and the 2019 Royal Society Summer Science Exhibition. Without Bristol’s physical validation work, the UK’s AGRs would have shut from 2018 onward, posing serious risks to energy security and costing billions in lost clean energy production. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic advance understandings of mental health and promote the development of sustainable, patient-centred support systems across a range of settings. Research informed policy and practices in institutions such as government, healthcare, the military, education, and social services, foregrounding mental health and wellbeing as essential aspects of public health. Many highlight the needs of underserved or misunderstood groups, particularly in low-resources or culturally specific contexts for more informed, resilient and inclusive mental health provisions. Strong emphasis is placed on developing understandings of the relationship between mental health and media. There is particular emphasis on the role of media in shaping body image, eating disorders and mental wellbeing in young people and women, as well as safeguarding against digital addiction and social media ‘echo chambers’.
narrative:
Living With Feeling: Transforming Understandings of Emotional Health

Explored the difference between healthy and unhealthy human emotions through a Wellcome Trust funded project ‘Living with Feeling: Emotional Health in History, Philosophy, and Experience’ (LWF). Team engaged extensively through broadcast media, particularly Prof. Dixon. He has appeared on high-profile programmes on BBC Radio 3 and 4 with a circulation of 10,754,000, and his series on ‘Five Hundred Years of Friendship’ aired in a slot that attracted 2,500,000 listeners weekly. His podcast series, ‘The Sound of Anger’ has been nominated for 3 British Podcast Awards and won in the ‘Smartest’ and ‘Wellbeing’ categories. It has been streamed 14,200 times. The LWF collaborated with The Kemnal Academies Trust (TKAT) to design and deliver the Developing Emotions programme, a series of lessons for primary school children to enhance the emotional vocabulary and understanding of primary school children. Children’s emotional vocabulary expanded by 75%, and teachers reported an improvement in behavioural issues. Read more...

Intensive post-discharge support for child and adolescent mental health clients

The period after discharge from a mental health facility is associated with the highest risk of suicide and self-harm in adolescent mental health clients, due to a lack of social support and effective treatment upon discharge. Supported Discharge Service (SDS) was set up to fill this gap. SDS offers detailed assessment and evidence-based, individual, group and family treatment without significant disruption to education, family or leisure. The efficiency and cost-effectiveness of SDS has contributed to a shift away from inpatient treatment to an intensive community service delivery for longer term and more cost-effective results (average of £3,700 per patient). NHS England has now allocated £50,000,000 to post-discharge support for these patients. SDS has received international interest, with German adoption under the name ‘Hot-BITs’ (Home Treatment Brings Inpatient Treatments outside), with estimated treatment cost saving of over EUR 6,000 per patient. Read more...

Improving the management of physical health in people with severe mental illness in the UK NHS and internationally

This research identified the widening mortality gap for people with severe mental illness (SMI) and led to efforts to improve the management of physical health in people with severe mental illness in the UK NHS and internationally. This research has contributed to the development of new prediction tools and management strategies for people with severe mental illness (SMI) that have been adopted across the NHS, such as the use of the Lester tool for cardiovascular screening. This research led to the inclusion of annual cardiovascular screening for all patients with SMI as a central principal of the NHS 2019 Long Term Plan. It was fundamental to the development of a RightCare pathway for people with SMI in local health systems in England -- recommending use of the PRIMROSE intervention, an evidence-based, nurse-led service. It has also driven new guidelines worldwide on the need to effectively manage physical health among people with SMI, including The American Association Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients with Schizophrenia (2019), The Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety Treatments and International Society for Bipolar Disorders (2018), the physical health of people with severe mental illness (Ireland’s Mental Health Commission, 2018), and the Excess Mortality in Persons with Severe Mental Disorders (2016). Read more...

Sleeping on it: using history to understand and address today's 'sleep crisis'

Partnered with the National Trust (NT) in a public programming project to provide a series of exhibitions, workshops, outreach events, films, blog posts, and staff training exercises to bring public attention to the ‘sleep crisis’ and offer information and solutions based on historical research of how we used to sleep. The Tudor properly, Little Moreton Hall (LMH), hosted the bulk of the programme of events. 79,000 visitors in 2017 participated in the ‘Sleep Walk’ that demonstrated historic bedtime routines, bi-phasic sleep patterns, and sleep remedies. An increase in the number of visitors from 76,000 to 79,000 in 2017 was attributed to this attraction. The success of this partnership contributed to the NT being awarded the status of Independent Research Organisation by the AHRC on behalf of UKRI in 2019. The Children’s Sleep Charity and the British Academy partnered with ICS researchers to repurpose the educational materials developed through the NT outreach and events to engage school communities, comparing past and present healthcare strategies in relation to sleep and wellbeing, and improving public understanding of sleep’s importance for physical and mental health. The partnership with the CSC achieved the Foundation for Social Impact Award for ‘Small Charity, Big Achiever’, and the Royal Society for Public Health Award for ‘Children and Young People’. Read more...

Super Skills for Life: Transforming access to evidence-based mental health interventions for young people

Research on mental disorders in young people has underpinned the development and dissemination of Super Skills for Life (SSL), a transdiagnostic mental health intervention manual for children and adolescents. The SSL is designed for ease of dissemination, for example, in Malaysia one practitioner alone delivered SSL to 718 young people and trained 781 other practitioners. It has shaped the practice of 24,906 practitioners in 24 countries and has produced positive mental health outcomes in around 600,000 young people. Read more...

The HeadStart Learning Programme: changing policy and practice for young people’s mental health and wellbeing

HeadStart Learning Programme led by the Evidence Based Practice Unit at UCL was the first large-scale investigation of resilience-based approaches to support mental health and wellbeing of young people in England. Results have changed how 6 local authorities and 300 schools with 75,000 pupils identify and support young people experiencing mental health difficulties. A further 90 secondary schools outside the HeadStart Programme, serving an additional 15,000 pupils, have also been able to experience the benefits by implementing the findings and recommendations of the programme. Read more...

Mental health in early fatherhood: evidence-based development of the first NHS screening programme

As a result of Mayers’ research, the NHS introduced routine mental health checks and treatment for new and expectant fathers as of 2018. Mayers frequently appears in media to spread awareness, including The Washington Post, The Guardian, Sky News, Channel 5 News, BBC Radio 5 Live. He also worked with BBC Radio 4 on a documentary on fathers’ mental health (2019). The Movember charity worked with these research findings to launch the Movember Fathers Mental Health Business Plan, launched in 2021. Read more...

The Friendship Bench for common mental health problems

The introduction of the Friendship Bench approach in Zimbabwe, allowing grass roots, community-led mental health support, has been highly successful and attracted large additional funding. The course of training for lay health workers (non-professionals trained in ‘peer-supporting’ conversation) has been funded by international bodies, e.g., Grand Challenges Canada’s award of $852,000 in 2016 to enable Friendship Benches to be available to a further 14,000 people across 33 clinics in Zimbabwe. 112 Friendship Benches have provided therapy to over 63,000 people in areas that previously had little primary healthcare. The Friendship Bench intervention has been recognised in the WHO Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 2019 action plan. In its 2018 Depression and Anxiety Forum, the World Innovation Summit for Health (WISH) highlighted how Friendship Benches can reduce depression and increase adherence to HIV medication. Read more...

Transforming Green Exercise practice, strategy, funding and reach for vulnerable groups with complex needs

Essex Green Exercise (GE) researchers were the first to demonstrate that being active in nature resulted in significant improvements in mental health. GE researchers evaluated over 60 GE programmes, enabling organisations to deliver an increased number of improved programmes with greater funding opportunities. The Wilderness Foundations built resilience in 647 vulnerable teenagers with complex mental health issues, reaching 6,000 people per year on average. The Wildlife Trusts secured £550,000 fin unding for additional programmes. Future Roots (a Dorset-based care-farming charity) secured £140,000. Read more...

Changing how we understand and respond to the rising demands of beauty

Professor Widdows’ research contributed to the theory of ‘lookism’ (used to name appearance discrimination in activist circles) and the integration of the #EverydayLookism campaign into NGO practices and campaign messaging. In the three weeks following its launch, the #EverydayLookism campaign received 74,886 video views, 13,449 engagements, and 1.03 million people saw the campaign. To date (at time of ICS authorship), the EverydayLookism blogs have over 46,000 views and the campaign has received over 800 story submissions. Anti-bullying campaign Ditch the Label included a chapter on lookism in the Annual Bullying Survey for the first time in 2019. The Mental Health Foundation’s briefing paper ‘Image-editing Apps and Mental Health’ recommended engagement with #EverydayLookism. Widdows’ comments in support of this paper were quoted in 264 outlets, reaching an audience of 11.6 million. Widdows’ work was instrumental in the intervention of the Nuffield Council of Bioethics (NCoB) in the report ‘Cosmetic Procedures: Ethical Issues’ (2017). Read more...

Journey into SPACE: evidence-based design of an app to reduce digital addiction

The SPACE app offers users real-time harm-reduction strategies for those struggling with digital usage. It promotes self-control and helps users achieve life/phone balance. It has been downloaded more than 2,000,000 times and has 1,000,000 active users in 21 countries. It has a user rating of 4.2/5 and was featured as an ‘Essential App’ on Google’s Play Store. User data suggests that app users spend an average of 2h46m on their phones per day compared to the average US citizen usage of 3h54m. Read more...

ICD-11 Complex Posttraumatic Stress Disorder: Introduction of a new psychological disorder and a tailored diagnostic assessment tool

This research contributed to the World Health Organisation's (WHO) classification of C-PTSD as a recognised disorder, and the development of the only globally recognised and utilised tool for its assessment, the International Trauma Questionnaire (ITQ). The ITQ is freely available online in 22 languages and is recommended by the President of the UK Psychological Trauma Society and the lead of the Royal College of Psychiatrists. Organisations have used the ITQ for research on around 50,000 participants. Read more...

The Improving Access to Psychology Therapies (IAPT) programme: better recovery for people with anxiety disorders and depression

The (Improving Access to Psychology Therapies) IAPT programme has trebled in sized from 2013-2020, from seeing 434,000 people a year with depression and/or anxiety related problems to ~1,200,000 people per year. In its Long Term Plan, the NHS has committed to increase this usage further. The recovery rate for those who received a course of psychological treatment has improved from 43-52% in England during the REF period (meaning that 230,000 more people recover and 314,000 more improve than in 2013). The media and international impact has been such that an article discussing IAPT in the Canadian Globe and Mail was simply titled ‘For better mental health care in Canada: look to Britain’. Read more...

Hellblade: engaging video game players with Viking culture and contributing to success and innovation within the creative sector

Researchers brought together Anglo-Saxon and Viking history and Neuroscience to aid game developers in designing an accurate depiction of a Viking world and of the experience of psychosis. The resulting game, Hellblade, allows players to engage with a unique depiction of psychosis in a particular historical context as the main character embarks on a journey to rescue their dead lover from the underworld while suffering from a curse that causes them to experience the voices of spirits in their head. This case study is an excellent example of interdisciplinary research helping to develop public understanding by repackaging the issues at hand in innovative and engaging ways. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic address the complex relationships between food, diet and health across a range of contexts. Research in this topic informed NGOs, governments and the food industry on issues such as food marketing, insecurity, accessibility and sustainability. Work supports the fostering of healthy eating habits and contributes scientific understanding of diet-related diseases and development of interventions to reduce their impact. A number of case studies focus on education and early-life intervention, influencing school-based policies and lifelong health education to promote informed, sustainable dietary habits from an early age.
narrative:
Breakfast research informs national school breakfast provision, local public health breakfast interventions, and Corporate Social Responsibility marketing

Research demonstrating the positive impact of breakfast consumption on cognitive function, academic performance, and classroom behaviour of children and adolescents. This research led policy change in England, including the expansion of a government funded national school breakfast programme to an additional 650 schools. It also underpinned the process that brought the School Breakfast Bill into Parliament. It has had similar impacts on a food industry-funded national breakfast club programme by Kellogg, expanding to an additional 300 schools. A Local Authority Public Health breakfast intervention has been introduced to ease the impact of COVID-19 lockdown on over 2,500 children in areas of deprivation. Read more...

Unhealthy food advertising to children: Impacting on a watershed policy

Research directly informed change of government policy around unhealthy food advertising to children. The research proved that the earlier legislation introduced in 2009 to prevent unhealthy food advertising during children’s television programming was ineffective. The recommendations of the research were taken up by various government bodies and NGOs. The report submitted to the Childhood Obesity Inquiry in 2018 was cited as a major factor in reassessment of the policies, particularly the predictions that a watershed would reduce childhood obesity by around 5% and save the NHS £7,400,000,000. The recommendation of a watershed on unhealthy food advertising was corroborated by the Department of Health and Social Care and the UK Government implemented a 9pm watershed on unhealthy food advertising. Read more...

Mindful Construal Reflection: A novel intervention which promotes healthier eating habits

The Mindful Construal Diary and the online version, the Mindful Construal Reflection tool, allow users to identify and change their eating behaviours, particularly in relation to grazing and comfort eating. The MCR has been adopted for clinical use in several NHS trusts in the UK and has influenced practice of care internationally. Read more...

The Sensory Play Toolkit for Parents and Professionals: A Game-Based Intervention to Increase Food Acceptance in Picky Eaters

The Sensory Play Toolkit (SPT) is a free, caregiver-led, evidence-based intervention for children with ARFID (Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder – ‘extreme picky eating’). The SPT is comprised of a 28-page paper workbook that parents and children can fill in together, designed to integrate new food experiences through play. It has provided strategies and support for parents, professionals, and organisations from 38 countries. It has been accessed by 2,500 individual families directly through download from the internet, as well as distribution by 1,500 professionals to ~52,339 users. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic worked to preserve Welsh and Gaelic languages and promote their learning to safeguard and broaden current and future usage. Several provided practical means by collating and improving access to resources such as dictionaries and online databases. Case studies also worked to recognise and improve language diversity, recognising the social and economic benefits of such multilingualism. This included introducing their official use in more settings, such as schools, workplaces and courts of law. Many underpinned governmental policies to support their acquisition and wider use. This was largely seen in language teaching in schools and online classes enabled by case studies providing resource access, teacher training and development of curricula. Addressing ‘linguistic fragility’ in native-speaking communities reconnected with heritage and supported rich cultural partnerships that fostered a strong sense of community and identity on local, regional and national scales.
narrative:
GPC: The authoritative dictionary of the Welsh language

The Geiriadur Prifysgol Cymru (GPC) is a historical dictionary similar to the Oxford English Dictionary. It plays a key role in standardising and promoting access to the Welsh language, receiving funding from the Welsh Government in 2016 as part of its Cymraeg 2050 project to increase the number of Welsh speakers to a million by 2015. The number of entries consulted has risen from 216,418 in 2014 to 3,236,543 in 2020. Mobile app usage increased from 303,239 in 2016 to 1,263,384 in 2020. Read more...

Language technology for Welsh as a less-resourced language

This research has influenced policy as part of the Cymraeg 2050 project, fostering daily use of Welsh, providing assistive technology, and supporting the use of Welsh in industry. Cysgliad, a Welsh spelling and grammar checker, the only of its kind, is licenced to 492 public and private authorities, with an additional 5,392 individual licenses. 270,000,000 words were added to the free-use online Cysill Ar-lein corpus between 2015-2020. Read more...

Rediscovering Ireland’s Past in Words

The Electronic Dictionary of the Irish Language is a historical dictionary that reveals the development of the language over a millennium. The dictionary has had 200,000 unique users over the last five years with nearly 3,400,000 million page views. Read more...

description: This topic addresses reasearch into healthcare ethics and health data governance and their translation into policy frameworks, regulatory standards, and clinical practice guidelines. The research encompasses studies on patient privacy and data protection, clinical research governance, end-of-life care ethics, as well as digital security methods, anonymization frameworks, and ethical decision-making tools. Case studies often demonstrate how ethical research influences healthcare policy, regulatory approval processes, and professional practice standards. The topic includes examples of successful ethics-to-policy translation that improve patient safety, data security, and ethical standards across healthcare systems.
narrative:
