The ethical approval of mitochondrial replacement therapy

In December 2014, the UK Parliament approved regulations allowing the licencing of mitochondrial replacement treatment, a pioneering medical intervention to prevent the transmission from mother to child of extremely serious genetic conditions. The process was guided by input from ethics philosophy on the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority (HFEA). Read more...

Improving the Governance and Efficacy of Rare Disease Research by Ensuring the Integration of Patients’ Perspectives

Woods’ and McCormack’s research led to the inclusion of a patient representative in the governance structures of the TREAT-NMD Alliance (The Alliance). The Alliance is made up of 258 organisations. Forty percent of members of the TREAT-NMD Project Ethics Council (PEC) established by Woods and McCormack are patient advocates, bringing patient voices to responses to ethical issues related to rare disease research. The principles and consent guide, produced through workshops organised by Woods and McCormack between 2013-2018, was adopted by the International Rare Diseases Research Consortium and was translated into a code of conduct in 2015. Written compliance with the code of conduct is now a condition of access to the RD-Connect platform, thereby committing signees to implementing patient-centred values. Read more...

description: This topic addresses software engineering, hardware development, and digital technologies research and their translation into commercial products, industrial applications, and societal benefits. The research encompasses studies on software verification, embedded systems, semiconductor design, as well as open-source development tools, formal modeling approaches, and digital platform technologies. Case studies often discuss product development, industry standards, and technological innovation across a vast range of applications. The topic includes examples of successful technology transfer including new start-up companies, open-source software adoption, hardware optimization, and digital solutions that improve efficiency, reliability, and accessibility across multiple sectors.
narrative:
The Infer Tool for Automatic Verification of Memory Violations in Software System

The University of Greenwich’s Computational Mechanics and Reliability Group (CMRG) has transformed high-reliability electronics design through advanced modelling techniques that predict how and when components will fail. Their work has directly informed the design protocols of aerospace leader Leonardo, removing over £30 million in design and qualification risk for critical radar systems. Collaborations with Micross Semiconductors improved understanding of hot solder dipping, enabling growth in high-reliability component refinishing services. In partnership with Microsemi, CMRG’s models enabled the adoption of 3D-printed electronics, cutting production costs and time-to-market by 10% and reducing material waste by up to 3%. Globally, the group's research has shaped IEEE standards and industry roadmaps, with Professor Bailey leading the “Modelling and Simulation” chapter of the Heterogeneous Integration Roadmap—downloaded over 24,000 times—guiding global best practice beyond Moore’s Law. Their design-for-reliability methods are now embedded in practice across aerospace, defence, and electronics industries, driving quality, safety, and cost-efficiency worldwide. Read more...

UltraSoC Technologies - On-chip debug, monitoring and analytics infrastructures to accelerate semiconductor product development and ensure trust

Essex University’s research into scalable, low-overhead on-chip debug and analytics infrastructure for complex multiprocessor systems-on-chip (MPSoCs) led to the formation of UltraSoC Technologies, a spinout that transformed semiconductor development. The novel debug architecture—compact, vendor-agnostic, and capable of real-time monitoring—enabled dramatic reductions in development time and cost, doubling profitability and improving safety and reliability in consumer, industrial, and automotive chips. UltraSoC licensed its technology to over 20 major semiconductor firms including ARM, Intel, Huawei, and Seagate, and became the de facto debug standard for RISC-V processors. Its capability to detect faults, bugs, and cyber threats in deployed systems led to its acquisition by Siemens in 2020, integrating into the global giant’s silicon lifecycle management strategy. UltraSoC’s technology, built on Essex’s foundational research, now underpins mission-critical chips across AI, automotive, storage, and cybersecurity domains, and continues to shape industry standards in silicon trust, resilience, and performance analytics. Read more...

GraphicsFuzz: Reliable and Secure Graphics Programming

GraphicsFuzz, developed at Imperial College London, is a groundbreaking tool that uses metamorphic testing to automatically uncover critical bugs in GPU compilers and drivers. Originating from research into reliable many-core programming, it found serious security vulnerabilities in compilers from all major GPU vendors, prompting the spin-out of GraphicsFuzz Ltd., which was acquired by Google in 2018. Now integrated into Google's Android and Chrome platforms—used by billions of people—GraphicsFuzz is essential to ensuring graphics driver reliability, with its tests embedded in the Android Compatibility Test Suite and Vulkan Conformance Test Suite. The research also led to GPUVerify and CLsmith, tools adopted by ARM and Codeplay to improve verification and testing of GPU software, collectively making GPU applications safer, more secure, and more robust for global users. Read more...

Sensorless control of high efficiency drives for consumer appliance

Newcastle University’s research into sensorless control of electric motors has delivered major advances in electronics for consumer appliances. By eliminating the need for physical position sensors, the technology uses voltage and current measurements to digitally estimate rotor position—significantly reducing component count, cost, and control complexity. This innovation enables highly compact, ultra-high-speed brushless motors (over 110,000 rpm), which are smaller, lighter, and more energy efficient than traditional designs. Adopted by UK-based manufacturer Dyson in its Supersonic hair dryer and extended to next-generation vacuum platforms, the sensorless control system supports advanced motor integration, improved production consistency, and streamlined electronics architecture. It enables simplified drive electronics, better thermal management, and more ergonomic product design, while saving £7–10 million annually in production costs and helping to reduce global emissions from small electric appliances. Read more...

description: This topic brings together research that has shaped the design, regulation, and integrity of democratic processes in the UK and internationally. Case studies address the mechanics of democracy—from electoral system design and boundary reform to the regulation of campaign finance and polling practices. Contributions include improving election polling methodologies and informing public understanding of polling accuracy, as well as shaping electoral policy, such as campaign regulation. Internationally, research has informed electoral integrity efforts, supported peaceful transfers of power, and improved democratic oversight through legislative reform and election monitoring. These impacts have strengthened public confidence in democratic institutions and enhanced the fairness and functionality of electoral systems.
narrative:
Improving the Quality of British Elections: Balancing Access with Integrity

This research informed policy changes and the introduction of safeguards to improve the integrity of British elections. The Electoral Commission (EC) started its Crimestoppers campaign ‘Your Vote is Yours Alone’ on the basis of research findings concerning fear of reporting fraud among vulnerable groups, especially women who might not speak English very well. The research report was welcomed by Parliamentarians, helping to correct the issue of MP’s often relying on local knowledge and a few high-profile cases to make unrepresentative legal judgements. In 2019, the research recommendations became manifesto promises, election manifestos, and appeared in the Queens Speech. This work has influenced organisations and campaigns working to improve under-registration, e.g., the Democracy Fund hosted by the Joseph Rowntree Reform Trust which raised over £1 million. Read more...

Influencing the 2017 Supreme Court judgment to overturn the Presidential election result in Kenya

Cardiff University research demonstrated the failure of the Kenyan Supreme Court to reinforce gains in electoral integrity made in the new constitution in 2010, and the court's risk of undermining those gains. This research underpinned challenges to the presidential election result in Kenya in 2017. AfriCOG, a leading civil society organisation monitoring issues in Kenya, drew on the research in its 2015 Policy Forum, and it was also cited by AfriCOG in their case to the International Criminal Court at the Hague in 2015 against sitting President Uhru Kenyatta and Vice-President William Ruto for their roles in post-election violence in 2007-8. The research was used in training for the Kenyan Judiciary ahead of the 2017 petition. Read more...

Informing British Democracy: The Impact of the British Election Study on the Media, Polling, and Political Party Decision-making

The British Election Study (BES), led by the University of Manchester team since 2013, collaborated with ITV News to shape coverage of the 2015, 2017, and 2019 General Elections, as well as the 2016 EU Referendum. Traditional coverage relied on analysis of aggregate level data, leading to false representation of individual voters and groups. The new approach, using survey date collected before and during election campaigns, allowed ITV to better inform the audience of voter opinions and motivations. The BES research was increasingly cited following the UoM team taking over, with a more than ten-fold increase in print media articles mentioning the BES in the 6 years since UoM took over. BES research has impacted British democracy by providing data which shapes the behaviour of the Conservative and Labour parties through understanding of voter movements, campaign resources, and post-election analyses. Read more...

Securing Elections, Defending Democracy, and Protecting Human Rights in Europe, Africa and North America

Dr. Klaas’s research has led to changes in international policy to prevent authoritarian regimes that agree to hold elections from using pseudo-democratic strategies. Klaas has consulted with institutions including NATO, the UK Foreign and Cabinet Offices, the European Union, and the Italian Foreign Ministry. His work helped to enable NATO to intervene in Tunisia to ease exclusion politics and pseudo-democratic strategies related to water scarcity. Other reports have aided the Transatlantic Commission on Election Integrity (2019) to put pressure on Western governments and the Ukrainian government to safeguard early-stage democracy. His research has led to human rights lobbying in Madagascar, particularly related to human rights abuse by Chinese investors, and a greater public understanding of the debates around the ongoing decline of global democracy. His How to Rig an Election lecture given in answer to Indian President Narendra Modi’s claim that it is impossible to rig an election gathered 11,966 views on YouTube. He has appeared in over 500 media interviews since 2018 as a political expert. He has appeared on BBC Radio 4’s The Today Programme 9 times, with an average of 1,000,000 listeners each time, and his Washington Post column has an average page view of 80,062 people. His podcast series, ‘Power Corrupts’, has been downloaded 1,670,000 times across 207 countries. Read more...

description: This topic addresses air pollution research and its translation into policy, regulation, and technological solutions to protect public health and environmental quality. The research encompasses studies on the health impacts of both outdoor and indoor air pollution, as well as sampling/sensing technologies, statistical modeling approaches and air quality data are included. Case studies often demonstrate how scientific evidence influences policy interventions and applications extend across public health policy, environmental regulation, urban planning, industrial compliance, climate change mitigation, and technological innovation in air quality monitoring and pollution control systems.
narrative:
Improving Indoor Air Quality and Ventilation Standards in UK Housin

Glasgow School of Art’s Mackintosh Environmental Architecture Research Unit (MEARU) has significantly advanced understanding of how airtight, low-energy housing can compromise indoor air quality (IAQ), with profound implications for occupant health. Their research exposed how poor ventilation and lack of occupant awareness result in high levels of carbon dioxide, humidity, and airborne pollutants—conditions linked to respiratory problems and other health risks. MEARU’s findings directly influenced changes to Scottish Building Standards in 2015, improving ventilation design in over 86,000 new homes. Their work has also shaped architectural practice, public health guidance, and housing association policy, contributing to reduced emissions in retrofit housing, improved occupant wellbeing, and wider recognition of indoor pollution as a key health issue in energy-efficient homes. Read more...

Robust and reliable digitalisation of the automotive industry: improvements in 3D CFD modelling of particulate matter emissions

Oxford Brookes University’s Engine Modelling Team developed cutting-edge 3D CFD models that uncovered how low piston surface temperatures in gasoline direct injection (GDI) engines lead to the formation of harmful ultra-fine particulate matter (PM), a major contributor to air pollution and global health risk. Their discovery of ‘Limiting Temperatures for the Retainment of Liquid Film’ revealed a key mechanism behind pollution spikes during engine acceleration and warm-up. This insight has driven a shift in practice at Ford Motor Company, informing new piston technologies and calibration strategies to reduce PM emissions at the source. The models have also been embedded into Siemens and Ricardo’s global engine simulation platforms, enabling industry-wide adoption of cleaner, low-emission engine design and helping meet future air quality regulations without relying solely on filtration technologies. Read more...

Improving air quality in Scotland’s cities using statistical modelling

University of Glasgow researchers developed advanced statistical modelling tools, including a fast and accurate emulator of the ADMS-Urban air quality model, enabling the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (SEPA) to assess compliance risks and predict pollution levels across Scottish cities. These tools directly informed the National Modelling Framework and supported the design and implementation of Scotland’s Low Emission Zones (LEZs), starting in Glasgow in 2018. UofG’s high-resolution pollution mapping and health impact analyses provided critical evidence of the links between air quality and cardiovascular and respiratory diseases. Their modelling now underpins policy decisions to reduce emissions and improve urban health across Scotland. Read more...

Definitive demonstration of the adverse cardiovascular effects of air pollution leads to policy change at the local, national and international level

Groundbreaking research by the University of Edinburgh definitively demonstrated that air pollution, especially ultrafine particles from vehicle exhaust, directly harms cardiovascular health—causing vascular dysfunction, exacerbating heart disease, and crossing into the bloodstream to accumulate in diseased tissues. This work shifted scientific consensus from correlation to causation, influencing major policy changes. It prompted the British Heart Foundation to make air pollution its top prevention priority, spurred UK and Scottish clean air strategies (including Low Emission Zones), informed WHO guideline revisions, and shaped legislation across Europe. The research underpins public health campaigns and new clinical guidance, contributing to global efforts to reduce pollution and prevent cardiovascular disease. Read more...

description: This topic considers the area of veterinary science and animal welfare, covering companion animal health, livestock management, and wildlife conservation. Development of improved diagnostic tools, treatment methods, and welfare assessment techniques is a large component of this topic. This topic includes case studies that demonstrate advances in disease prevention, vaccine development, genetic testing, and surveillance systems that improve animal health outcomes, as well as welfare standards through housing improvements, pain assessment tools, and evidence-based management practices across domestic, farm, and laboratory animals. Applications span across veterinary medicine, agricultural production, food safety, policy development, and conservation amongst others.
narrative:
Reduction of antibiotic use and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) in livestock agriculture

Research by the University of Cambridge identified a novel strain of MRSA (mecC) and uncovered previously unrecognized livestock-associated MRSA (LA-MRSA) in the UK food chain. These discoveries revealed significant public health risks and reshaped understanding of antimicrobial resistance transmission between animals and humans. The findings influenced UK and EU policy, including new EU legislation restricting antibiotic use in farming, and informed national risk assessments and professional guidelines. These efforts contributed to a 45% reduction in antibiotic use in UK agriculture (2014–2019), a 90% drop in use of critical cephalosporins in dairy cows, and the eradication of detectable mecC and mecA MRSA in UK food-producing animals by 2019. Read more...

Simultaneous administration of multiple live respiratory vaccine viruses in day-old broiler chicks for better production worldwide

Research led by the University of Liverpool has transformed global vaccination practices in broiler poultry production by demonstrating that simultaneous administration of live infectious bronchitis (IB) Mass, IB Variant (793B), and Newcastle disease (ND) vaccines in day-old chicks is safe and effective. This co-vaccination strategy simplifies hatchery protocols, reduces stress, and improves bird welfare. It has been widely adopted in over a dozen countries, replacing traditional staggered vaccine schedules. Producers have reported enhanced flock performance, including reduced mortality, better feed conversion, higher body weights, and fewer carcass condemnations—translating into millions of pounds in additional revenue and benefits for commercial and smallholder farmers worldwide. Read more...

Animal welfare impact assessment, Brexit and sentience policy

This research has significantly influenced post-Brexit policy on sentient species in the UK. It has provided expert input into the founding of the ‘Better Deal for Animals’ (BDA) coalition, with membership of over 40 national and international UK-based NGOs. BDA has lobbied the UK government for animal welfare impact assessment and the establishment of an Animal Welfare Commission. A 2018 Parliament Petition received over 100,000 signatories, leading to debate of these matters. The Labour Party Official Opposition publicly supported an Animal Welfare Commission – as of July 2020 the implementation of sentience policy is still being decided. Read more...

Extending high quality life of dogs with asymptomatic canine mitral valve diseas

Research at the Royal Veterinary College led by Professor Adrian Boswood showed that early treatment of dogs with asymptomatic degenerative mitral valve disease (DMVD) using pimobendan (Vetmedin®) extends their symptom-free life by an average of 15 months. The pivotal “EPIC” trial provided strong evidence for treating dogs in the preclinical B2 stage, leading to regulatory approval for expanded drug use across the EU, UK, Australia, Japan, and China. This work has influenced international clinical guidelines, improved canine quality of life, and supported the development of a diagnostic algorithm (now a patent-pending app) to identify suitable candidates for treatment in general veterinary practice. Read more...

description: This topic considers the treatment and prevention of breast cancer, ovarian cancer, and their related conditions. Development of improved therapeutic approaches, diagnostic tools, and personalized treatment strategies is a large component of this topic. Case studies for improved patient outcomes include improved treatments through risk assessment tools, radiotherapy innovations, and patient-centered care approaches, as well as cancer prevention strategies, therapy optimisations, surgical techniques, and supportive care. Initiatives often focus on clinical implementation and evidence-based decision-making to improve survival rates and quality of life for cancer patients.
narrative:
Approval of Tamoxifen for Breast Cancer Preventio

Research at Queen Mary University of London demonstrated that a five-year course of tamoxifen provides a 20-year preventive effect against breast cancer in women at increased risk. This pivotal evidence led to major changes in international clinical guidelines and regulatory approvals. Since 2013, tamoxifen has been recommended in the US by bodies such as the US Preventive Services Task Force and the American Cancer Society. In 2016, Australia licensed tamoxifen for preventive use and added it to the national Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme. In 2018, the UK approved tamoxifen for primary prevention, potentially benefiting 500,000 women. The research has significantly expanded access to low-cost, effective breast cancer prevention. Read more...

Reducing breast and ovarian cancer occurrences in women at high risk

The University of Cambridge developed BOADICEA, a personalised, web-based tool that predicts breast and ovarian cancer risk by integrating genetic, lifestyle, and clinical data. Widely adopted across 91 countries and endorsed by NICE, the American Cancer Society, and other global health bodies, BOADICEA empowers women and clinicians to make informed decisions about preventive actions such as prophylactic surgery and enhanced screening. Its use has improved clinical outcomes, reduced unnecessary procedures, and informed national guidelines and major international screening trials, contributing to earlier cancer detection and prevention and ultimately saving lives. Read more...

description: This topic considers the area of meteorological and climate science, covering weather forecasting, climate modeling, and atmospheric research. Development of improved prediction systems and observational technologies is a large component of this topic. Case studies demonstrate advances in forecasting accuracy and extreme weather attribution that improve public safety and economic outcomes, as well as climate resilience through satellite data analysis, risk assessment, and automated prediction systems. Applications are broad and span across aviation safety, urban planning, disaster risk reduction, insurance analysis, and international development amongst others. The topic also includes initiatives focused on technology transfer and capacity building to promote climate adaptation and societal resilience.
narrative:
Policy implications of revised uncertainties related to climate change

Research at Durham University developed foundational Bayesian statistical methods to quantify uncertainties in complex computer models of physical systems—methods that were directly adopted by the UK Met Office in the UK Climate Projections (UKCP09 and UKCP18). These projections underpin the UK’s statutory Climate Change Risk Assessments (CCRA) and the National Adaptation Programmes (NAP), informing government climate policies, infrastructure planning, and investment decisions across sectors. Durham’s work enabled more rigorous risk quantification, making probabilistic climate scenarios accessible to planners and decision-makers, and significantly enhancing the UK’s capacity for evidence-based adaptation to climate change. Read more...

Satellite data processing and analysis techniques enabled better forecasting for improved drought resilience in Africa

Swansea University’s GEMEO group developed new satellite-based techniques to more accurately measure atmospheric aerosols and surface albedo—two critical variables for climate and weather modelling. These methods led to high-quality global datasets that improved weather and air quality forecasts by major agencies including the UK Met Office and ECMWF. Swansea’s aerosol data significantly reduced modelling error and was integrated into ECMWF’s CAMS Reanalysis, used by the WHO and others. Their albedo data improved temperature forecasts in the Met Office’s global model and informed simulations submitted to the IPCC. Swansea’s products are now part of operational satellite services, and serve as international benchmarks for climate model evaluation. Read more...

Global satellite data for improved climate and weather predictions

Sussex University’s AstroCast project, building on astrophysics methods originally developed for space telescopes, enabled highly accurate short-term forecasting of vegetation health to support drought early warning systems (EWS) in sub-Saharan Africa. By adapting astronomical data techniques, the team developed novel models predicting Vegetation Condition Index (VCI) up to six weeks in advance with exceptional accuracy. These forecasts are now integrated into Kenya’s national EWS, influencing government and Red Cross preparedness actions and contingency funding. The tools have also been adopted by regional bodies and are guiding anticipatory drought response across Africa, strengthening institutional capacity and resilience to climate shocks. Read more...

Improved turbulence forecasts for the aviation sector

Research at the University of Reading led to the development of a new clear-air turbulence forecasting algorithm—the Lighthill–Ford method—now operationally used by the US National Weather Service and private weather companies, improving flight safety, efficiency, and environmental outcomes for nearly 5 billion passengers by 2020. The algorithm significantly outperforms previous systems, extending forecast lead times and reducing unpredicted turbulence encounters. Furthermore, Reading’s discovery that climate change is increasing turbulence has catalyzed innovation across the aviation sector, prompting Airbus to develop automated turbulence-reporting systems and IATA to launch a global platform for real-time turbulence data sharing, marking a transformative shift in aviation safety and operations. Read more...

description: This topic focuses on high-performance computing, data analytics, and distributed systems applications across business, scientific research, and public sectors. It encompasses supercomputing, cloud platforms, big data processing, and data governance for improved computational efficiency and decision-making. Some studies demonstrating industrial transformation including manufacturing optimization, financial services, and public sector digitalization are incorporated. Case studies also cover computational infrastructure, data science methodologies, and associated security considerations. Key themes include system scalability, algorithmic optimization, and commercial applications across finance, healthcare, manufacturing, and defense.
narrative:
New computer systems for exploiting big environmental data for worldwide usability, model and policy development

Research at the University of Reading has transformed the global handling of massive environmental datasets through pioneering technologies enabling petascale data analysis. Central to this achievement is the design and implementation of JASMIN, a unique computational facility supporting over 1,500 users and enabling key scientific and policy outputs, from UK biodiversity monitoring to African climate insurance services. The work also shaped the global Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF), underpinning the IPCC’s climate assessments. Standards and tools developed at Reading have been adopted by major organisations like EUMETSAT and the UK Met Office, significantly enhancing interoperability, operational efficiency, and global scientific collaboration. Read more...

A secure and scalable cloud computing platform to support SMEs and public sector organisations through economic impact and efficiency gain

A suite of cloud computing technologies developed at the University of Westminster—including the CloudSME Simulation Platform (CSSP), CloudiFacturing Platform (CFGP), and MiCADO—has enabled over 86 SMEs across Europe to improve efficiency and competitiveness. These tools have directly supported the creation of 550+ new products or services, generated over €100 million in turnover growth, and helped establish more than 1,100 new commercial partnerships. A commercial provider based on this technology reported strong financial returns, and public sector users in Spain and the UK have achieved measurable gains in service delivery, efficiency, and customer satisfaction. Read more...

Impact Lab: An Environmental and Big Data Hub for SMEs

The University of Plymouth’s Environmental Futures & Big Data Impact Lab has directly supported 43 SMEs—16 via the university’s Centre of Mathematical Sciences—using advanced data analytics and machine learning techniques. Its research enabled the creation of predictive tools that reduced costs and improved efficiency in the insurance sector (e.g., for Software Solved), and increased sales for leading digital printing firm Harrier through improved demand forecasting. The Lab also addressed regional skills shortages by delivering CPD courses in Data Science and Big Data to over 200 participants, contributing to workforce upskilling and innovation adoption across multiple sectors. Read more...

description: This topic showcases case studies addressing the representation, rights and experiences of LGBTQ+ communities across a range of social, legal and cultural contexts. Research in this topic informed legal frameworks, policy and institutional practices to improve understanding of diverse sexual and gender identities and provide better protection against discrimination and hate crime. Areas of focus include cultural heritage and visibility, mental health and wellbeing, and LGBTQ+ experiences in institutions such as the police, military, education and government. Case studies also explore issues in areas such as adoption, marital law, and asylum, working to advance equity, representation and social justice for LGBTQ+ communities.
narrative:
Re-shaping Approaches to LGBT+ History in the Museums, Archives and Heritage Sectors

The researcher written guidebook, Prejudice and Pride, was central to the National Trust’s flagship project of the same name, broadening access to LGBT+ heritage and setting up a 2017 programme that drew over 350,000 visitors. Read more...

Sexualities, History and Heritage: Bringing LGBTQ Heritage into the Mainstream

This project encouraged heritage sites in Britain to reference their LGBTQ (lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer) histories in their interpretation. It led Historic England to commit to a greater diversity of histories in their properties and achieved 22 new and amended listings of nationally protected sites on the National Heritage List for England. Read more...

Changing hearts and minds: How the stories of older LGBT people are changing attitudes, education and care

RUFUS STONE is a research-based drama exploring the life of an older gay man in rural England, developed to challenge discrimination around sexuality and ageing. Grounded in in-depth qualitative research, the film addresses loneliness, marginalisation, and social stigma. It has had global impact, screened in festivals, community cinemas, and universities across 73 countries, earning awards and critical acclaim, including coverage in The New York Times.In education, the film has been adopted into teaching at universities in the UK, Portugal, Turkey, and Kazakhstan, prompting student-teachers to reconsider inherited social values. In frontline care, it has shaped diversity training at Hampshire County Council, the Alzheimer’s Society, and Help and Care UK. Staff reported a shift in awareness and empathy, with some institutions crediting the film with long-term cultural change, including inspiring the county’s first Gay Pride. RUFUS STONE has proven to be a catalyst for inclusivity in both education and care sectors. Read more...

topic_name_long: Military: Personnel, Ethics, Equipment, Strategy & Intelligence
description: This topic showcases research that has strengthened military effectiveness, ethics, and support systems across defence institutions in the UK and internationally. Case studies span improvements to personnel performance and wellbeing—including training protocols, equipment upgrades, and digital support services for veterans and families—as well as research that shaped ethical frameworks for military decision-making, drone operation, and cultural property protection. Strategic insights informed UK foreign and defence policy, enhanced defence intelligence tradecraft, and contributed to doctrine development and preparedness. Other work supported transparency in biodefence, improved weapons acquisition practices, and shaped regulation of emerging technologies such as autonomous weapons systems.
narrative:
Novel biodetection technologies: protecting armed forces and civilians from biological attacks, strengthening crop protection and delivering economic impact.

The University of Hertfordshire’s Centre for Research in Biodetection Technologies (CRBT) developed advanced microfluidic systems that significantly enhanced the UK’s ability to detect airborne biological threats. Their research underpinned the Biological Surveillance and Collector System (BSCS), now in service with the RAF, protecting troops from biological attacks. The system also became an export product for civilian security (Spinnaker), contributing to national safety and economic growth. CRBT’s innovations additionally led to SporeSentry, an early warning system for crop disease, now integrated with the UK-wide CropMonitor Pro platform, improving agricultural resilience and food security. Read more...

SafeSeas: Building Effective Capacities for Maritime Security

The University of Bristol’s SafeSeas programme has significantly shaped global maritime security policy and practice by providing the first systematic analysis of maritime security capacity building. Its research informed the UK’s cross-government maritime strategy, securing a £9 million increase in maritime security spending and contributing to the creation of the UK Joint Maritime Operations and Coordination Centre. SafeSeas' Best Practice Toolkit has been adopted by the US, Nigeria, the EU, and international organisations like UNODC and the Djibouti Code of Conduct, guiding training, strategy, and investment in the Western Indian Ocean, Gulf of Guinea, and South East Asia. Read more...

The mental health of military personnel, veterans and their families: informing policy, interventions and investmen

Research from the King’s Centre for Military Health Research has provided the UK’s most authoritative evidence on the mental health of serving personnel, veterans, and their families, directly informing national policy, service provision, and investment. Through its large-scale longitudinal study, the research dispelled harmful stereotypes, influenced the UK Defence Mental Health and Wellbeing Strategy, and underpinned the creation of services like the NHS Veterans’ Transition, Intervention and Liaison Service. It shaped decisions not to adopt post-deployment screening and supported policies on women in combat roles. By identifying both unmet needs and effective interventions, the research led to tangible improvements in mental health support and reduced stigma across the Armed Forces community. Read more...

UoP17Drones: Killing by Drone: Implementing professional ethics training in the induction and practice of the UK’s Royal Air Force Reaper drone operators

The Royal AIr Force (RAF) Reaper drones are widely deployed in combat missions in Afghanistan, Iraq and Syria since 2007.Detailed research with Reaper crews, highlighted the increased psychological and emotional jeopardy faced by crews undertaking remotely piloted air operations. This led to advocacy to both the Inquiry by the All-Party Parliamentary Group on Drones and the RAF, on the urgency of introducing military ethics training to provide a moral framework and vocabulary to support the decision-making and mental wellbeing of Reaper crews as they make life-or-death choices. The RAF acted on the advice, introduced bespoke professional ethics training into the initial induction and asked researchers to develop and deliver training to all Reaper personnel (around 400 staff - exact number not available for security reasons) in 2018. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic explore the representation, rights and heritage of Islamic communities, particularly within the UK. Research shaped how Islamic communities, and the Middle East more broadly, are understood in British culture and governance. It supports efforts to combat Islamophobia through clearer definitions and improved policing practices, both online and offline. Many case studies focused on fostering cross-cultural and interfaith dialogue through collaborative outreach, education, and cultural exhibitions, involving schools, councils, law enforcement, and faith communities. They also highlighted the cultural contributions of Islamic communities, promoting recognition, inclusion and social cohesion in historically divided contexts.
narrative:
Creating Historical and Cultural Recognition of the British Mosque

This research contributed to the recognition of several mosques by Historic England, protecting them for future generations, and integrating the architectural contribution of British Muslims into the narrative of British culture and heritage. The announcement of this Grade Listed status resulted in over 30 press articles around the world. A Ramadan Pavilion designed by Shahed Saleem was the headline installation for the V&A’s London Festival of Architecture 2021 which focused on mosque architecture. Prior to this collaboration, the history of the mosque in Britain was not represented in the V&A’s collections or programming. The Muslim Council of Britain has credited this research and its outcomes with consolidating a place for British Muslims in the history of the nation and with providing a sense of legitimacy and belonging in public discourse. Read more...

Changing Attitudes to Muslim Migration and the Muslim World: shaping public discourse and giving voice to migrant communities

This research by Professors Sarah Hackett and Yasir Malik explores the histories and contemporary experiences of Muslim migration, identity, and integration in Europe and beyond. Their work has significantly shaped public understanding, influenced heritage practices, and supported public sector training.Through over 100 media appearances, public talks, and contributions to platforms like BBC Urdu and Critical Muslim, the researchers have challenged stereotypes and enhanced global understanding of the Muslim world. Their work has reached millions and inspired young Muslims and non-Muslims alike to re-examine Islamic history and identity.Hackett’s research changed museum and archive practices, leading to more inclusive exhibitions - like ‘Destination Tyneside’ - and new approaches to recording Muslim migrant histories. Together, the researchers have trained over 140 civil servants, diplomats, and military personnel in cultural awareness and cross-cultural communication. Their research continues to inform public discourse, enrich collective memory, and improve professional practices across sectors in the UK and internationally. Read more...

description: This topic highlights research that has significantly enhanced the collection, analysis, and application of economic, demographic, and policy-relevant data. Case studies include improvements to numerous population censuses, mortality estimates, and life tables; the development of more accurate measures of income inequality and economic performance; and novel modelling of international development metrics. Research also shaped official statistics used by the UK Office for National Statistics and other national and international agencies. It provided important methods improvements for official statistics, e.g. better geospatial methods for boundary design as well as improved data visualisation and communication. Work in this area underpinned policymaking in fields ranging from pensions and insurance to tourism and regional governance.
narrative:
How Long Do We Live? Improving the life expectancy estimation in English Life Tables 17 for better social policy

Research at the University of Southampton developed advanced statistical methods for estimating mortality that underpinned the official English Life Tables No. 17, published by the ONS. These life tables, a cornerstone of UK population statistics, now offer more accurate and granular life expectancy estimates—particularly at older ages—enabling more effective policymaking in pensions, social security, and healthcare. The methods are also used by insurers and actuaries to assess longevity risk, improving the pricing and regulation of life and health insurance products. This work has been widely adopted across government and industry and was recognised with a 2020 ESRC award for its public policy impact. Read more...

Improving population censuses around the worl

Southampton’s research on census design and estimation has driven improvements in population censuses globally. Their statistical methods improved the 2011 UK census and informed coverage survey designs and cost models for the 2021 census, contributing to £500m in national benefits and saving £750k in survey costs. In the Netherlands, their techniques enhanced estimates of the resident population, increasing the country’s representation in the European Parliament. In Ireland and New Zealand, their methods are critical to transitioning to administrative data-based censuses, addressing overcoverage and enabling accurate estimates for marginalised groups like the Māori, ensuring inclusive policymaking and more efficient, robust censuses. Read more...

description: This topic brings together research that has shaped emergency medical care, ambulance services with those focussed on disaster response at national and international levels. It includes innovations in pre-hospital care to better patient outcomes, improved triage systems, and improvements to ambulancing in emergency as well as analysis to reduce unnecessary hospital transfers. Work in this area also addressed systemic challenges like emergency department overcrowding and improved health outcomes through bettering community response and medical device access for medical emergencies. Beyond medical emergencies, research has influenced disaster preparedness and response strategies globally—enhancing community resilience, informing financial strategies for disaster recovery, and shaping UN and Red Cross policies as well as governmental, corporate and volunteer efforts to protect and support populations in crisis contexts.
narrative:
Designing and implementing a digital platform to reduce A&E peak time demand across the South West through the provision of real time information to empower patient decision-making

NHSquicker app enabled patients to choose the appropriate type of treatment facility for their condition, given real-time data on A&E/MIU wait times. The app was made available to 1.7 million patients since 2017, with 40,000 patients using it. It has lead to enhanced patient experience of acute care services by improving access to and use of NHS services and reducing A&E pressures during peak periods. Two early adopters of the app, TSDFT and North Devon Healthcare Trust, reported that between 2017-Feb 2019 there was a reduction in A&E attendances and an increase in MIU attendances compared to the previous year. Future work focused on scaling up the app from a regional to a national service, and to use the data collected by NHSquicker to improve the performances of services like Pathway (used by the NHS to triage 111 calls). Read more...

Improving pre-hospital emergency care

Research at the University of Stirling has significantly improved pre-hospital emergency care, leading to national and international changes in clinical practice. Findings on impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia informed updates to UK ambulance guidelines, ensuring tens of thousands of patients receive more effective care and follow-up advice, reducing repeat emergencies. The research also shaped service delivery and policy in leading third-sector health organisations. Separately, a low-cost handover tool developed from Stirling’s research has been adopted across the Scottish Ambulance Service, improving communication and patient safety during emergency handovers. The tool is also influencing prehospital care practices internationally, including in the United States. Read more...

Enhancing community preparedness for disasters in Sri Lanka

Salford’s research transformed disaster preparedness in Sri Lanka by creating MOBILISE, a digital platform enabling real-time, multi-agency collaboration for flood and landslide risk management. Replacing fragmented decision-making with shared data and situational visualisation, the platform is now integrated into national disaster systems, reaching over half the population with early warnings and improving responses for around 50,000 families. It supports the World Bank’s strategy in Sri Lanka and has improved flood alerts, community mobilisation, and post-disaster resettlement practices, significantly enhancing resilience and saving lives in climate-vulnerable areas. Read more...

Transforming national operational guidance for the UK emergency service

Research at the University of Sheffield led to a major overhaul of ambulance services in England and Wales, directly shaping NHS policy through the Ambulance Response Programme. Sheffield’s evaluations demonstrated that new triage protocols, revised call categories, and updated response time targets improved response rates for the most critical emergencies and enabled more efficient use of resources. Based on this evidence, the reforms were implemented nationwide and incorporated into the NHS Constitution, improving care for millions of 999 callers annually. The model is now influencing ambulance service redesign in Canada, highlighting its international significance in enhancing emergency medical response. Read more...

description: This topic brings together research that has informed and reshaped international relations, diplomacy, and foreign policy in complex and contested global contexts. It encompasses work on the strategic use of soft power, religious engagement; on border relations and identity politics as factors in regional stability; and on historical narratives that shape modern political alignments. Research has influenced UK and international policy on regions including the Balkans, East Asia, the Arab world, and even the polar zones, while also advising on constructive diplomatic engagement in both adversarial and friendly contexts. Other work has helped broker international agreements, guided policy on maritime and border security, and informed the rights and political situation of stateless populations. Across these contributions, a shared focus lies in supporting peaceful cooperation, cross-cultural understanding, and evidence-based foreign policy.
narrative:
Informing national and international security policy for a changing Arctic

Research at Loughborough University on geopolitical and security developments in the Arctic has directly influenced defence and foreign policy at national and international levels. It informed the UK Ministry of Defence’s first Defence Arctic Strategy and shaped its thinking through expert briefings and feedback on strategic planning documents. The work also contributed to NATO’s Strategic Foresight Analysis 2021, guiding long-term planning for all 30 member states, and supported Estonia’s successful development of its Arctic Council observer application. By highlighting the implications of climate change, increased military activity, and great power competition, the research has helped key institutions anticipate and respond to emerging Arctic security challenges. Read more...

Public Policy on Russia, Ukraine and Eastern Europe

Research on politics in Post-Soviet States helped underpin the development of policy planning towards Russia and the six countries of the Eastern Partnership by European Union ( EU) Member States, the EU and other international institutions. Regular closed-door briefings at the Foreign and Commonwealth Office and Cabinet Office have informed new UK ambassadors to the region and helped with the drafting of in-house policy papers.The Prime Minister was briefed in the context of Ukraine's revolutionary Maidan events in February 2014. A researcher led team of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe ( OSCE) experts conducted a Needs Assessment Report for the deported peoples in Crimea in 2013-14. Read more...

description: This topic brings together research that has shaped how workplaces promote wellbeing, manage risks, and organise work. A key focus is improving mental health, emotional resilience, and job quality through changes to HR policies, health and safety practices, and support systems across sectors—from policing and law to gig economy platforms. Case studies explore how organisations address workplace conflict, bullying, and stress; how they embed ethical practices; and how work design influences both productivity and employee wellbeing. Research has also guided public bodies and trade unions in reforming employment relations, modernising management structures, and promoting fair and decent work. At its core, this topic reflects a commitment to creating more humane, effective, and sustainable workplaces through evidence-based policy and practice.
narrative:
Fairwork: Improving Working Conditions in the Digital Gig Economy

Research led by the University of Oxford’s Fairwork project developed five principles for fair digital labour—covering pay, conditions, contracts, management, and representation—which are now used to evaluate platform work in 23 countries. These principles directly improved working conditions in South Africa, where platforms like NoSweat, SweepSouth, and GetTOD changed practices to align with Fairwork standards. In the UK, Fairwork research contributed to a legal judgment extending PPE rights and health protections to 4.7 million gig workers during COVID-19. The principles have also been adopted into labour policy by the Berlin state government and embedded in Germany’s national digital strategy, supported by over €670,000 in federal funding for a global secretariat. Read more...

Transforming worldwide policy and practice to prevent psychosocial risks at work and work-related stress

Research at the University of Nottingham led to the development of PRIMA-EF, a best-practice framework for managing psychosocial risks and work-related stress. Adopted by the WHO’s 193 member states and used by global and national organisations including the ILO, ISO, and national standards bodies in the UK, Canada, Denmark, Ireland, and Australia, PRIMA-EF has directly shaped international policy and workplace practices. It informed Canada’s national standard, Italy’s workplace regulation, Ireland’s “Work Positive” tool, and ISO 45003, the first international standard on workplace psychological health. It has also been adopted as corporate practice in major organisations like Equinor. Read more...

Delivering optimal solutions to enhance organisational capability

The University of Wolverhampton’s applied research in the Architecture, Engineering and Construction (AEC) sector has enhanced organisational capability across people, processes, and technology. Key impacts include a globally available stress management app adopted by over 50 companies; health and safety improvements via collaboration with the Institution of Civil Engineers; and co-created innovations through the Sustainability and Construction Futures Research and Innovation Centre. This work has transformed high-value manufacturing processes, increasing business turnover and job creation, and led to the formation of a new VR/AR company delivering services to the construction sector. Read more...

Changing Employment Policy and Practice in Adult Social Care in England and Wales.

The Welsh Government used this research showing the relationship between employment conditions for adult social care (ASC) workers and the quality of domiciliary care to change employment regulations and introduce legislation that curbs zero-hour contracts and ensures that travel and care times are clearly identified. This change has affected the employment conditions of 19,500 workers and the care provided to 23,000 people. Read more...

description: This topic addresses vehicle engineering and includes case studies across modelling, analysis and design of vehicles and their components. Case studies are often concerned with improving sustainability of vehicle manufacture and operation, reducing emissions and improving efficiency. Further considerations are developments in safety, maintenance requirements, performance and reliability. Some works also consider vehicle care, maintenance and preservation.
narrative:
Improving the competitiveness and sustainability of UK Automotive Industries

Loughborough University’s research in automotive simulation, calibration, and aerodynamics has significantly enhanced the competitiveness and sustainability of the UK automotive and motorsport sectors. Collaborations with Ford and Jaguar Land Rover led to new powertrain calibration technologies saving Ford $12 million annually and reducing CO₂ emissions by an estimated 7.5 million tonnes per year. Vehicle drivability and design were improved through new engine mapping and aerodynamic solutions, such as a novel flow-through rear spoiler at Jaguar Land Rover. Off-road tyre models and dynamic simulation tools were also integrated into industry-standard software, improving vehicle safety and performance while reducing development costs. Read more...

Optimisation of Railway Wheel Profile Design and Maintenanc

Research at the University of Huddersfield’s Institute of Railway Research led to optimised wheel profile design and maintenance practices that improved safety, performance, and cost efficiency across the UK rail network. A tram-train wheel profile developed for dual use on tram and heavy rail lines was instrumental to the success of Sheffield’s pioneering £125m tram-train pilot and has influenced plans in over ten UK cities. The team’s work on Economic Tread Turning (ETT) resulted in changes to national railway standards, enabling cost savings estimated at £880k–£5.1m annually. Trials by Alstom and Porterbrook extended wheelset life by up to 43% and 25%, respectively, while predictive maintenance tools based on this research were commercialised in Alstom’s Trainscanner and MRX Technologies’ Surface Crack Measurement system. Read more...

Multi-parametric dynamic analysis of lightweight car parts

Collaborative research between Keele mathematicians and TPV Automotive led to the development of advanced multi-parametric dynamic modelling methods for lightweight, high-contrast car components. These methods allowed engineers to optimise material and geometric configurations for components such as cross-car beams and control arms, reducing weight by 15% and lowering carbon emissions and energy consumption by up to 21% and 15%, respectively. The techniques were applied within major EU-funded projects (EVA4green and EAGLE), contributing to 22 new products, 40 innovations, and 16 international patent applications. Keele researchers also helped upskill TPV’s R&D team through professional development workshops and co-authored a Slovenian-language textbook, changing design practices and shortening development cycles. Read more...

topic_name_long: Virtual Reality, Video Games, Creative Digital Industries
description: This topic focuses on immersive technologies (VR/AR) and Human-Computer Interaction applications across healthcare, manufacturing, education, and entertainment. It encompasses user experience design, industry collaboration, and research translation for improved business processes and creative economy development. Case studies cover immersive technologies, digital innovation, and academia-business collaboration. Key themes include user experience design, accessibility, economic impact, and applications in gaming, healthcare, education, and cultural sectors. Public engagement and industry transformation through knowledge transfer are also incorporated.
narrative:
Project Cars: impact in the games industry from practice-based research in soundtrack and audio design

Creative research practice in composition, audio direction, and sound design contributed to the development of 3 globally-distributed, commercially succesful racing simulation games that reached over 5,000,000 gamers. Read more...

Using immersive technology research and collaboration to catalyse creation and development of an SME

Research into using Virtual Reality (VR) for pedagogical purposes led to the development of a startup and over GBP 700,000 in government investment for design and delivery of 10 VR learning environments. Responding to Covid-19 constraints, this project shifted from teaching in VR labs to enabling delivery of a VR experience via software like Zoom, allowing students to participate even without VR equipment. This effort attracted GBP 1,300,000 additional investment and was rolled out to 26 UK HEIs and 27 additional HEIs across 5 continents in autumn 2020. Read more...

Using Virtual Reality for the Benefit of Patients and Medical Practitioners

Research team developed a suite of immersive, interactive Virtual Reality (VR) rehabilitation systems for patients with neurological and musculoskeletal conditions, orthopaedic trauma, and chronic pain. Immersive VR experiences physically and/or psychologically enhanced the health and wellbeing of patients. Researchers further increased public awareness and improved understanding of the technology and established commercial and medical collaborations to improve healthcare and cost-effectiveness in the NHS. Read more...

description: Research in this topic address the understanding, diagnosis, treatment and prevention of metabolic diseases and obesity. Case studies informed national and global public health policy, improving risk assessment and shaping preventative strategies. Work shaped governmental, health institutional and public understandings of these diseases and factors underpinning. New medical approaches enhanced treatment effectiveness and patient outcomes. Public health initiatives promoted health literacy and lifelong behavioural change from childhood through adulthood, reducing risk factors.
narrative:
POWeR – cost effective online support for weight management

POWeR (Positive Online Weight Reduction) helps users sustain weight loss. POWeR has been made directly available to over 2,000,000 people through partnerships with Local Health Authorities and the NHS. POWer has developed a partnership with ‘Changing Health’ for further national and international dissemination. The POWeR app has been delivered to 4,000 patients as part of the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme and will be rolled out to a further 12,000 patients from 2020-2050. The POWeR web application has been delivered to 4,000 patients as part of the National Diabetes Education Programme and will reach a further 600,000 diabetic patients from 2020-2050. Read more...

A web/app based probability calculator is used worldwide to improve diagnosis and treatment of genetic diabetes

Researchers developed the MODY Probability Calculator - a clinically validated, CE-marked tool that helps healthcare professionals identify patients with Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY), a rare but often misdiagnosed genetic form of diabetes. Since its launch, the calculator has transformed clinical practice in the UK and globally, with over 170,000 uses across 187 countries and widespread uptake through mobile apps and online platforms. The calculator has improved diagnosis rates (32% vs 24%), led to correct and more cost-effective treatments, and is now embedded in NHS genomic testing guidelines and endorsed by major international diabetes bodies including the WHO and ADA. Correct diagnosis often allows patients to stop unnecessary insulin, improves quality of life, and enables genetic testing of family members. By guiding targeted testing, it saves the NHS millions in healthcare costs, with projected savings of £20-40 million, while improving outcomes for thousands of patients and families. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic aimed to deepen public engagement with environmental issues and inform policy for the protection of the environment through artist and cultural production, exhibition and collaboration. Research highlighted the cultural, social, economic and health value of nature, landscapes, and ecology, promoting sustainable change, environmental awareness, advocacy, and activism.
narrative:
Atmospheric art; Portraying the climate emergency with air

The Pollution Pods art instillation enabled a range of visitors, from the general public to policy makers and UN delegates, to experience various levels of air pollution, prompting better understand the implications of declining air quality for health and wellbeing. The interactive design provoked emotions and cognition to most effectively create positive behavioural change in audiences. The Pods toured globally, creating discourse across language barriers and inspiring sustained interest in air pollution among researchers, governmental bodies, and the general public Read more...

Enhancing public understanding of the cultural significance of trees, and assisting preservation of trees and woodlands

Stafford’s research has had measurable impact on public engagement with trees, conservation, and policy. Her authorship of the Charter for Trees, Woods and People -developed with input from 130,000 people and 70+ organisations - resulted in 144,413 individual signatories and 639 active Charter Branches across the UK. The Woodland Trust honoured each signature by planting one tree, totalling 114,000 by the 2018-19 cycle.Her book The Long, Long Life of Trees sold 25,521 copies by December 2020, significantly raising public awareness. As a ‘breakout’ success for Yale University Press, it shifted perceptions in publishing, enabling broader commercial reach in nature writing. Her 15 BBC Radio 3 programmes and 17 public book talks helped engage diverse audiences, including 230 attendees at an Oxford Botanic Garden lecture that led to a new ‘literary garden’ seen by 178,344 visitors in its first year.Stafford’s talks to professional bodies (e.g. Royal Forestry Society, 229 delegates) bridged forestry and the arts, influencing biodiversity planning in councils and the £5.7M Northern Forest Scheme. Her work inspired international initiatives, including a Dresden urban tree trail and informed Richard Powers’ Pulitzer-winning novel The Overstory. Stakeholders credit her with transforming conservation narratives, embedding emotional and cultural dimensions into environmental policy and education. Read more...

Nature Connections: relational engagement with nature through (co) creative practice

Darlington’s research has led to measurable changes in public engagement with nature. Her book Owl Sense sold 11,618 copies and featured as BBC Radio 4’s Book of the Week (audience: 4.5 million), while her Times ‘Nature Notebook’ column reached 11.5 million monthly readers. Thematic analysis of 97 reader reviews and 64 event feedback cards (from 23 events reaching over 2,900 people) showed behaviour changes: 50% began birdwatching, 25% joined wildlife charities, 10% volunteered, and others took up nature writing. The Owl Watch campaign, based on her work, generated 380 public submissions and recorded 405 owls. Darlington’s creative methodologies were adopted by key organisations. A pilot with Effervescent and Hack Back CIC led to a 28-30% reduction in conduct issues among vulnerable children and £120k follow-on funding. At Paignton Zoo, she co-developed a creative education programme for Key Stage 2 pupils, now central to the Wild Planet Trust’s strategy. Her work with the British Trust for Ornithology led to a national education pack distributed to 16,769 schools. She also advanced women’s participation in nature. A women-only birdwatching initiative with the Barn Owl Trust saw 100% of attendees increase their knowledge, 82% gain confidence, and 73% report stronger conservation attitudes. Read more...

description: This topic showcases how research has influenced the development of social enterprises and transformed entrepreneurship education globally. Impact includes support for small businesses and social ventures in embedding sustainability and social responsibility into their practices, often in alignment with the international development goals. Case studies highlight new models for social innovation and co-operative practice, support structures for entrepreneurship in justice and fair trade contexts, and practical tools for inclusive enterprise development in Africa and Latin America. In parallel, research has shaped entrepreneurship education across multiple sectors and continents, from developing creative pedagogies to inspiring entrepreneurial thinking among scientists, students, and youth. Together, these case studies demonstrate how entrepreneurial capacity can be built to generate both economic and social value.
narrative:
Creating and growing social enterprise

Research at Middlesex University’s CEEDR has driven national and international growth in social enterprise by shaping UK government policy, including strategies for Public Service Mutuals, and informing EU social enterprise guidance. Their online courses attracted over 50,000 learners globally, leading to the creation of more than 1,900 new social enterprises. CEEDR’s work also improved practices among support providers and funders, influencing major programmes like the Access Foundation and Power to Change, and helping social enterprises grow through consultancy, training, and strategic support. Read more...

Inspiring science and engineering researchers: entrepreneurial career development and economic impact from the YES programme

Research at the University of Nottingham led to the transformation and expansion of the Young Entrepreneurs Scheme (YES), an experiential programme for early career researchers to develop entrepreneurial skills and explore commercialising scientific research. Drawing on longitudinal and pedagogical studies, the programme introduced cross-disciplinary collaboration, online integrative learning, and industry mentoring. From 2013–2020, 2,089 researchers from 88 institutions participated, supported by 400 partners including GSK and Syngenta. An independent evaluation estimated YES contributed up to £1.8 billion in economic impact. Alumni have launched ventures in biotechnology, green energy, and science education, including a drug development firm that raised £8 million and a social enterprise reaching 40,000 schoolchildren in Malaysia. Read more...

description: This topic focuses on pharmaceutical research and biotechnology innovation to advance drug discovery, diagnostics, and therapeutic development. Case studies show development of treatments, therapies, and drug delivery systems that improve patient outcomes. Case studies also cover enhanced diagnostic capabilities through point-of-care testing, biomarker identification, and advanced screening technologies. The topic also incorporates novel scientific methods for protein engineering, synthetic biology, and computational drug design, leading to faster and more cost-effective pharmaceutical development. Initiatives are often focused on commercialisation and technology transfer, particularly through spin-out companies and industry partnerships, to promote therapeutic innovation and economic growth in the life sciences sector.
narrative:
Optimised human cell products to improve therapy development

Research at the University of Cambridge significantly advanced stem cell science by uncovering the mechanisms that direct the differentiation of human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs). This led to the development of 13 patents and the founding of the spin-out company DefiniGEN in 2012, which became the first to produce customised predictive liver models from hPSCs for pharmaceutical applications. DefiniGEN has since raised £9 million in investment, employs 17 staff, and supplies liver, pancreas, and gut cell models to clients in Europe, the US, and Japan. The research has also underpinned the creation of three additional companies—bit.bio (90 employees, $50 million investment), Hepatotarget Therapeutics, and Bilitech—which develop hPSC-derived technologies for disease modelling and regenerative therapies. These developments have improved drug development efficiency, supported international biotech innovation, and facilitated public engagement, including with the cystic fibrosis community, through accessible communication of scientific advances and contributions to patient understanding. Read more...

PARP inhibitors as a therapeutic to treat BRCA-defective cancers

University of Sheffield researchers pioneered the use of PARP inhibitors to treat BRCA-deficient cancers by demonstrating, in 2005, that targeting the DNA repair enzyme PARP induces synthetic lethality in tumour cells lacking functional BRCA genes. This groundbreaking discovery led to a global patent, licensed initially to Kudos and later to AstraZeneca, catalysing development of the first-in-class drug Lynparza® (Olaparib). Approved in over 70 countries and used to treat multiple cancer types—including ovarian, breast, prostate, and pancreatic—Lynparza® and other PARP inhibitors have significantly extended progression-free survival in patients with few treatment options. The Sheffield research underpins four clinically approved PARP inhibitors and spurred an $8.5 billion collaboration between AstraZeneca and Merck. Lynparza® alone has generated over $1.2 billion in sales since 2017 and was recognised by Universities UK as a ‘Nation’s Lifesaver’, highlighting its transformative impact on global cancer therapy. Read more...

Software for crystallography supporting new drug development

Software developed at the University of York for macromolecular crystallography—especially the COOT platform—has become a cornerstone of global pharmaceutical research, underpinning drug discovery efforts across academia and industry. Licensed to over 150 commercial sites, COOT’s powerful tools for molecular modelling, validation, and ligand fitting are central to structure-based drug design and fragment-based drug discovery (FBDD), which has produced at least 17 known clinical trial candidates and four approved drugs since 2010. Major pharmaceutical companies including AstraZeneca, Pfizer, and Novartis have used COOT in developing blockbuster treatments, with applications extending to COVID-19 therapeutics and vaccines. The software has enabled high-throughput screening, reduced development costs, and accelerated discovery timelines, with broader impacts seen in over 240–1000 commercial drug discovery publications and citations in 278 patents globally. Read more...

C4X Discovery: generating market-leading drug candidates from cutting-edge technology

University of Manchester researchers developed a breakthrough NMR-based technology that enables precise measurement of flexible 3D molecular shapes, accelerating drug discovery. Spun out into C4X Discovery (C4XD), this innovation underpinned the development of market-leading drug candidates at a fraction of traditional costs. It enabled rapid creation of C4X3256, a novel therapy for substance addiction now in clinical development via a USD294 million licensing deal with Indivior. C4XD also applied the technology to inflammatory and cardiovascular diseases, forming strategic partnerships with Takeda, Evotec, and others. The company floated on the London Stock Exchange in 2014, raising £31 million, and continues to attract investment, generating high-quality R&D jobs and expanding Manchester’s life sciences sector. Read more...

Oxford Nanopore: Nucleic acid sequencing and diagnostics on any scale from laboratory to point of care

Research on nanopore-based single-molecule sensing at the University of Oxford led to the founding of Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT), whose revolutionary portable DNA and RNA sequencing devices have transformed global genomics. Since 2013, ONT has raised over £507 million, expanded to 600 employees, and achieved a valuation of approximately £1.7 billion. Its technology enables rapid, low-cost, in-field sequencing and has played a critical role in public health responses to Ebola, Zika, Lassa fever, and COVID-19, including identifying SARS-CoV-2 and supporting real-time surveillance. ONT also developed LamPORE, a rapid SARS-CoV-2 diagnostic test adopted by the UK government, with 450,000 units ordered and proven near-perfect accuracy in NHS trials. Read more...

description: This topic contains case studies describing developments in the treatment and care of corectal cancers. This incorporates screening, diagnostics, surveillance, prevention, and adjuvant care, generally resulting in improved patient outcomes and/or reduced treatment costs. Case studies often detail impacts in clinical trials, as well as updates to guidelines and policy for corectal cancer.
narrative:
Lynch syndrome cancer prevention with aspirin

Research at the University of Leeds demonstrated that regular aspirin use significantly reduces colorectal cancer risk in people with Lynch Syndrome, a genetic condition affecting up to 200,000 in the UK. The landmark CAPP2 trial showed a 44–59% long-term reduction in cancer risk after daily aspirin use, leading to its adoption as standard preventive care in UK NICE guidelines and influencing international clinical practice across Europe, Australia, and the USA. This shift has empowered patients with a low-cost, accessible cancer prevention tool and transformed global management of Lynch Syndrome, while also driving further clinical trials to determine optimal dosage. Read more...

Improving surveillance for bowel cancer in the NHS

Research at Imperial College transformed NHS post-polypectomy surveillance by showing that most patients previously recommended for regular colonoscopy after adenoma removal did not face increased colorectal cancer risk. This led to revised 2020 UK guidelines—endorsed by key national bodies—that now restrict surveillance to genuinely high-risk patients. As a result, colonoscopy workload has dropped by up to 80%, freeing up NHS resources and reducing patient exposure to unnecessary procedures. Imperial’s findings were central to the guideline revision and its national rollout, improving care targeting and system efficiency. Read more...

description: In this topic research relating to volcanology and seismology is collated, with case studies primarily covering aspects of monitoring, modelling & prediction of events, as well as prevention and disaster response. This includes studies into public health, monitoring and sensing, and development of technologies for this. Broadly; increasing safety, public wellbeing and reducing disruption are key themes of the topic.
narrative:
University of Cambridge volcanic gas monitoring systems protect life, property and livelihoods

University of Cambridge research transformed volcano monitoring by developing the first automated UV spectrometer networks to track sulphur dioxide gas emissions—critical indicators of impending eruptions. First deployed on Montserrat in 2002, this system has since been adopted at 42 volcanoes across 18 countries, enabling real-time gas flux monitoring that informs life-saving evacuation and exclusion decisions. The Cambridge model helped forecast activity at sites including White Island (NZ) and Tungurahua (Ecuador), directly influencing public safety alerts. In Montserrat, it has guided safe geothermal redevelopment, while UAV-based innovations from Cambridge’s ABOVE project have empowered local communities in Papua New Guinea to remain on their land by enabling real-time, low-cost monitoring. The tools and training provided have reshaped hazard response protocols, protected at-risk populations, and enabled sustainable economic development in volcanic regions globally. Read more...

Increasing resilience to earthquake risk in developing countries

University of Cambridge research into earthquake hazard and risk led to the creation of the Earthquakes without Frontiers (EwF) partnership, which has increased resilience to seismic risk across 11 developing countries with a combined population of over one billion. EwF supported the retrofitting of buildings and the introduction of new building codes in Nepal, where all retrofitted structures withstood the 2015 earthquake, and improved hazard assessment and urban planning in cities such as Tehran, where identification of a previously unrecognised fault led to revisions in development plans. By strengthening local scientific capacity and shifting focus from short-term prediction to long-term preparedness, the partnership influenced public safety policy in several countries. In parallel, Cambridge research on seismic hazards in the Caspian region informed risk assessments for major oil and gas infrastructure projects, enabling safer and more cost-effective energy development in an area with investments exceeding $50 billion. Read more...

description: This topic focuses on healthcare professionals (HCPs) and management of the healthcare workforce and services. This includes case studies in key areas such as; HCP education and training, from assessment to professional development and ongoing training, developing best practice and compentency; workforce management, including staff planning, performance, operational effiency and organisation; and case studies in training and support of community healthcare practitioners such as support workers and carers. Aspects of healthcare policy and regulation are naturally encompassed within this topic, and improved patient satisfaction, treatment outcomes, and service costs are often key metrics considered.
narrative:
Creating better leaders in the NHS in England and Wales
