Research by the University of Birmingham’s Health Services Management Centre (HSMC) reshaped NHS leadership training through the co-design and delivery of the Elizabeth Garrett Anderson (EGA) and Nye Bevan programmes. These programmes, now considered the gold standard for NHS leadership development, have reached over 4,300 mid- and senior-level NHS leaders, equipping them to challenge poor practice, support staff wellbeing, and lead cross-sector collaborations. Independent evaluations show participants gained the skills and confidence to create open, inclusive cultures and deliver more person-centred care. Leadership practices improved in over 97% of NHS Trusts, with many participants promoted to influential roles and driving measurable improvements—such as raising Care Quality Commission ratings and transforming end-of-life services. The programmes have been recognised for their nationwide cultural impact and direct benefit to patients and staff across the NHS. Read more...

Transforming thoracic trauma surgery education and training by design

Research by Arm at Nottingham Trent University’s Flexural Composites Laboratory led to the creation of highly realistic thoracic manikins that transformed training for emergency thoracic trauma procedures. These manikins simulate organs and tissues with high bio-fidelity using composite elastomers and 3D-printed moulds, allowing surgeons and first responders to practise life-saving techniques like thoracotomy in realistic, low-risk environments. Used by the NHS, air ambulance services, UK armed forces, NATO partners, and emergency medics worldwide, the manikins have enhanced team preparedness, confidence, and competence in critical care scenarios. Commercialised by Trauma FX, the product generated over £900,000 in revenue and catalysed a merger forming Safeguard Medical, opening access to major international markets and creating new skilled jobs. Read more...

‘Taking Care’: Enhancing UK nursing training using mixed-methods drama research to reconceptualise, teach and promote embodied ‘care’ in clinical interactions

Project has helped nursing educatiors at 16 HEIs integrate resources for ethical care, ethical communication skills, and workplace empathy into the nursing curricula, benefiting 2,500 nursing trainees. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic focus on the planning, management, and long-term impact of sporting and public events. This includes practical provisions such as ticketing systems, advertising, accessibility, and infrastructure. Research promoted environmental sustainability and sustainable development, with focus on the social and economic legacies of such events at both local and national levels. Work contributed to policy development in areas such as para-sports, anti-corruption, and public safety, as well as future investment strategies.
narrative:
Anti-Match Fixing: Improving Global Sports Governance and Bringing Perpetrators to Account.

Previously, physical evidence was required to prosecute match fixing cases. ICS research helped have this requirement removed, allowing the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) to rule that evidence from betting markets was sufficient to identify match fixing. Following this ruling, FIFA ordered the replay of a match in which the referee was found to be involved in match-fixing. This was the replay that enabled Senegal to qualify for the 2018 World Cup. ICS research has also underpinned the education of athletes and coaches on match-fixing. A follow-up project, ERASMUS+, saw Liverpool partner with EU Athletes to introduce whistle-blowing apps for 3,000 athletes in 7 countries across a range of sports. Read more...

Sports Events as Agents of Change

McPherson and McGillivray’s research has significantly shaped international sport policy, embedding diversity and inclusion into the planning and legacy of major sporting events. At the global level, McPherson advised the OECD in 2018 on its Recommendation on Global Events and Local Development, adopted by all 38 member countries. This influenced legacy planning for events in Japan, Korea, France, China, and Italy, and established McPherson as a key figure in the OECD’s ongoing steering group for global events policy. In Japan, their Paralegacy 2020 project led to policy engagement at the House of Councillors and the development of bilingual resources on disability-inclusive research. Their work directly influenced teaching materials for the ‘I’mPossible’ programme, reaching 36,000 schools nationwide. In Canada, research underpinned legacy planning for the 2015 Toronto Pan/Parapan American Games. It led to strategic changes in the Canadian Paralympic Committee’s approach, impacting five municipalities, training hundreds of parasport coaches, and improving accessibility at eight sports facilities. Locally, their findings shaped policy in Glasgow post-2014 Commonwealth Games. Engagements with Scottish Parliament and Glasgow City stakeholders influenced the city’s legacy strategy, with the research earning a Herald Game Changer Award. The Canadian partner’s workshops further supported alignment with Ontario’s Accessibility Act across five provinces. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic encompass the prevention and treatment of accidental injuries. This incorporates awareness, preventative measures and interventions in public health and in sports, as well as studies into diagnosis, treatment and therapy for injuries (including traumatic injuries). Aspects of public health that impact injury rates (i.e. exercise plans, nutrition, care of children and elderly/vunerable populations) are included in this topic.
narrative:
A lifecourse approach to reducing the burden of osteoporotic fractures

Research from the MRC Lifecourse Epidemiology Unit at the University of Southampton has directly influenced national and global clinical guidelines and policy on osteoporosis prevention and fracture care. Their work showed that Fracture Liaison Services (FLS) reduce mortality and are cost-effective, leading to over 400 FLS implementations worldwide and a 40% increase in UK osteoporosis treatment rates. Their SCOOP trial demonstrated that screening using the FRAX® tool reduces hip fractures by 28%, helping to shape 22 national guidelines and NICE quality standards. Their maternal vitamin D research led to UK and WHO recommendations on supplementation in pregnancy, contributing to better bone health in children. This lifecourse approach has improved care across all ages and reduced healthcare costs, with FLS alone estimated to have saved £800 million in the UK over five years. Read more...

Falls prevention amongst older people: Increased reach and further impact of interventions, uptake and adherence

Research from the University of Manchester has led to large-scale adoption of the Falls Management Exercise (FaME) programme, helping reduce falls, fractures, and associated healthcare costs. Since 2014, FaME has been included in Public Health England, NICE, and US CDC guidelines. Over 1,100 new FaME instructors have been trained, and by 2019, an estimated 172,000 older adults in the UK participated, potentially preventing over 420,000 falls and up to 21,000 fractures. The programme has also been adapted into digital formats and widely distributed during COVID-19 lockdowns. Additionally, Manchester’s research changed how services promote falls prevention—shifting from fear-based messaging to emphasising the benefits of participation—and developed key tools such as the Falls Efficacy Scale-International (FES-I), now used in over 120 countries. Read more...

Reducing the risk to brain health in youth football: the science that generated public debate, policy U-turns, and the banning of heading practice

Research at the University of Stirling provided the first direct evidence that routine football heading causes immediate disruption to brain function. This work fundamentally changed how football heading is viewed, triggering global debate and prompting football authorities to act. Within days of publication, the Scottish Youth Football Association began reviewing its guidance, and by 2019 had advised coaches to stop heading in training for under-11s. In 2020, the Football Associations of England, Scotland and Ireland implemented UK-wide restrictions on heading for all under-18s. UEFA followed with its own Europe-wide youth heading guidelines. Stirling’s research also featured centrally in the BBC documentary Alan Shearer: Dementia, Football and Me, further raising public awareness and contributing to the commissioning of the FIELD study, which confirmed elevated dementia risk in former footballers. This body of work has had lasting public health and policy impacts, protecting millions of children across Europe from unnecessary brain injury risk. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic are concerned with monitoring, understanding and preventing hate crime and hate speech, with strong emphasis on informing public policy, legislation, and community responses. Research improved legal recognition, judicial responses, and victim support. Novel scientific approaches developed methods for identifying and measuring hate-related incidents both online and offline. Initiatives focused on raising awareness and providing accessible resources particularly within schools and community networks to promote tolerance, inclusion and understanding.
narrative:
Redefining Islamophobia and Influencing anti-Muslim hate crime policy in Britain

Professor Awan’s work with Tell MAMA was directly used by the All Party Parliamentary Group on Islamophobia to address the threat of online Islamophobia, and Awan has informed various other committees. This research informed social media guidelines and current policy and legal guidance in relation to racial and religiously aggravated hate crime. Awan provided training for practitioners to implement case management, recording, and reporting. The training enabled Tell MAMA to find hard-to-reach groups and support them to report Islamophobia online. These tools have been accessed by 100 mosques across the UK. Further training for Faith Associates has resulted in changes in policies and strategies, that has enabled over 200 mosques and imams to have a greater understanding of how to effectively report Islamophobia. Research contributed to the Government’s National Hate Crime Action by presenting arguments for further funding to secure buildings from attacks. The Home Office allocated £1.6 million over 3 years for the protection of faith institutions. Awan has been commissioned by the government to establish a new working definition for Islamophobia which is now officially adopted by over 800 organisations Read more...

The Searchlight Archive and British Extreme Right Culture

Dr. Paul Jackson’s research on the extreme right has provided guidance for combatting far right extremism in Britain to professionals, organisations, and the wider public. His main work in based on analysis of historical materials of the Searchlight Archive which documents such extremism since the 1960s, collated by the anti-fascist organisation Searchlight, and available to the public since 2013 through the University of Northampton. This historically informed research was used to create Continuing Professional Development (CPD) tools for institutions and organisations supporting anti-fascist and anti-racist campaigning, such as city councils. The team also contributed to a digitisation project with Gale Cengage (2018-present) to make Searchlight accessible online and raised £10,000 in royalties for Searchlight to put towards its campaigns. The research also contributes to ongoing analysis of developments in extremism for Janes' Terrorism and Insurgency Centre, as well as national and international media outlets to raise public awareness. Read more...

HateLab: Preventing the rising tide of hate crime and speech through influencing policy and policing

Research outlining prevalence, impacts, and prevention of hate crimes formed the primary source of information for the Welsh Government’s Framework for Action on Tackling Hate Crime (2014). Researcher developed technologies were also embedded within the National Cyber Hate Crime Hub (run by the UK’s National Police Chiefs’ Council), allowing policymakers and police to more effectively address the problem of hate crimes. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic focused on understanding and supporting the evolving role of religion and theology in contemporary society. Many case studies addressed challenges to religion in the modern world, and how institutions, governments and communities interact with religious groups, ideas and practices to support worship, affirm religious and spiritual identities, and foster interfaith dialogues. They engaged with diverse religious perspectives to promote mutual understandings, informing institutional policy changes, novel educational approaches, cultural collaboration, and frameworks for inclusivity.
narrative:
The Alevi Religion and Identity Project

The Research and Identity project found that the Alevi community’s social invisibility negatively impacted their sense of belonging in school and in wider society. Researchers, working closely with Alevi groups elsewhere, such as the Alevi Federation in Turkey, developed educational resources and training to facilitate the teaching of Alevism in UK schools. These materials can be accessed for free online, and the education site was accessed 23,874 times as of July 2020. The educational resources, particularly those describing Alevism, were vital supporting evidence in the community’s 2015 application to be officially recognised as a religious charity, denoting state-recognition of the religion. Researchers designed the first comparative survey that would provide empirical data about the community, map Alevi settlement in the UK, and describe the community and their transnational connections. Data collected in this survey has allowed an estimate of the size of the UK Alevi community, and ‘Alevi’ was included in the 2021 national census as a distinct religious group. This research has done much to redress the exclusion felt by Alevis from communities and institutions in the UK. Read more...

Demonstrating Jesus as a Historical Figure in the Public Consciousness

The research had a significant impact on public understanding, media discourse, and individual well-being through its wide dissemination and engagement. The Guardian article, grounded in the scholars’ work on mythicism and the historical evidence for Jesus, attracted over 1.16 million views in four days, with more than 146,000 shares by early 2019 - figures far surpassing other pieces in the same series. This extraordinary reach indicates a strong public appetite for accessible, evidence-based discussion of Christian origins. The article provoked substantial online debate, with nearly 1,000 comments in just a few hours, and was cited in sermons, shared by prominent clergy, and used in talks across universities and churches, reaching thousands. Emails from Christian readers reveal how the article answered longstanding questions, strengthened faith, and improved well-being, especially during challenging periods like Easter. Non-Christian and interfaith readers also reported shifts in understanding and greater engagement with historical questions. The article influenced further media coverage, including responses to mythicist claims in outlets such as The Independent, MSN, and international radio and newspapers. It also led to a longer academic article that received unexpected lay readership and pastoral feedback. Overall, the research met a clear public need and produced lasting, widespread intellectual and emotional impact. Read more...

description: This topic brings together research that has shaped how societies govern, access, and experience digital technologies. It includes efforts to tackle digital exclusion by improving skills, access, and outcomes for underserved communities, particularly in rural areas and across the Global South. Research has influenced national and international policy on digital inclusion, supported the development of digital skills frameworks, and guided NGOs and governments in measuring and addressing digital inequalities. Case studies also highlight how digital platforms have enhanced citizen engagement in policymaking and transformed public service delivery. Broader governance issues feature prominently, including challenges around internet privacy, ethical computing, and digital profiling, with research leading to changes in global professional standards, intellectual property debates, and the regulation of digital markets. Collectively, these studies demonstrate how digital access, infrastructure, ethics, and governance are increasingly central to public policy, civic participation, and social justice.
narrative:
‘Human Rights are Digital Rights’: Humanizing the Internet

This research on internet policy-making processes has led Professor Franklin to lead the Internet Rights and Principles Coalition (IRPC). Since 2014, the IRPC has contributed to official recognition that there is a fundamental relationship between online information, communication technologies, and human rights. IRPC information has informed internet governance at the UN, in Europe, Cameroon, Brazil, Latin America, the Middle East, and North African regions. In 2014, the IRPC Charter was cited as a best practice document by the European Agency for Human Rights. In 2014, the Council of Europe published the Guide to Human Rights for Internet Users modelled on the IRPC Charter Booklet. The IRPC Charter continues to hold influence on public debates and government policies. In 2019, Sir Tim Berners-Lee, Director of the World Wide Web consortium and founder of the World Wide Web Foundation, cited the IRPC Charter as a source in his Contract for the Web, a manifesto calling on governments, organisations, and individuals to ‘safeguard [the internet] from abuse and ensure it benefits humanity’. The Contract for the Web is backed by over 150 organisations. Read more...

Cloud Legal Project- Responding to the Challenges of Disruptive Technologies

This research led to the launch of the Cloud Legal Project (CLP) in 2009. CLP identifies legal and regulatory issues with the Cloud. The CLP's work was the first legal research focused entirely on the Cloud, and was funded by Microsoft, Hewlett Packard, and the European Commission. It has enabled the development and implementation of legal and governance structures for Cloud Computing services to solve legal uncertainties. These legal governance structures have allowed users to negotiate better terms from Cloud service providers, such as the changing of standard terms to better reflect the needs of organisations including 1,000 UK tertiary education and research institutions. CLP research has also been used to draft European Commission legislation that enables criminal investigations by allowing access to Cloud data. Read more...

Digital inequality, exclusion and inclusion

Researchers identified that over 11 million UK citizens are non-users or limited users of digital systems. By identifying the consequences and inequities resulting of digital exclusion, researchers were able to support new policy development for digital inclusion and skills by charities, such as the Good Things Foundation and the Carnegie UK Trust. Researchers also supported the development of the UK national digital policy, including the first UK Digital Culture policy and regional digital inclusion policy for social housing organisations and local government. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic are concerned with wildlife conservation and management. They cover key areas such as species identification and conservation strategies (i.e. relocation and reintroduction programmes), and value biodiversity. Scientific research, policy and regulatory frameworks form a key part of this topic, including international and national conservation policies, risk management and planning to mitigate biodiversity loss, hunting regulations, and scientific studies that support these policies. Finally, community engagement, education and awareness - including eco-tourism and outreach initiatives - are a valuable component of this topic.
narrative:
Protecting threatened birds and their habitats across the tropics

Research at Manchester Metropolitan University has significantly influenced global bird conservation, especially in tropical regions. Findings on bird population declines and habitat threats have informed the IUCN Red List status of 71 species and helped secure a global trade ban for the African Grey Parrot under CITES. The work also led to changes in conservation legislation and protected area management in Brazil, the Philippines, and Peru. The team’s distance sampling methods have been widely adopted, including in the LAWIN monitoring system used across 6 million hectares of Philippine forest, and have guided local training and data collection in 15 countries. Read more...

The discovery and protection of a new orangutan species, the Tapanuli orangutan, and sustaining and protecting existing orangutan species

Research at the University of Portsmouth played a crucial role in the discovery and protection of a new great ape species—the Tapanuli orangutan—based on acoustic analysis of orangutan long calls. This discovery, confirmed in 2017, led to the species being classified as Critically Endangered, triggering global conservation measures, legal protections, and international advocacy. In parallel, the research informed new rehabilitation strategies for orangutans in Malaysia, co-developing methods to assess individual readiness for release. These methods have improved survival rates and shaped release policies, contributing significantly to the preservation of critically endangered orangutan populations. Read more...

Transforming Practice: Novel Statistical Models for Biodiversity Monitoring

Statistical research at the University of Kent has transformed biodiversity monitoring by enabling organisations to analyse large, error-prone datasets from citizen science and environmental DNA (eDNA) surveys with greater accuracy and speed. New models developed by Kent’s Statistical Ecology team underpin official biodiversity indicators published by UK and European agencies, shaping conservation policy and informing environmental reporting. The methods have also improved species prioritisation and monitoring practices for organisations such as Butterfly Conservation, Natural England, and the Bumblebee Conservation Trust. Widely adopted training and free software have further enabled conservationists worldwide to apply these advanced tools, reshaping biodiversity assessments and enhancing global responses to ecological decline. Read more...

description: This topic focuses on the use of data to enhance healthcare for improved patient outcomes, service efficiency and cost effectiveness. It encompasses data analysis for healthcare system and workforce management. Additionally, it covers evidence-based practices for clinical trials and patient care; including data collection, data analysis, decision making, risk analysis and healthcare interventions. Furthermore, studies demonstrating impact in public health strategy including evidence-based improvements to commnunications, self-management tools and disease risk stratification are incorporated.
narrative:
A solution to staff rostering problems in hospitals by means of a ‘fair’ algorithm

A mathematical algorithm developed at City, University of London led to a rostering system that improves junior doctor well-being, patient safety, and cost efficiency in NHS hospitals. First implemented at Whittington Hospital, the system replaced traditional fixed rotas with personalised, fair e-rosters that reduced fatigue, ensured equitable shift allocation, and accommodated leave and training needs. All doctors using the system reported improved morale and reduced fatigue, and the department saw savings in locum costs and rota management time. The algorithm informed NHS workforce policy, supported negotiations during the 2016 junior doctors' contract dispute, and was cited in government reports and parliamentary discussions. It has since been used to enhance surgical training capacity, guide pandemic-era staff redeployment, and serve as an exemplar in NHS improvement initiatives. Read more...

Improving Clinical Trials by Innovative Statistical Design

Statistical research at the University of Bath has significantly improved the design of clinical trials, enabling faster, more flexible, and more cost-effective evaluation of treatments. New methods in group sequential and adaptive designs allow for early stopping or mid-trial modifications without compromising statistical validity, reducing sample sizes by 20–30% on average and expediting access to effective therapies. These methods have been applied in high-impact trials, including GATSBY and TAPPAS, and are embedded in industry-standard software used globally by pharmaceutical companies and regulators. The research has informed FDA guidance for adaptive clinical trials and has supported ethical, efficient trial conduct that saves money, protects patients, and accelerates innovation in global healthcare. Read more...

Estimating Health Opportunity Costs

Research at the University of York on the health effects of changes in healthcare expenditure has informed impact assessments of the UK Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC). Based on the team’s findings, DHSC now uses £15,000 per Quality Adjusted Life Year (QUALY) as an empirical estimate of health opportunity costs. Since 2014, DHSC has carried out 23 impact assessments using this estimate, with a reported financial impact of £1.9billion. The York research also introduced new health opportunity costs to be considered in these assessments, which brought the total of QUALYs to be 125,846, which the DHSC values at £7.5billion. Research showing where the cost per QUALY remains less than £15,000 was key to securing rebate payments from manufacturers to the NHS, including £841,000,000 in 2019 alone. The impact of this research on policy and practice in relation to healthcare resources has aided in maximising health gains from limited resources in national and international settings. Read more...

topic_name_long: Marginalized & Underrepresented Communities: Histories, Rights and Inclusion
description: Case studies in this topic foreground the histories, rights, and identities of marginalised and underrepresented communities across local and global contexts. They explore a wide spectrum of ethnic, racial, religious, and cultural experiences, using diverse methods such as education, exhibition, writing, artistic collaboration, and curation to amplify voices and promote dialogue. Engaging with complex and often contentious topics, including colonialism, slavery, apartheid, and migration, research deepened public understanding and fostered inclusion. Many case studies influenced policy and public opinion, working to bridge divides between communities and support the recognition and inclusion of historically silenced groups in cultural, social, and political life.
narrative:
Breaking the impasse on global reparations for Afrikan enslavement

Based on this research, the International Network of Scholars, and Activists for Afrikan Reparations (INOSAAR) has broken an impasse between activists and academics over reparations for transatlantic trafficking of enslaved peoples. INOSAAR has built trust between stakeholders in Europe, the Americas, and the Afrikan continent, and is the only group to have members of civil society and grassroots academia on the platform. It has developed a global community of over 30 member organisations committed to the shared Principles of Participation. INOSAAR has brought about a global declaration, the Porto-Novo Declaration, calling for the active participation of Afrikan states in the reparations movement. In the UK, INOSAAR influenced the discussion of reparations policies in the UK, resulting in Bristol, Lambeth, and Islington Councils passing motions on Atonement and Reparations for the United Kingdom’s Transatlantic Traffic in Enslaved Africans. Read more...

Identifying and promoting community owned solutions within marginalised communities, practitioners and policy

Project COBRA researchers and staff launched the Cobra Collective Community Interest Company (CIC) to help empower marginalised communities to identify, record, promote and practice community owned solutions. This expanded the number of trained community researchers to 60, working in 13 countries. Project COBRA provided visual materials on how community owned solutions could be implemented to tackles issues such as food insecurity, domestic abuse, and environmental degradation. 30 indigenous facilitators trained in Project COBRA have been hired by more than 10 civil society organisations around the world to spread this training on the community owned solutions approach. Key policy makers are now implementing the ‘community owned’ and System Viability Framework approaches, including in DEFRA/DFIS’s work to help develop Guyana’s National Action Plan for Traditional Knowledge, which is now being used as a best practice model for other countries. Read more...

topic_name_long: Drugs, Substance Abuse, Alcohol, Psychoactive Substances
description: This topic contains case studies pertaining to substance abuse, substance control and the treatment of affected individuals. Studies may explore drug policy and regulation, whether at local, government or international level. Also included are case studies of healthcare and support for individuals, as well as implementation of broader public health measures, as well as some relevant scientific research and neurological investigations.
narrative:
Development of ground truth datasets of controlled substances to understand Global drug use

Research at the University of Dundee has transformed forensic responses to synthetic drugs through the creation of unique “ground truth” datasets of novel psychoactive substances (NPS). By synthesising and characterising over 250 bespoke drug samples, researchers enabled forensic chemists, law enforcement, and prison services to rapidly identify emerging compounds, including synthetic cannabinoids and opioids. This work has helped prevent drugs entering Scottish prisons, informed new prison safety protocols, and directly contributed to the development of global drug detection policies. It has influenced national early warning systems, supported WHO drug scheduling decisions, and underpins United Nations guidance used across 193 member states. The research has also shaped operational procedures and technology deployment in Scottish prisons, informed national policy on drug use and overdose prevention, and enhanced international forensic practice via contributions to UN and UK expert panels. Read more...

Take-home Naloxone: developing a nasal spray and making it widely available in the community to prevent deaths from heroin and other opioid overdose

Naloxone saves lives by reversing the effects of opioid overdose. Researchers pioneered the concept of pre-providing naloxone to laypeople, known as Take-Home Naloxone (THN), which led to the development of a medically approved naloxone nasal spray as a safer, easier mode of administration than injection. The United Nations (UN) and World Health Organisation (WHO) subsequently endorsed THN and recommended its wider provision globally. Over 23 countries have now implemented THN programmes, with the US alone having committed an extra $180 million in funding. Increased distribution of this intervention across the world ensures that opioid users, carers, and families have THN ready for when they need it, to save lives. Read more...

Improving the lives of individuals at risk of Alcohol Related Brain Damage

Research by the University of South Wales has significantly improved the recognition, diagnosis, and treatment of Alcohol Related Brain Damage (ARBD), a severely underdiagnosed yet treatable condition linked to alcohol misuse. The research provided the first accurate prevalence estimates of ARBD in the UK, highlighted diagnostic shortcomings, and informed best practice in assessment and treatment. These findings directly shaped the Welsh Government’s national Substance Misuse Treatment Framework (SMTF) for ARBD, which is now influencing UK clinical guidelines. The research also underpinned professional training delivered to over 90% of frontline staff at The Pobl Group, Wales’s largest housing association. This resulted in a major increase in staff awareness, confidence, and capacity to support individuals at risk. The work has improved service delivery, prompted changes in care protocols, and received endorsement from the Royal College of Psychiatrists, positioning Wales as a leader in ARBD policy and care. Read more...

description: Work in this topic raises awareness of important historical writers and literary traditions. Case studies enhanced education around reading and literature both in schools and public settings like literary events. Research influenced provision of literary access, including library policies and online databases. Case studies showcase the social, cultural, and economic benefits of literature across communities, cities, regions and countries. They also promote the use of literature for engaging with heritage and individual and community wellbeing.
narrative:
Magical Realism and Augmented Reality: Using Digital Technology to Bring Archives to New Audiences, Build Children’s Engagement with Place, and Change Ways of Working at a Cultural Organisation

This case study used digital tools purposefully designed to present archival material to new public audience in novel, interactive ways. The team developed an app in partnership with Seven Stories, at the National Centre for Children’s Books, which presents literary archives to children by using Augmented Reality Technology to embed content from the Seven Stories collections into the landscape around the visitor centre. The app development brought together museum professionals, teachers, children, designers, and developers as partners in co-design. The initial trial in 2019 impacted 150 children over 5,400 hours of participant engagement. It enabled children to engage with reading and cultural heritage in new ways, and to rediscover their local environments through a new perspective. Reported impacts were particularly powerful for children from disadvantaged areas. Read more...

Widening Access to Literature by Providing New Insights into the Lives of Writers

Bradford’s research on Larkin’s photography led to major cultural engagement, including his advisory role in Hull’s 2017 City of Culture and an exhibition linking Larkin’s verse and visual art, which attracted significant public and media attention. His book inspired BBC TV’s Through the Lens of Larkin, where Bradford served as advisor and interviewee, and features in major newspapers shifted public perceptions of Larkin’s work. Similarly, Bradford’s Orwell biography generated widespread media invitations, reaching audiences of up to 2.2 million, and sparked new public debates on contemporary political issues. His success led to a £250,000 publisher investment for a literary biography series, further bridging academic research and general readership. Kennedy-Andrews and Ó Dochartaigh’s research fostered a new archival network that supported a touring exhibition on Jews in Irish literature, attracting over 5,500 visitors at PRONI alone and engaging Jewish communities in Northern Ireland and beyond. This project also enhanced public understanding and cultural preservation of underrepresented histories, gaining political support and media coverage. Murphy’s work has strengthened local cultural tourism through festivals linked to Steinbeck and Cather, engaging diverse audiences and generating international interest. White’s Beckett research influenced major arts festivals in Northern Ireland, expanding cultural participation. Overall, this research has created new cultural artefacts, broadened audience engagement, stimulated tourism, and enhanced preservation of local traditions. Read more...

The Centre for New Writing: Developing New Writers and Audiences, Enriching Public Debate and Informing Arts Policy

The Centre for New Writing (CNW) has advanced public understanding of gender, race, identity, and inequalities through research closely linked to community engagement in Manchester and beyond. Its work supports underrepresented writers and new audiences, influencing arts policy such as Ireland’s ‘Next Generation’ scheme, which has awarded bursaries to over 100 emerging artists since 2016. Jeanette Winterson’s 2018 Richard Dimbleby Lecture, broadcast on BBC1 and BBC2, was viewed by tens of thousands and sparked widespread online discussion, enhancing public debates on feminism and AI. Kamila Shamsie’s Orwell Lecture (350 attendees, 3,000+ YouTube views) and media appearances shaped conversations on race and citizenship, reaching millions through BBC Radio 4’s Today programme (6.8 million listeners). CNW’s ‘Literature Live’ series expanded from 6 events in 2005 to nearly 20 annually (2013–2019), hosting 120+ international writers and attracting 7,740 attendees from 2013–2018. School initiatives engaged 218 pupils from deprived areas (2017–2020), providing mentoring and fostering creative skills. Workshops in 2019 supported 33 trans and non-binary writers in safe, creative spaces. John McAuliffe’s leadership in the Irish Arts Council contributed to a €5 million funding increase and the ‘Making Great Art Work’ strategy, influencing cultural investment and artist support. CNW played a central role in Manchester’s 2017 UNESCO City of Literature designation, co-designing key cultural programs and helping secure funding for a dedicated City of Literature team. These efforts have raised Manchester’s literary profile nationally and internationally, engaging thousands and strengthening global creative networks. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic worked with visual media in the preservation, representation, and sharing of heritage and culture. Through exhibitions, public events and museum practices, and use of novel technologies, case studies used visual media to foster greater visibility, dialogue, and inclusion, particularly for historically overlooked groups such as ethnic minorities, marginalised peoples, women, and children. They informed public understanding and promoted cultural integration and learning. Photography featured prominently in this topic, with many case studies involving exhibitions, curation practices, and wider archival access for photography.
narrative:
Beyond the Physical: visual technologies and contemporary choreographic practice

Multi-disciplinary research that is changing contemporary dance practice by inserting cutting-edge digital technologies into the choreographic process, such as allowing dancers to interact with animated 3D counterparts. This research is central to acclaimed modern dance works, such as SWM’s Olivier Award winning Woolf Works, and Atomos, which reached a combined audience of 778,904. Read more...

Raising Voices: Visualising Untold Stories

UAL’s research in photography, filmmaking, and curation has reshaped the ethical and creative representation of marginalised communities by challenging dominant visual tropes and curatorial norms. Central to this impact is Justine (2013), Rughani’s award-winning short film (BAFTSS Research in Practice Award), used by social services and universities internationally to train assessors and students. It anchors UAL’s Ethics for Making, a global teaching tool promoting empathic documentary practices, and was screened at the UN International Day of Persons with Disabilities (2015).Through the Photography and the Archive Research Centre (PARC), Williams co-curated Seaside: Photographed (2019), funded by a £220,000 ACE grant and £10,000 from Turner Contemporary. Attracting 12,500 visitors, the exhibition revealed unseen or forgotten photographic works via an open ‘Call for Works’, expanding how British life is curated and understood. Her archive joined the Martin Parr Foundation in 2019, reflecting her significance in UK photography. Davidmann’s Ken. To Be Destroyed (2016), supported by a Philip Leverhulme Prize and nominated for the Deutsche Börse Photography Prize, included six solo and two group exhibitions, three V&A events, a book, and a co-authored article, raising awareness of trans histories globally. Hunter’s A Journey Home (2019) drew 14,252 visitors, received Arts Council funding, and featured national media coverage. Zimmerman’s Estate and Here for Life (Artangel, 2019) staged screenings in community settings and earned her the 2020 Film London Jarman Award. Together, this work has advanced inclusive, participatory methods that foreground dispossessed voices and reshape cultural narratives in museums, galleries and public discourse. Read more...

The Cartonera Publishing Project: Empowering Vulnerable Communities for Sustainable Social Change

Cartonera publishing, a grassroots Latin American movement, has proven to be a sustainable and socially transformative tool for empowering marginalised communities and reshaping cultural institutions. Working with four key cartonera collectives in Mexico and Brazil, researchers co-designed arts-based workshops that reached over 1,000 participants, including homeless individuals, indigenous communities, and imprisoned people. In Brazil’s Cerrado region, 13 workshops engaged 200+ participants, including quilombola women who created Buriti-Dão, a book that fostered storytelling, income generation, and environmental awareness. In São Paulo, 18 homeless participants co-produced Mutirão, a book and housing intervention that visibly improved living conditions. In Mexico, a prison-based programme led to the creation of Wind & Mirrors and Bote Cartonero, the country’s first inmate-run publisher, inspiring the UK’s first prison cartonera initiative - Unlocked - where 100% of participants reported enjoyment and 80% noted improved literacy. On the cultural front, a São Paulo exhibition showcased 350 books from 40 collectives, drawing 2,500+ visitors and over 5 million media views. In the UK, partnerships with major libraries resulted in a 700+ book collection and events involving 1,000+ participants, including the London Cartonera Festival. These efforts are helping embed activist, decolonial approaches in libraries and empower new community-led publishing initiatives globally. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic cover areas of artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics, and the associated ethical considerations in their use. Within AI and machine learning (ML) policies and legislation is a key theme, with topics covering aspects of human rights, data protection, usage regulations, representation and social/cultural impacts of AI. Robotics topics also consider ethics of humanoids and applications within society. Public awareness, understanding and perception of these technologies - including outreach and exhibitions - are also incorporated.
narrative:
Improving the oversight and regulation of advanced digital surveillance

Research at the University of Essex on the human rights implications of digital surveillance has shaped legal standards, oversight practices, and public debate in the UK and internationally. Groundbreaking independent analysis of live facial recognition (LFR) trials exposed significant legal and ethical deficiencies, influencing national guidance issued to all police forces and directly informing a landmark Court of Appeal ruling that found police use of LFR unlawful. The work underpinned surveillance policy issued by the UN and EU Fundamental Rights Agency, was cited in UK Parliament and national policy frameworks, and informed oversight by bodies such as the Investigatory Powers Commissioner’s Office. By highlighting disproportionate harms to civil liberties and marginalised groups, the research reframed the debate beyond privacy to broader rights and freedoms, catalysed civil society campaigns, and helped drive demands for stronger regulation of AI-driven policing technologies. Read more...

AI: Alignment, Policy and Governance

Research at the University of Oxford’s Future of Humanity Institute has significantly shaped global understanding and governance of long-term risks from advanced artificial intelligence. The publication of Superintelligence (2014) reached over 7 million people, catalysing public debate and reframing AI as not only a technical challenge but also a societal and philosophical one, requiring new approaches to policy, ethics, and international coordination. The research introduced core concepts now foundational in AI alignment and risk discourse, influencing UK parliamentary recommendations on regulation and funding, and shaping institutional policies at leading AI labs and international bodies. It also played a key role in establishing AI safety as a philanthropic funding priority, helping direct over $110 million in global grants toward work on responsible AI development and long-term safety. Read more...

description: This topic considers the area of materials science, covering areas such as investigation of material properties and behaviours, manufacturing innovations, and performance enhancement. Development of new materials or advancement of existing material technologies is a large component of this topic. Applications are broad and span across textiles, coatings, optics, aerospace, electronics, infrastructure amongst others.
narrative:
Driving a Carbon Negative Market in Europe

Brunel University London’s research into sustainable wood polymer composites (WPCs) enabled Ecodek—a small importer—to transform into the UK’s leading manufacturer of durable, fully recyclable decking. With over 1 million metres produced annually and products used in 6,000+ projects including the London Olympic Stadium and Dubai’s Jumeirah Beach Walkway, Ecodek’s growth was driven by Brunel’s innovations in material formulation and waste utilisation. The company locks up 600,000 kg of CO₂ annually, recycles the equivalent of 100 million milk bottles, and supports a circular economy through buyback schemes. This partnership catalysed £8.5M acquisition, expanded R&D capacity, created 50 jobs, and established a model for carbon-negative manufacturing in Europe. Read more...

Global economic and performance impact through world-leading innovations in optical thin film manufacturin

Research from the University of the West of Scotland’s Institute of Thin Films, Sensors & Imaging has led to global advances in high-performance optical coatings, addressing the demand for scalable, low-temperature, high-throughput precision manufacturing. Novel plasma-assisted deposition technologies—patented and deployed across the UK, China, and the USA—have enabled enhanced coating performance on temperature-sensitive substrates. The technology is now in production use at leading companies including Helia Photonics, Orion Photonics, Teer Coatings, and Shanghai Jason Vacuum Company, supporting markets from laser optics and photonics to inertial confinement fusion. This has generated an estimated £11 million in economic impact, new high-level physics jobs, and international equipment sales of over £7 million annually. Read more...

High strength recyclable extrudable aluminium alloys for light-weight automotive structures

Brunel University London's research into high-strength, fully recyclable aluminium alloys has transformed the automotive industry’s approach to lightweight structural components. Working with Constellium, Brunel developed HSA6 alloys and the melt-conditioned direct chill (MC-DC) casting process, enabling stronger, more recyclable aluminium extrusions without costly post-processing. These innovations have been adopted in crash management systems for vehicles from Tesla, JLR, BMW, and Audi—contributing to nearly £200 million in vehicle sales and cutting 225,000 tonnes of CO₂ emissions. The work has underpinned 80% of Constellium's new business and helped double its automotive revenue, while driving strategic R&D investment, reshoring UK manufacturing, and creating jobs. Read more...

Designing innovative materials from waste streams to increase sustainability in Scottish product development

Research showing innovative uses of waste materials in design and manufacturing has influenced practices at multiple Scottish manufacturers, leading to improved projections for sustainable manufacturing and revenue. The main beneficiary and long term collaborating organisation, The Scottish Leather Group, which is the UK’s only automotive leather manufacturer, confirm the research has supported them in using 2,300t of waste material each year, at a potential yield increase of 5-10 percent. This research has also helped The Scottish Leather Group eliminate or replace their current estimated plastic bag usage of over 40,000 bags per year. Read more...

description: This topic highlights how research has advanced the sustainability, resilience, and performance of infrastructure and construction. Case studies span innovations in low-carbon materials, offsite timber construction, and life-extension techniques for roads, bridges, and buildings—contributing to greener, more cost-effective infrastructure. Work on overheating in buildings, landslide forecasting, and resilient infrastructure has helped mitigate environmental and public health risks. Studies have also influenced the environmental standards applied to millions of buildings globally. Research shaped planning policy, urban liveability, and biodiversity through tools adopted in UK cities and by national agencies. Other case studies show how sustainable development goals (SDGs) and environmental impact assessments are being embedded into infrastructure governance, while collaborative contracting models and digital tools support more efficient, transparent delivery of construction projects.
narrative:
Collaborative construction contracts: A new way to deliver improved value

To reduce legal disputes and improve value for money during construction projects, law scholars developed the Framework Alliance Contract (FAC-1). FAC-1 was rapidly adopted by the construction industry and its clients. It (i) improves integration of consultants, contractors and subcontractors; (ii) ensures timely sharing of and agreement to accurate designs, costs, programmes and risk information; and (iii) embeds knowledge gained from one project to the next. Procurements of social housing, schools, highways and public buildings with an estimated total value of GBP 45,000,000,000 have been completed under the new framework. Read more...

ICS1: Prolonging the Life of our Roads and Highways with No CO2 Emission Construction Material

This research resulted in the production of new emulsions and techniques for sustainable, low emission, and low-cost repairs. It also led to the surfacing and maintenance of existing asphalt, and the laying over 850,000 m2 of roads in 2018 and 2019. Read more...

Adaptation of existing buildings to boost resilience in a changing climate

This research on the adaptation of post-war buildings to increase resilience to a changing climate, reduce carbon emissions, and improve comfort guided the development of the NHS Energy Efficiency Fund (EEF) specifically to mitigate climate change effects by improving energy efficiency across the retained NHS Estate. 117 energy efficiency projects in 48 NHS organisations are predicted to save 100.6Mkg CO2 pa, which is 2.4% of the entire NHS building energy related carbon footprint. Researchers also redrafted the primary NHS guidance on energy efficiency, promoting EEF findings and advocating refurbishment over newbuild in most scenarios. Read more...

topic_name_long: Taxes, Public Sector Finance, Welfare, Charities
description: This topic explores how research has shaped taxation, public finance, and welfare systems to improve transparency, fairness, and effectiveness. Case studies include reforms to audit practices and financial reporting in local government, better tax compliance strategies, and modernised gambling taxation. Research informed UK and international tax policy, addressed tax evasion, and improved measurement of the tax gap. In welfare, contributions influenced Universal Credit reform, the Funeral Payment scheme, and tools for assessing the social impact of budget cuts. Work on charitable giving and nonprofit reporting reduced burdens and increased donations, while big data tools helped combat corruption in public procurement.
narrative:
Tackling Tax Evasion and Maximising Revenue

Research at the University of Warwick led to major changes in UK tax enforcement. The work revealed which types of taxpayers are most likely to underpay and showed that tax audits have strong long-term effects—bringing in more than half their revenue impact in the years after the audit. Based on these findings, the UK government committed in 2020 to funding 1,300 new auditors at HMRC, projected to generate £3.9 billion in additional revenue over five years. The work also influenced HMRC policy discussions and featured in the Labour Party’s 2019 election platform. Internationally, tax authorities in countries including Norway, India, and South Africa have drawn on the findings to shape their audit strategies. Read more...

The modernisation of gambling taxation

Research at Nottingham Trent University transformed gambling taxation policy in the UK and internationally. Economic modelling demonstrated that taxing operator profits rather than turnover would boost both government revenue and industry viability. This directly informed HMRC’s shift to a Gross Profits Tax (GPT) system for betting and gambling machines, nearly doubling UK gambling tax revenues to £3 billion annually and generating £3.87 billion from Machine Games Duty alone (95.8% during the REF period). The approach has since been adopted in Australia and the United States, where it underpins new state-level gambling tax regimes. Read more...

Establishing A New Era for Not-for-Profit Financial Reporting

Research at Sheffield Hallam University led to major reforms in not-for-profit financial reporting in the UK and internationally. It directly informed the UK government’s decision to raise the charity audit threshold from £500K to £1M, enabling thousands of charities to use independent examination instead of audit—saving the sector an estimated £40 million between 2015 and 2020. The findings also drove structural reforms to the UK and Ireland Charities SORP development process, strengthening representation of smaller charities. Internationally, the work catalysed the creation of a global initiative to develop international financial reporting standards for NPOs, now led by an international consortium with anticipated implementation by 2024. Read more...

Direct payment of Housing Benefit and the development of Universal Credit

The Centre for Regional Economic and Social Research (CRESR) research team engaged with government ministers and other senior policy makers in the Department of Work and Pensions (DWP) to initiate three major changes: the introduction of a data sharing policy between DWP and social landlords,the implementation of additional safeguarding politics, and the development of a ‘Local Services Support Framework’. These policy changes benefitted Government policy makers, 1,855 registered local landlords, and 1,179,940 Universal Credit social renter households subject to Direct Payment and Universal Credit policies. Read more...

description: Case studies in this topic are examples of mechanical engineering and manufacturing developments. This topic is largely focussed on improving manufacturing processes in efficiency and/or sustainability, often integrating new technologies and materials to the pipeline. The topic also encompasses aspects of product design/testing, engineer training and materials considerations as relevant to the mechanical engineering and manufacturing of products and devices.
narrative:
Improved Software and Service Systems that Deliver Sales, Efficiency, and Access Opportunities in the European Manufacturing Industry

Developed software systems that enable collaboration among companies on complex manufacturing activities. Software modules and service systems that enabled manufacturing companies to collaborate more effectively in the supply chain for European aerospace created savings of EUR 10,000,000 per annum in operating costs, a 30% increase in speed of procurement and a 10% increase of throughput for a major European aerospace company. Read more...

Advancements in flexographic printing technology for graphic image printing and functional device fabrication

Research at Swansea University significantly advanced flexographic printing, leading to improved print quality, reduced waste, and increased productivity across the global packaging industry. Swansea’s work underpinned new metrology tools used in 1,500 installations by Troika Systems, saving an estimated £428 million in production costs and £90 million in waste annually. It also informed Asahi Photoproducts' CleanPrint plate technology, cutting run times by 30% and boosting global sales by 20%. Strategic research partnerships with UTECO supported €20 million in R&D investment. Swansea’s contributions were formalised in FTA Europe’s industry-endorsed best practice guide, now used internationally for training and process improvement. Read more...

Optimising the Performance of Safety Critical Industrial Valves

University of Huddersfield research revolutionised the design of safety-critical industrial valves by replacing trial-and-error methods with rigorous mathematical modelling. Partnering with Weir Valves through two Knowledge Transfer Partnerships, researchers developed new design tools that improved valve sizing accuracy by up to 250%, reduced costs through smaller, more efficient valves, and enabled additive manufacturing of complex components. These advances led to a 640% increase in sales, a £3M contract win, and enhanced competitiveness for the company. The research also influenced design practice across the industry, informing CPD training and adoption by major firms such as ExxonMobil and Equinor. Read more...

description: This topic encompasses engineering and technology advancements for aerospace and naval applications. It includes impactful work that leads to an improvement in aerospace and naval equipment/practices such as vessel components, manufacturing, dynamic modelling, or usage procedures across the aerospace and nautical sectors. Studies in this topic tend to consider safety, efficiency and economic viability as important metrics for the innovations showcased and be industrially and/or commercially relevant.
narrative:
Compressor Elliptical Leading Edge

Research at the University of Cambridge’s Whittle Laboratory led to a new elliptical compressor blade design that now features in all modern Rolls-Royce civil aero engines. First introduced on the Trent 1000 and now standard across newer and retrofitted engines, this design improves airflow, reducing fuel burn by 0.5–0.7%. Nearly 2,500 engines with the technology were delivered between 2014–2020, with ~2,000 more on order. In service with 45 airlines, the innovation is delivering estimated annual fuel savings of USD219 million and has strengthened Rolls-Royce’s competitiveness in the global aviation market. Read more...

Research into new maritime structures and systems exploited in novel designs by commercial and naval designers and builders.

UCL’s research into innovative maritime structures and systems has shaped global naval and commercial shipbuilding. Its trimaran designs led to 13 US Navy vessels and new high-speed ferries, while structural research informed safety engineering for offshore platforms at Hyundai Heavy Industries and Daewoo, cutting costs by up to USD5 million per vessel. UCL’s design tools and safety models have been embedded in industry-standard software used in over 23 countries, supporting efficient, reliable ship design. Its environmental modelling underpinned the IMO’s key GHG strategy and UK maritime climate policy, contributing to emissions reduction and improved marine energy efficiency. Read more...

Using advanced textiles to enhance UK-based technology and manufacturing capability in the US dominated space satellite telecommunication industry

Enhanced UK space technology capability by developing a pioneering, lower-cost, lightweight and deployable knitted metal mesh reflector for Oxford Space Systems' (OSS) new generation antennae. The Advanced Textile Research Group (ATRG) created this new technology for use in UK/EU space telecommunication satellites as an alternative to costly US-made warp-knitted metal fabrics. The micro-knitting technology utilised computerised flat-bed knitting with ultra-fine metal wires to create a seamless, 3D parabolic mesh reflector that can be unfurled in space. Read more...

Design and Optimisation of Laminar Flow Wing Technology for Next Generation Aircraft.

Research in applied mathematics at Imperial College led to the development of advanced computational tools that optimise wing design by accurately predicting the transition from laminar to turbulent airflow. These innovations directly supported Airbus’s efforts to reduce drag and fuel consumption through laminar flow wing technology. The tools were used in Airbus’s €200 million BLADE project and validated in flight tests, predicting laminar-turbulent transitions with high accuracy. The resulting improvements in aerodynamic modelling have saved design time and reduced the need for expensive physical tests. This work is now shaping the aerodynamic design of Airbus’s next-generation low-emission aircraft, contributing to industry goals of reducing CO₂ emissions by 5% per aircraft, or 3,000 tonnes annually. Read more...

topic_name_long: Economic Governance, Regional Development, Industrial Policy
description: This topic brings together research that has informed the governance of economic policy, regional development, and industrial strategy in the UK and internationally. Case studies include efforts to shape national frameworks for public investment through new modelling tools, appraisal methods, and the calculation of social discount rates. Others demonstrate how research has supported local and regional development—from guiding Growth Hubs and inward investment strategies to influencing policy on rural economies, subnational devolution, and spatial inequalities. Research has also played a central role in advancing place-based industrial strategies, smart specialisation, and mission-oriented innovation. At the global level, projects have influenced investment frameworks in developing countries, reshaped corporate environmental transition monitoring, and supported development oriented industrial and innovation policies. Taken together, the studies show how academic insights are shaping innovation and industrial investments and place-sensitive economic policymaking.
narrative:
Creating the Borderlands Initiative: political innovation driving economic development on the Anglo-Scottish Border

Research into the economic potential of the Anglo-Scottish border region led to the establishment of the Borderlands Initiative—a new cross-border political and institutional collaboration involving five local authorities. The research identified the benefits of sub-regional cooperation and the need for strategic frameworks to unlock growth in a geographically remote and historically underfunded area. This evidence informed the development of the Borderlands Inclusive Growth Deal, which secured over £394 million in joint UK and Scottish Government funding. Resulting investments include £65M for Carlisle Station, £31M for green energy projects, and £19M for a Biking Innovation Centre, alongside other initiatives in tourism, skills, and natural capital. The research directly shaped local and national policymaking, fostered new collaborative structures, and provided the economic rationale for a lasting programme of place-based regional development. Read more...

Supporting the Rural Economy: Forming Policy for Rural Business and Shaping the UK Industrial Strategy

Research by Newcastle University’s Centre for Rural Economy (CRE) has reshaped national policy on rural business and productivity, challenging assumptions about rural underperformance and revealing rural firms’ strong export and innovation capabilities. Their work directly influenced the UK Government’s £177M Rural Growth Strategy and informed the design and evaluation of Rural Growth Networks, which created or safeguarded over 2,200 jobs. Through a five-year initiative, Rural Enterprise UK, and its successor, the National Innovation Centre for Rural Enterprise (NICRE), the team helped embed rural considerations into the UK Industrial Strategy. Their evidence was instrumental in influencing parliamentary debates, shaping statistical reporting in official government releases, and advising high-level bodies including BEIS, Defra, and the Cabinet Office on levelling-up and post-COVID economic recovery. Read more...

Building state and societal capabilities to maximise the developmental effects of inward foreign direct investment (FDI).

Research by academics at Manchester Metropolitan University has significantly influenced global investment policy by demonstrating how host countries can better harness foreign direct investment (FDI) for development. Their work informed major reforms through the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), including tools adopted by over 150 countries and 400 policy roadmaps across 50 economies. Their findings shaped the 2018 UN World Investment Report and influenced Special Economic Zone policy across Africa. Domestically, the research contributed to UK parliamentary inquiry recommendations and improved guidance for unions and investors on partnership labour relations. Their stakeholder-driven approach to FDI policy has directly shaped investment strategies, industrial development, and labour frameworks globally. Read more...

Transforming global and national policies on innovation in Low Income Countries

Research on the Diffusion of Innovation in Low Income Countries (DILIC) established the importance of focusing on innovation in LICs and generated a new approach to innovation at the UN. This work influenced Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 9 and 17 and led to the creation of the UN Technology Facilitation Mechanism supported by the new UN Technology Bank. Read more...

topic_name_long: Operation Management, Supply Chains, Industrial Engineering
description: This topic brings together research that has advanced the efficiency, sustainability, and resilience of operations, supply chains, and industrial systems across a wide range of sectors. Many case studies focus on optimising complex supply chains—whether in infrastructure, logistics, construction, or manufacturing—by developing new tools, standards ), and statistical models to support more efficient production and better procurement and engineering processes. Research has also informed ‘green-lean’ and low-carbon operational strategies, enhancing productivity while improving environmental outcomes. Other projects address optimisation and scheduling challenges using advanced algorithms and software, often achieving large-scale savings for industry partners. Work in areas like demand forecasting, digitalisation, and predictive maintenance has improved operational reliability in sectors including gas distribution, aerospace, and process industries. Overall, the research supports smarter, more sustainable operations and supply chain systems both in the UK and globally.
narrative:
Process Systems Engineering

Research from Imperial College’s Centre for Process Systems Engineering underpinned the success of spin-out company Process Systems Enterprise Ltd (PSE), which became a global leader in process simulation and was acquired by Siemens AG in 2019 (valued at over £100M). The research enabled the development of PSE’s gPROMS™ platform, now central to Siemens’ digital process industry tools. Widely adopted across sectors including energy, chemicals, and pharmaceuticals, gPROMS supports digital twin technologies and advanced modelling for design, optimisation, and operations. Additional societal impact includes training over 200 universities through the PATH initiative, equipping engineers with next-generation digital skills. Read more...

Saving time and money through industrial scheduling and optimisation algorithms

University of Stirling research on combinatorial optimisation and metaheuristics delivered significant technological and economic benefits across three industries. At BT, advanced scheduling algorithms underpinning the “iRoster” system improved workforce logistics for 23,000 engineers, saving £1.3M by 2020. In Iceland, Stirling’s automated bug-fixing and predictive modelling tools helped Janus Rehabilitation Centre save £1.46M in software costs and contributed an estimated £4.2M in wider societal value. At KLM Royal Dutch Airlines, optimisation of scheduling software improved reliability for 200,000 flights and saved two years of developer time, driving lasting changes to software development practices across Air France-KLM. Read more...

Transforming the North Sea logistics supply chain

Robert Gordon University’s AI-driven optimisation research transformed freight logistics in the North Sea oil and gas sector, delivering major economic and environmental gains. Partnering with firms including ARR Craib and Nexen, the team developed algorithms that improved vehicle utilisation and vessel scheduling, leading to cost savings of £6M and £6.5M respectively. The research underpinned the creation of two spin-outs—Celerum and PlanSea—and informed a multi-operator initiative supported by the Oil & Gas Technology Centre, with projected industry-wide savings of £100M annually. The software also contributed to reduced emissions and enhanced operational resilience across complex supply chains. Read more...

description: Research in this topic improved the efficacy, accessibility and accountability of legal systems worldwide. Case studies informed reforms to legal aid, litigation processes, and judicial and legal training, improving access to justice for all, and particularly for vulnerable and underrepresented groups. Work addressed systemic barriers, enhanced witness protection, reduced wrongful convictions, and promoted diversity within the legal profession, contributing to more equitable and accountable legal outcomes.
narrative:
CLOCK, a transformative methodology for access to justice

Community Legal Outreach Collaboration Keele (CLOCK) co-designed the Community Legal Companion, helping to lessen the impact of a significant withdrawal of other forms of legal aid. Based on Dr. Krishnadas’ ‘transformative method’, it provides litigant-centred, community-based training to improve access to justice, including signposting and monitoring access. Since 2015, CLOCK has directly impacted 3,712 litigants-in-person and been adopted into the teaching of 12 law schools in England, operating in 9 court centres, with 70 partners. It has also informed the development of policy by providing invaluable data on legal access by vulnerable groups to the Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders (LASPO) review. During the COVID-19 pandemic, CLOCK supported 160 litigants in person to expose domestic violence in the lockdown as a social crisis. Internationally, it has assisted 1,200 disaster affected families through the All India Access to Justice Strategy. Read more...

Closing justice gaps: Improving the effectiveness of and confidence in Out of Court Disposals

In 2019, over 200,000 Out Of Court Disposals (OOCD) were issued in the UK, helping reduce court costs and re-offending. Barry Godfrey’s research has been pivotal in establishing Scrutiny Panels—first in Cheshire in 2013 and then nationally from 2016 -comprising magistrates, police officers, and himself to oversee OOCD use, enhancing confidence among sentencers, victims, and the public. Between 2013 and 2020, these panels reviewed more than 3,300 cases, focusing on youth, BAME, and child offenders or victims. Initially, panels disagreed with 20% of OOCD decisions; by 2020, this fell to 10%, reflecting improved police practices informed by feedback and training based on Godfrey’s research. Cheshire’s model influenced Merseyside and Greater Manchester Police to adopt similar panels. Godfrey also organises annual conferences at Cheshire Police HQ attended by senior officials, reinforcing trust in the OOCD system. His research on victims has been integrated into training videos for about 100 new Cheshire police recruits yearly, emphasizing victim-centred policing. In 2020, Godfrey helped oversee police use of Covid-19 OOCDs in Cheshire, reviewing 20 of 240 cases to ensure equitable enforcement. His work continues to strengthen justice outcomes, public confidence, and policing standards nationally. Read more...
